# PIANISTpy ver. 1.0.0: the manual as one text file

Every page of https://pianistpy.com/docs/ as markdown, in the manual's reading order (the order of the tabs and their menus). Each page opens with its title and its address; a line of three dashes separates the pages.


---

# What PIANISTpy does

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/overview

- [Density profiles.](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/profiles) Analytical double-power-law density profiles with a finite central
potential, including the Navarro-Frenk-White, Hernquist and Plummer profiles.

- [Velocity anisotropy.](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/anisotropy) Isotropic, constant-anisotropy, Osipkov-Merritt and
Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) models. The Osipkov-Merritt and COM models are radially (Type I) or tangentially
(Type II) biased.

- [Distribution functions.](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/df) Each anisotropy model’s distribution function, inverted from the
input density with exact symbolic expressions up to the final numerical integration, with extensively validated
numerical accuracy ([Accuracy tables](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/accuracy)) and checks that the distribution function is
non-negative (physical) and monotonic (a sufficient condition for dynamical stability).

- [Truncation in phase space.](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/truncation) Model truncation performed in phase space. The
truncation boundary is self-consistent and in dynamical equilibrium. Method I preserves the model’s anisotropy
profile, and Method II gives different anisotropy models an identical truncated density.

- [Particles.](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/particles) Particle initial conditions drawn from the truncated distribution
function, with a finite, dynamically stable truncation boundary. The particles are given in internal, model or
physical units.

- [Observables.](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/observables) Radial, tangential and line-of-sight velocity dispersions,
line-of-sight velocity distributions and their Gauss-Hermite moments, and the local velocity distribution at a 3D
radius. Projected quantities are averaged over centered or offset circular and rectangular apertures.

- [Superposition.](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/superposition#guide-superposition) Distribution functions of different anisotropy models on one
truncated density, linearly superposed into one equilibrium model. The superposed model’s anisotropy profile can
differ from every analytical family, for example an anisotropy profile fitted to simulated halos.

- [Inference.](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/superposition#guide-inference) End-to-end differentiable in JAX: the likelihood of a model against
kinematic data, with gradients in the superposition weights, the mass and length scales (*M*<sub>0</sub> and
*r*<sub>0</sub>) and, for Method II components, the anisotropy parameters, for gradient-based Monte Carlo inference.


---

# Install

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/install

```bash
pip install pianistpy
```

PIANISTpy needs Python 3.11 or later and runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.

To check an installation, run the package’s tests:

```bash
pip install "pianistpy[test]"
pytest --pyargs pianistpy
```

For a shorter check, `pytest --pyargs pianistpy -m "not slow"` skips the slowest tests, which carry the marker
`slow`.

## Dependencies

The dependencies are installed by pip with the package. The Standard column of the table gives the version of each
dependency that the release was tested with. The Minimum column gives the oldest version of each dependency, and the
minimum versions together pass the full test suite.

Package

Minimum (oldest that passes the suite)

3.11

2.4

7.2

mpmath

1.3

1.1.0

SymPy

1.14

1.2

JAX

0.9.2

0.6.0

Diffrax

0.7.2

0.7.1

Optimistix

0.1.0

0.1.0

By default, pip installs the newest version of each dependency that PIANISTpy allows. The newest allowed version can
differ from the Standard version, the version of the tested environment. To reproduce the tested environment, install
each dependency at its Standard version, for example `pip install "jax==0.9.2"`. In ver. 1.0.0, PIANISTpy requires a
JAX version below 0.10.2.

## CPU and GPU

PIANISTpy runs on the CPU with the default installation. With a CUDA build of JAX installed, PIANISTpy runs
every step that has a GPU implementation on the GPU, with no setting in PIANISTpy. The
[Representative computing time](https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/computing-time) page shows which steps run on the GPU. JAX’s CUDA builds are
for Linux only, so macOS runs the CPU-only mode. A native Windows Python also runs the CPU-only mode. On Windows,
PIANISTpy reaches the GPU through the Windows Subsystem for Linux or a Linux virtual machine. Results on the GPU and
on the CPU agree to better than \(10^{-10}\) in relative terms, and every accuracy check holds on the GPU and on
the CPU. To
choose the CPU or the GPU explicitly, see [Runtime options](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/runtime).


---

# Quick start

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/quickstart

The example below builds an NFW halo of concentration 10 with a constant velocity anisotropy of 0.25. Method I
([Truncation in phase space](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/truncation)) truncates the halo in phase space so that the truncated mass
equals the virial mass of the untruncated halo. The model is then given in physical units, with a virial mass of
\(10^{12}\,M_\odot\), about the mass of the Milky Way, and a scale radius of 20 kpc.

```python
import pianistpy as pp
import astropy.units as u

# an untruncated NFW density profile with a constant velocity anisotropy of 0.25
halo = pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.nfw(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25))

# the untruncated distribution function
df = pp.compute_df(halo)

# Method I: truncate the distribution function so that the truncated mass equals the virial mass of the
# untruncated NFW halo of concentration 10 (the mass inside 10 scale radii)
model = pp.truncate(df, pp.Truncation(mass_t=1.0, concentration=10))

# physical units: a halo of 1e12 solar masses with R_vir = c * r_0 = 200 kpc
model = model.to("physical", mass_0=1e12 * u.Msun, r_0=20 * u.kpc)

# draw ten million equal-mass particles centered at the origin and write them to a file
particles = pp.Sampler(model).sample(10_000_000, seed=1)
particles.write("NFW_Const0p25_Mt1e12_PARIC.h5")

# the line-of-sight velocity dispersion at three projected radii
sigma = pp.sigma_los(model, [2, 20, 100] * u.kpc)
```

`pp.solve(halo, pp.Truncation(mass_t=1.0, concentration=10))` runs `compute_df` and `truncate` in one call.

The [Examples](https://pianistpy.com/docs/notebooks/index) page shows self-contained Jupyter tutorial notebooks, and the notebooks
that reproduce the result figures of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758).


---

# Representative computing time

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/computing-time

The tables below give the computing time of each step of one PIANISTpy workflow, from a density profile to the
observables. The example truncates an isotropic NFW halo by Method I. Method II then builds a model with a constant velocity
anisotropy of 0.2 on the truncated density of that Method I model ([Truncation in phase space](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/truncation)). Each time in the tables is the time of a repeated
call. The first call of a session takes longer due to JAX compilation, as does the first aperture call on a
table (14.7 s on spock’s CPU). The times were measured with the default settings on two machines. The first machine
is the [spock GPU cluster](https://github.com/calab-ntu/gpu-cluster/wiki/System-Overview#spock) of
[NTU CALab](https://calab-ntu.github.io/) (PI: [Hsi-Yu Schive](https://www.phys.ntu.edu.tw/enphysics/hyschive.html)),
with an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5975WX CPU (32 cores, Linux) and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Ti GPU. The second
machine is a laptop with an Intel Core Ultra 9 185H CPU (16 cores, Windows 11). The steps that run in parallel
processes used 28 processes on spock and 12 processes on the laptop, set by `set_cores()`.

† A `LosTable` is built once per model, and every later call given the same `LosTable` reads it without a
rebuild. Every observable in the table “Observables from the line-of-sight table” reads a `LosTable`. `losvd` and `aperture_losvd` called on a
model build a `LosTable` first. Each row of a `LosTable` is the line-of-sight velocity distribution at one
projected radius. The integral of each row agrees with the surface density, and the second moment of each row agrees
with the projected dispersion, each to a relative error of at most \(10^{-6}\). For a distribution read between
two rows, the estimated error is at most \(10^{-8}\) relative in the second moment, and at most
\(10^{-7}\) of the row’s largest value at each velocity. A GPU-accelerated build, and builds of
only the part of a `LosTable` that a call needs, are listed on the
[Upcoming features](https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/upcoming-features) page.

# Models

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/models

A model (`Model`) is an equilibrium of one or more components, untruncated or truncated in phase
space. Each component is a density profile with a velocity anisotropy, and the model holds the distribution
function of each component. A model is built in the four main steps below.

- [Density profiles (DoublePowerLaw)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/profiles)

- [Velocity anisotropy (Anisotropy, Component)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/anisotropy)

- [Distribution functions (compute_df)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/df)

- [Truncation in phase space (truncate, solve)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/truncation)


---

# Density profiles

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/profiles

`pianistpy.DoublePowerLaw`

`DoublePowerLaw(rho_alpha, rho_beta, rho_gamma)` is the analytical double-power-law density profile
\(\varrho(R) = C\,R^{-\gamma}\,(1 + R^{\alpha})^{(\gamma-\beta)/\alpha}\), with \(R\) the radius in units of
the scale radius and \(C\) a normalization constant. The class takes three arguments:

- `rho_alpha`, the sharpness \(\alpha\) of the transition between the inner and the outer slope, at least
1/2;

- `rho_beta`, the outer slope \(\beta\), greater than 2 for the profile and at least 3 for a component;

- `rho_gamma`, the inner slope \(\gamma\), with \(0 \leq \gamma < 2\), so that the central potential is
finite.

In internal units ([Units](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/units)), the scale radius and the central potential of a `DoublePowerLaw`
profile are 1. The NFW, Hernquist and Plummer profiles are parameter sets of `DoublePowerLaw`, not classes of
their own:

```python
pp.DoublePowerLaw.nfw()        # Navarro-Frenk-White
pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist()
pp.DoublePowerLaw.plummer()
pp.DoublePowerLaw(1.0, 3.0, 1.0)   # the NFW profile, given by (rho_alpha, rho_beta, rho_gamma)
```

The methods `rho(r)`, `mass(r)` and `p(r)` of a `DoublePowerLaw` profile return the density, the enclosed mass
and the relative potential in closed form.

A component (`pianistpy.Component`) of a model is a density profile together with a velocity anisotropy
([Velocity anisotropy](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/anisotropy)). The density profile of a component needs an outer slope
\(\beta \geq 3\). In ver. 1.0.0, a component whose profile has \(2 < \beta < 3\) raises
`InputError`, with a message that begins `OUTER SLOPE`.


---

# Velocity anisotropy

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/anisotropy

`pianistpy.Anisotropy`, `pianistpy.Component`

One class, `Anisotropy(beta_c, r_a, kind)`, covers every analytical anisotropy model of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758):

- the default, `Anisotropy()`, is isotropic;

- a nonzero central anisotropy `beta_c` alone, with \(\beta_{\rm c} < 1\), gives constant anisotropy;

- a finite anisotropy radius `r_a` gives the Osipkov-Merritt model (with `beta_c = 0`) or the
Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) model (with a nonzero `beta_c`). `kind="I"` (the default) is radially biased,
`kind="II"` tangentially biased.

The anisotropy model is chosen by exact comparison of the parameters. `beta_c=0.0` gives the isotropic model, and
`beta_c=1e-12` gives a constant-anisotropy model. The attribute `Anisotropy.model` gives the anisotropy model:
`"isotropic"`, `"constant"`, `"om"` or `"com"`. Results are continuous across \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0\) and
across an infinite \(R_{\rm a}\). A model with \(\beta_{\rm c} = 10^{-12}\) agrees with the isotropic model
within the accuracy of the settings ([Accuracy](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/accuracy)).

```python
pp.Anisotropy()                           # isotropic
pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)                # constant anisotropy
pp.Anisotropy(r_a=10.0, kind="I")         # Osipkov-Merritt, radially biased
pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=-0.25, r_a=10.0)     # COM, Type I by default
```

`Component(profile, anisotropy)` joins a density profile and an anisotropy. A `Component` is the input of
`compute_df()` and `solve()`. In ver. 1.0.0, `compute_df` and `solve` take one
component. Several components in one potential are among the [Upcoming features](https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/upcoming-features).


---

# Distribution functions

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/df

`pianistpy.compute_df()`, `pianistpy.DistributionFunction`

`compute_df(component)` returns the untruncated distribution function of a component as a
`DistributionFunction`. `compute_df` computes the distribution function by the analytic inversion
of the density. `compute_df` returns the distribution function even where the distribution function is negative or
not monotonic, and the result states the energies at which the distribution function is negative or not monotonic.
The attribute `k_t_min` is the lowest truncation energy that `truncate` accepts. `k_t_min` is zero when the
distribution function is non-negative and non-decreasing everywhere and the model is not a Type II model. One result serves every Method I truncation of the
same component, so a scan over
truncation energies needs one `compute_df` call.

```python
halo = pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.nfw(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25))
df = pp.compute_df(halo)
```

`DistributionFunction.from_function(component, f)` validates a distribution function from elsewhere, such as a
fitting function or the output of another code, with the checks of `compute_df`:

- `f(k, depth)` takes an array of energies \(\mathcal{K}\) in internal units and the array of their depths
below the center, \(P_0 - \mathcal{K}\). It returns the distribution function \(F\) at each energy, not
its logarithm. The depth carries no rounding error at every energy \(\mathcal{K} \ge 1/2\), so a fit written in
the depth near the center can use `depth`. A function of the energy alone may ignore `depth`.

- The function is tabulated on the energy grid that `compute_df` uses for the same component and settings. The
table is then continued beyond its ends, checked for sign and validated against the density, as for
`compute_df`.

- The function gives \(F\) only, so the validation report marks its check of the table’s logarithmic slope,
`slope_column`, as `"not judged"`.

- A file written from the result stores the table and the function’s name, not the function.

- A value that is not finite raises `InputError`, which states the first such energy.

- `truncate` raises `InputError` for a distribution function from `from_function`, because a
truncation needs values of the inversion that a distribution function from `from_function` does not carry.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.special import beta

# the isotropic Plummer model's DF in closed form, F = A K^(7/2)
plummer = pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.plummer(), pp.Anisotropy())
amplitude = 3.0 / (4.0 * np.pi * np.sqrt(2.0) * beta(4.5, 1.5))
df = pp.DistributionFunction.from_function(plummer, lambda k, depth: amplitude * k**3.5)
```

A `DistributionFunction` holds:

- the distribution function tabulated on its energy grid, with its logarithmic slope;

- the asymptotic forms of the distribution function at the center and at the outer end, which continue the
distribution function beyond the table;

- where it is negative or not monotonic, and `k_t_min`;

- the inputs and the settings it was computed from;

- its validation report and its identity string, a digest of the inputs, the settings and the package version.

A result can be written to a file and read back equal ([Input and output](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/input-output)). Only a `Model` can be
sampled or projected, and `truncate` builds the model from a distribution function
([Truncation in phase space](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/truncation)).


---

# Truncation in phase space

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/truncation

`pianistpy.Truncation`, `pianistpy.truncate()`, `pianistpy.solve()`, `pianistpy.Model`

## Method I

`truncate(df, truncation)` returns a `Model`, which holds the distribution function truncated at an
energy and the self-consistent potential-density pair of the truncated distribution function. If the untruncated
distribution function is everywhere non-negative and monotonic, the truncated distribution function inherits both
properties, and the truncation boundary is in dynamical equilibrium. A request with no physical model raises
`UnphysicalModelError`, which carries the distribution function, or the model without an edge, for
inspection.

At \(\beta_{\rm c} = -1/2\) and a steep inner density slope \(\gamma\), the iteration for the center of the
truncated model does not converge, and `truncate` raises `AccuracyError`. For example, with
\((\alpha, \beta) = (2, 4)\), \(\beta_{\rm c} = -1/2\) and \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t} = 0.3\), `truncate`
raises `AccuracyError` from \(\gamma = 1.735\) upward.

`Truncation` takes exactly one of three inputs:

```python
pp.Truncation(k_t=0.2)                          # the truncation energy, in internal units
pp.Truncation(mass_t=1.0, concentration=10.0)   # a target mass, in units of M_0 (model units)
pp.Truncation(r_t=5.0)                          # a target radius, in units of the scale radius
```

A target mass is given in units of \(M_0\), so it needs the concentration that defines \(M_0\). A target
radius or a truncation energy needs no concentration, and a concentration given with `r_t` or `k_t` raises
`InputError`.

`solve(component, truncation)` runs `compute_df` and `truncate` in one call. Without a `Truncation`,
`truncate` and `solve` return the untruncated model, or, for a Method II component, the model that ends at the
edge of the truncated density that the component uses.

A model holds:

- the truncated distribution function;

- the truncated density, potential and enclosed mass on one radial grid (`model.profile.r`, `.rho_trunc`,
`.p_trunc`, `.mass_trunc`);

- the truncation radius and the total mass;

- the validation report and the identity string, a digest of the inputs, the settings and the package version.

An untruncated model is not spatially finite. The untruncated model’s `spatially_finite` is false, and the
untruncated model’s truncation radius `r_t` is infinite. A function that needs a spatially finite model, such as
`Sampler` without `r_sample`, raises `InputError` for a model that is not spatially finite
([Flags and refusals](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/flags-refusals)).

### Type II models

A Type II model (Osipkov-Merritt or Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt) must end inside its anisotropy radius
\(R_{\rm a}\), where the model’s density \(\varrho_{\rm aux} / (1 - R^2/R_{\rm a}^2)\), with
\(\varrho_{\rm aux}\) the auxiliary density, has a pole.

- The truncation energy must satisfy \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t} > P(R_{\rm a})\). Where this bound sets `k_t_min`,
`k_t_min` is the next floating-point number above \(P(R_{\rm a})\).

- The bound is necessary, not sufficient. The bound keeps inside \(R_{\rm a}\) the radius at which the
untruncated potential equals \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\), but the truncated model’s own edge lies farther out than
that radius. Where the truncated model’s edge would reach \(R_{\rm a}\), `truncate` raises
`UnphysicalModelError` with a message that begins `TYPE II EDGE` and states the potential at
\(R_{\rm a}\) or the radius of the edge. A larger \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\) moves the truncated model’s edge
inside \(R_{\rm a}\).

### Osipkov-Merritt Type I models with a small anisotropy radius

An Osipkov-Merritt Type I model with a small \(R_{\rm a}\) and a low \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\) can have no edge
inside the largest radius at which `truncate` solves for the potential. `truncate` then raises
`UnphysicalModelError` with a message that begins `NO EDGE`. On the Hernquist density with the
quick settings, `truncate` raises `UnphysicalModelError` (`NO EDGE`) for the following
Osipkov-Merritt Type I models:

- \(R_{\rm a} = 1\) at every \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\) from 0.005 to 0.3;

- \(R_{\rm a} = 2\) below \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t} = 0.2\);

- \(R_{\rm a} = 5\) below \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t} = 0.03\);

- \(R_{\rm a} = 10\) at \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t} = 0.005\).

The Osipkov-Merritt Type I models on the Hernquist density with \(R_{\rm a}\) from 1 to 10 and
\(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\) from 0.005 to 0.3 that `truncate` builds have the tier `"recorded"`, above
\(10^{-6}\) and at most \(10^{-4}\) ([Accuracy](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/accuracy)). The check `high_k_slope_mismatch` of the distribution
function of each built model is \(3.4 \times 10^{-6}\), at \(\mathcal{K} = 1\).

## Method II

Method II gives a new anisotropy to a density that is already truncated. The new component takes the truncated
profile of a Method I model as its profile. `solve`, or `compute_df` and `truncate`, without a
`Truncation`, build the Method II model from the new component.

```python
truncated = pp.solve(pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.nfw(), pp.Anisotropy()), pp.Truncation(k_t=0.2))
model = pp.solve(pp.Component(truncated.profile, pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=-0.25)))
```

A Method II model exists only when its anisotropy is compatible with the edge of the Method I model’s truncated
density. Where that density goes as \(\hat{P}^q\) at the edge, with \(\hat{P}\) the Method I model’s truncated
relative potential, which is zero at the edge, the central anisotropy of the new component must satisfy
\(\beta_{\rm c} > 1/2 - q\). A `Component` whose \(\beta_{\rm c}\) is not above \(1/2 - q\) raises
`UnphysicalModelError` when the `Component` is created, and the error message states the bound.
The [Technical notes](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/notes) derive the condition \(\beta_{\rm c} > 1/2 - q\).


---

# Particles

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/particles

`pianistpy.Sampler`, [`pianistpy.particles.Particles`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/particles#pianistpy.particles.Particles)

`Sampler(model)` builds the sampling tables of a model once. `sampler.sample(n, seed)` then returns `n`
equal-mass particles in memory, as a `Particles` object that holds positions, velocities, masses and component
labels in the model’s unit system. The draw is reproducible particle by particle. Each particle depends only on the
seed, the particle’s component and the particle’s index, not on the hardware or on `n`. One call of `sample`
returns at most \(2^{31} - 1\) particles. A larger number of particles is drawn in several calls with distinct
seeds.

```python
sampler = pp.Sampler(model)
particles = sampler.sample(10_000_000, seed=1)
particles.write("halo.h5")                     # the native HDF5 layout
particles.write("halo_gamer.bin", layout="gamer")
particles.write("halo_gadget.hdf5", layout="gadget")
particles.write("halo.txt", layout="text")
```

The layouts are:

- `"native"` (the default): the package’s own HDF5 file, read back by `pianistpy.read()`;

- `"gamer"`: the particle file of [GAMER](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/sty2586);

- `"gadget"`: an HDF5 initial condition in the Gadget snapshot format 3;

- `"text"`: fixed-width text, with the units in its header.

Every writer reads the file back before returning, and raises `ResultError` if the file differs
from the particles written. A layout for another simulation code is added by one function decorated with
`pianistpy.particles.register_particle_writer`.

A model that is not spatially finite needs an explicit sampling radius, `Sampler(model, r_sample=...)`, in
internal units. The particles then carry the mass inside that radius (`Sampler.radius_table.mass_sample`, in
internal units).

## Particles in a range of radii

`Sampler(model, r_range=(r_lo, r_hi))` draws every particle between two radii, in internal units, with
\(0 \le r_{\rm lo} < r_{\rm hi}\) and \(r_{\rm hi}\) at most the outer radius of the sampling. Each
particle’s radius is drawn from the model’s enclosed mass restricted to the range, not selected from a full draw.
Every particle lies between \(r_{\rm lo}\) and \(r_{\rm hi}\), and the particles together carry the model’s
mass between \(r_{\rm lo}\) and \(r_{\rm hi}\). For a superposition, each component’s share of the particles
between \(r_{\rm lo}\) and \(r_{\rm hi}\) is the component’s weight, because the components share one
density.

## Constrained velocity draws

`Sampler.velocities(r, seed, v_range=(v_lo, v_hi))` draws one velocity at each given radius, in internal units, from the
model’s velocity distribution at that radius conditioned on the range. `Sampler.velocities` returns the velocities and, at
each radius, the fraction of the distribution inside the range. Where the range holds none of the distribution, the velocity is NaN.

- `v_lo` and `v_hi` are floats, for one range at every radius, or arrays that broadcast against `r`, for a
range at each radius. For example, a range from 0.5 to 0.6 times the escape velocity at each radius is one call,
with `v_lo` and `v_hi` given as arrays over `r`. A grid of such ranges in units of the escape velocity takes
one call per range.

- Every velocity lies in the range. A range from 0 to at least the escape velocity at every radius gives the velocities that
`sample` draws from the same random numbers at the same seed.

- For a superposition, the component of each velocity is drawn with a probability proportional to the component’s
weight times the component’s fraction of velocities in the range.

- `Sampler.velocities` takes isotropic and constant-anisotropy models only. A model with a finite anisotropy radius
raises `InputError`, because with a finite anisotropy radius the velocity depends on the drawn
velocity angle.

## Sampling accuracy near the smallest anisotropy radius

A model whose distribution function is non-negative cannot always be sampled to \(10^{-6}\). The velocity table
of a `Sampler` is refined until the table’s error is below the setting `sampling["row_error_goal"]`
(\(10^{-6}\) with the default settings, \(10^{-4}\) with the quick settings) or until the table holds
`sampling["n_rows_max"]` potential values. The validation report `Sampler.validation` records the velocity table’s
error, and a velocity-table error above \(10^{-2}\) raises `AccuracyError` ([Accuracy](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/accuracy)).

Let \(R_{\rm a,min}\) be the smallest anisotropy radius at which an Osipkov-Merritt (OM) or
Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) Type I distribution function is non-negative. Close to \(R_{\rm a,min}\), the
velocity table reaches `sampling["n_rows_max"]` potential values before the table’s error falls below
`sampling["row_error_goal"]`, and the error grows steeply as \(R_{\rm a}\) falls toward
\(R_{\rm a,min}\). For a truncated NFW density of concentration 10 (truncation radius 31.9 scale radii) with the
default settings, the velocity table’s error crosses \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-2}\) at the following ratios
\(R_{\rm a}/R_{\rm a,min}\):

model

\(\beta_{\rm c}\)

\(10^{-4}\) at \(R_{\rm a}/R_{\rm a,min}\)

\(10^{-2}\) at \(R_{\rm a}/R_{\rm a,min}\)

COM I

-0.75

1.62

1.16

COM I

-0.50

1.84

1.20

COM I

-0.25

1.38

1.10

OM I

0

1.27

1.07

COM I

+0.05

1.24

1.07

COM I

+0.25

1.14

1.04

COM I

+0.40

1.09

1.02

COM I

+0.45

above 1.23

1.02

Above the ratio for \(10^{-4}\), the velocity table’s error is below \(10^{-4}\). Between the ratio for
\(10^{-4}\) and the ratio for \(10^{-2}\), `Sampler` issues an `AccuracyWarning`. Below
the ratio for \(10^{-2}\), `Sampler` raises `AccuracyError`. At \(\beta_{\rm c} = 1/2\)
the distribution function is non-negative at every \(R_{\rm a}\), but the velocity table’s error is above
\(10^{-2}\) at every \(R_{\rm a}\) up to 0.32 scale radii. The velocity table of a constant-anisotropy model has an error below
\(10^{-4}\) up to \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0.4\) \((6 \times 10^{-5})\) and above \(10^{-4}\) at
\(\beta_{\rm c} = 0.45\) \((4 \times 10^{-4})\). The package sets no limit on \(R_{\rm a}\) or
\(\beta_{\rm c}\) for sampling. The tier of each `Sampler`’s validation report sets whether the `Sampler`
issues an `AccuracyWarning` or raises `AccuracyError`.


---

# Observables

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/observables

`pianistpy.sigma_los()`, `pianistpy.sigma_los_aperture()`, `pianistpy.aperture_losvd()`,
`pianistpy.Aperture`, `pianistpy.LosTable`

Observables are functions of a model. Given a model, `losvd` and `aperture_losvd` build the model’s
line-of-sight table (`LosTable`) at every call. For repeated requests on one model, build
`LosTable(model)` once. A `LosTable` tabulates the line-of-sight velocity distributions of the model, and every
observable accepts the `LosTable` in place of the model.

```python
sigma = pp.sigma_los(model, [0.1, 1.0, 10.0])        # at projected radii

circle = pp.Aperture.circle(r_ape=1.0, r_off=0.0)
slit = pp.Aperture.rectangle(side_x=2.0, side_y=0.2, r_off=0.0, angle=0.0)
pp.sigma_los_aperture(model, circle)                 # averaged over an aperture
pp.sigma_los_aperture(model, slit)

table = pp.LosTable(model)                           # once, for many requests
pp.sigma_los(table, [0.1, 1.0, 10.0])
pp.sigma_los_aperture(table, circle)
pp.aperture_losvd(table, circle, [0.0, 0.1, 0.2])    # the distribution in the aperture
```

[](https://pianistpy.com/docs/_images/projection_configurations.png)

The projection configurations of a spherical system truncated at \(R_{\rm t}\) (dashed circle), from
[Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Fig. 14. (a) The projected radial profile along the line of sight, as for a slit of negligible width.
(b) The average over a rectangular aperture of sides \(x\) and \(y\) (`side_x`, `side_y`), whose
center lies at the projected distance `r_off` from the center of the system, on a line at the angle
\(\theta\) (`angle`) to the rectangle’s \(x\) side, as for a slit of finite width. (c) The average
over a circular aperture, centered or offset, as for fiber-fed observations.

An `Aperture` is a circle or a rectangle, centered or offset. A rectangle also takes an `angle`, in radians,
between the rectangle’s x axis and the line through the center of the model and the center of the rectangle.
`sigma_los_aperture` and `aperture_losvd` take the same `Aperture` object. `sigma_r`, `sigma_t`, `losvd`
and `pdf_v` also take a model or the model’s line-of-sight table as the first argument. The
[Observables](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/observables) page of the API reference lists every call. The Gauss-Hermite
moments \(h_3\) and \(h_4\) of the line-of-sight velocity distribution have no top-level call. The inference
takes \(h_3\) and \(h_4\) as data ([`pianistpy.inference.Data`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/inference#pianistpy.inference.Data)).

`ProjectedSampler` draws pairs of projected radius and line-of-sight velocity on an annulus and, if given, in a
user-specified range of line-of-sight velocity. For every anisotropy model, the draw is conditioned exactly on the
velocity range. At each projected radius, the distribution of the projected radius is weighted by the share of the
line-of-sight velocity distribution inside the velocity range. The ranges and the drawn pairs are in the unit system
of the model or the line-of-sight table given to `ProjectedSampler`, as for the other observables. The attribute
`validation` of a `ProjectedSampler` is the validation report of the draw.

```python
sampler = pp.ProjectedSampler(table, R_range=(0.1, 3.0), v_range=(-0.2, 0.3))
pairs = sampler.sample(1_000_000, seed=1)   # pairs.r_2d, pairs.v_los, pairs.mass
```

Observables over an aperture of any other shape can be estimated by Monte Carlo. Draw pairs with
`ProjectedSampler` on an annulus that encloses the aperture, give each pair a uniformly random position angle
(the model is spherical), and keep the pairs inside the aperture. Sums over the kept pairs, each with its mass
(`pairs.mass`), give the aperture’s mass, dispersion and velocity distribution, with a statistical error that
falls as the inverse square root of the number of pairs.

- [Radial velocity dispersion (sigma_r)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_r)

- [Tangential velocity dispersion (sigma_t)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_t)

- [Line-of-sight velocity distribution (losvd)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/losvd)

- [Line-of-sight velocity distribution in an aperture (aperture_losvd)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/aperture_losvd)

- [Local velocity distribution (pdf_v)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/pdf_v)

- [Line-of-sight table (LosTable)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/lostable)

- [End-to-end differentiability](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiability)

- [Differentiable observables (Differentiable)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiable)


---

# Radial velocity dispersion

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_r

`pianistpy.sigma_r()`, `pianistpy.LosTable`

`sigma_r(source, r)` returns the intrinsic radial velocity dispersion \(\sigma_{\rm r}\) at user-specified 3D radii.
\(\sigma_{\rm r}^2\) is the second moment of the radial velocity over the model’s distribution function at a
fixed radius. As in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), \(\sigma_{\rm r}^2\) is the velocity moment of the augmented density
\(\varrho_{\rm aug}\), integrated over the energy \(\mathcal{K}\) up to the relative potential
\(P = P(R)\) at the radius \(R\),

\[\sigma_{\rm r}^2(R) = \frac{1}{\varrho_{\rm aug}(P, R)} \int_0^{P} \varrho_{\rm aug}(\mathcal{K}, R)\,
{\rm d}\mathcal{K}, \qquad P = P(R).\]

For the anisotropy models of the package, the augmented density separates as
\(\varrho_{\rm aug}(P, R) = \varrho_{\rm aux}(P)\,g(R)\), with \(\varrho_{\rm aux}\) the auxiliary density
and \(g\) the anisotropy factor (`Anisotropy.factor`). \(\sigma_{\rm r}^2\) is then the Jeans integral of
\(\varrho_{\rm aux}\) over the potential. The radius \(R\) of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758) is `r` in the package.

## Arguments and units

- `source` is a `Model` (one component, or a superposition) or the model’s
line-of-sight table (`LosTable`), which holds the same intrinsic profile.

- `r` is an array of 3D radii in the model’s unit system. In the internal and the model systems, the unit of `r`
is the scale radius. After `model.to("physical", ...)`, `r` is in parsecs, or an Astropy quantity of any
length unit.

- The result has the shape of `r`, in the model’s velocity unit (km/s in the physical system).

The members of a superposition, Method II models on one truncated density, share that density, so the members’ second moments
add with the weights:
\(\sigma_{\rm r}^2 = \sum_k w_k \sigma_{{\rm r},k}^2\).

## Accuracy

The profile is tabulated in radius once per model. Radii are added to the profile until \(\sigma_{\rm r}\) at
the midpoint of every interval between the profile’s radii is within a relative `profile_tolerance`:
\(10^{-7}\) with the default settings and \(10^{-6}\) with `Settings(quick=True)`. The default value of
`profile_tolerance`, \(10^{-7}\), is a tenth of \(10^{-6}\), so the profile adds little to the error of the
projected quantities computed from the profile. As for every observable, a model whose relative error is above
\(10^{-2}\) raises `AccuracyError`, unless the model’s settings set `write_anyway=True`
([Accuracy](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/accuracy)).

## Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

# a Hernquist density with a constant anisotropy of 0.25, truncated at K_t = 0.05
model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
r = np.array([0.1, 1.0, 10.0])
pp.sigma_r(model, r)                          # internal units

physical = model.to("physical", concentration=10.0, mass_0=1e9, r_0=500.0)
pp.sigma_r(physical, [50.0, 500.0, 5000.0])   # parsecs in, km/s out
```


---

# Tangential velocity dispersion

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_t

`pianistpy.sigma_t()`, `pianistpy.LosTable`

`sigma_t(source, r)` returns the intrinsic tangential velocity dispersion \(\sigma_{\rm t}\) at user-specified 3D radii.
\(\sigma_{\rm t}^2\) is the sum of the squared dispersions of the two tangential velocity components,
\(\sigma_{\rm t}^2 = \sigma_\theta^2 + \sigma_\phi^2\), with \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) the polar and the
azimuthal directions. As in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), \(\sigma_{\rm t}^2\) is the tangential velocity moment of the augmented
density,

\[\sigma_{\rm t}^2(R) = \frac{2}{\varrho_{\rm aug}(P, R)} \int_0^{P}
\frac{\partial}{\partial R^2}\Big[R^2 \varrho_{\rm aug}(\mathcal{K}, R)\Big]\,{\rm d}\mathcal{K},
\qquad P = P(R).\]

The velocity anisotropy is \(\beta_\sigma = 1 - \sigma_{\rm t}^2 / (2\sigma_{\rm r}^2)\). \(\beta_\sigma\)
is zero for an isotropic model, \(\beta_{\rm c}\) for a constant-anisotropy model, and
\(R^2 / (R^2 + R_{\rm a}^2)\) for an Osipkov-Merritt Type I model. The package evaluates \(\sigma_{\rm t}^2 = 2(1 - \beta_\sigma)\sigma_{\rm r}^2\),
with \(\sigma_{\rm r}\) from [Radial velocity dispersion](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_r) and \(\beta_\sigma\) in closed form from the model’s anisotropy.

## Arguments and units

As for [Radial velocity dispersion](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_r), `source` is a `Model` or the model’s line-of-sight table
(`LosTable`), `r` is in the model’s unit system, and the result has the shape of `r`, in the
model’s velocity unit. For a superposition,
\(\sigma_{\rm t}^2 = \sum_k w_k \sigma_{{\rm t},k}^2\).

## Accuracy

`sigma_t` has the accuracy of `sigma_r` ([Radial velocity dispersion](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_r)), because `sigma_t` reads the radial dispersion
profile of `sigma_r`. The factor \(2(1 - \beta_\sigma)\) is computed in closed form from the model’s
anisotropy.

## Example

The anisotropy computed from the two dispersions is the model’s own, here the constant
\(\beta_{\rm c} = 0.25\).

```python
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
r = np.array([0.1, 1.0, 10.0])
beta = 1.0 - pp.sigma_t(model, r) ** 2 / (2.0 * pp.sigma_r(model, r) ** 2)
np.max(np.abs(beta - 0.25))   # of the order of the floating-point rounding error
```


---

# Line-of-sight velocity distribution

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/losvd

`pianistpy.losvd()`, `pianistpy.LosTable`

`losvd(source, r_2d, v)` returns the line-of-sight velocity distribution \(D(R_{\rm 2D}, V_{\rm los})\) at
user-specified projected radii. \(D\) is the probability density of the line-of-sight velocity of the model’s
mass seen at a projected distance \(R_{\rm 2D}\) from the center. As in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), \(D\) is the distribution
function \(F(\mathcal{Z}, L)\), with \(L\) the angular momentum, integrated over the line of sight up to the
truncation radius \(R_{\rm t}\) and over the two plane-of-sky velocity components \(V_{\perp 1}\) and
\(V_{\perp 2}\), and divided by the surface density \(\Sigma\),

\[D(R_{\rm 2D}, V_{\rm los}) = \frac{2}{\Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})} \int_{R_{\rm 2D}}^{R_{\rm t}}
\frac{R\,{\rm d}R}{(R^2 - R_{\rm 2D}^2)^{1/2}} \iint F(\mathcal{Z}, L)\,{\rm d}V_{\perp 1}\,{\rm d}V_{\perp 2},
\qquad
\Sigma(R_{\rm 2D}) = 2 \int_{R_{\rm 2D}}^{R_{\rm t}} \frac{\varrho(R)\,R\,{\rm d}R}{(R^2 - R_{\rm 2D}^2)^{1/2}},\]

where the inner integral runs over the plane-of-sky velocities at which the truncated distribution function is
positive. The distribution is even in \(V_{\rm los}\) and integrates to one over all
\(V_{\rm los}\). The distribution is zero at every \(|V_{\rm los}|\) above the largest velocity that the
distribution function reaches on the line of sight. The second moment of \(D\) is \(\sigma_{\rm los}^2\)
(`pianistpy.sigma_los()`).

## Arguments and units

- `source` is a `Model` or the model’s line-of-sight table (`LosTable`).
Given a model, `losvd` builds the model’s `LosTable` at every call. For more than one call, build the
`LosTable` once ([Line-of-sight table](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/lostable)). In a script, a `LosTable` and a call of `losvd` on a model run under
`if __name__ == "__main__":`, as [Line-of-sight table](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/lostable) explains.

- `r_2d` and `v` are arrays that broadcast against each other. `r_2d` holds projected radii in the model’s
unit of length: internal units by default, parsecs or an Astropy quantity in the physical system. `v` holds
line-of-sight velocities in the model’s unit of velocity (km/s in the physical system).

- The result has the broadcast shape of `r_2d` and `v` and is a probability density per unit velocity of the
model’s unit system.

For a superposition, each component’s distribution is read from the component’s own table. The components are
summed with their weights times their surface densities, \(D = \sum_k w_k \Sigma_k D_k / \sum_k w_k \Sigma_k\).

## Accuracy

The accuracy of `losvd` is the accuracy of the `LosTable` ([Line-of-sight table](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/lostable)). The `LosTable` checks the norm
of the distribution at each tabulated projected radius (a row of the table) against the surface density, and the
second moment of each row against the projected dispersion. The `LosTable` also estimates the error of the distribution between rows. A
projected radius in an interval where the `LosTable` could not meet its tolerance raises
`ResultError`, whose message gives the interval and the reason.

## Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
table = pp.LosTable(model)

v = np.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 3001)
d = pp.losvd(table, 1.0, v)                    # at R_2D = 1, shape (3001,)
dv = v[1] - v[0]
d.sum() * dv                                   # one, to the accuracy of the sum on this grid
np.sqrt((v**2 * d).sum() * dv), pp.sigma_los(table, 1.0)

pp.losvd(table, np.array([[0.1], [1.0], [10.0]]), v).shape   # (3, 3001): radii by velocities
```


---

# Line-of-sight velocity distribution in an aperture

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/aperture_losvd

`pianistpy.aperture_losvd()`, `pianistpy.Aperture`, `pianistpy.LosTable`

`aperture_losvd(source, aperture, v)` returns the line-of-sight velocity distribution of the model’s mass inside
an aperture. \(\overline{D}\) is the line-of-sight velocity distribution \(D\) at each projected radius
([Line-of-sight velocity distribution](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/losvd)), averaged over the aperture with the surface density as the weight:

\[\overline{D}(V_{\rm los}) = \frac{\int_{\rm aperture} \Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})\, D(R_{\rm 2D}, V_{\rm los})\,{\rm d}A}
{\int_{\rm aperture} \Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})\,{\rm d}A}.\]

The distribution is even in \(V_{\rm los}\) and integrates to one over all \(V_{\rm los}\).
\(\overline{D}\) is zero at every \(|V_{\rm los}|\) above the largest velocity that the distribution function
reaches on the lines of sight through the aperture. The second moment of \(\overline{D}\) is the squared
dispersion inside the aperture, \(\overline{\sigma}_{\rm los}^2\). Given the same `LosTable`,
`pianistpy.sigma_los_aperture()` returns \(\overline{\sigma}_{\rm los}\).

## Arguments and units

- `source` is a `Model` or the model’s line-of-sight table (`LosTable`).
Given a model, `aperture_losvd` builds the model’s `LosTable` at every call. For more than one call, build
the `LosTable` once ([Line-of-sight table](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/lostable)).

- `aperture` is an `Aperture`: circular or rectangular, centered or offset ([Observables](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/observables)).
The aperture’s lengths are in the model’s unit of length.

- `v` is an array of line-of-sight velocities in the model’s unit of velocity (km/s in the physical system).

The result has the shape of `v` and is a probability density per unit velocity of the model’s unit system.

For a superposition, the call sums the components’ distributions in the aperture. The distribution of component
\(k\) is weighted by the component’s weight \(w_k\) times the component’s projected mass \(M_k\) inside
the aperture:
\(\overline{D} = \sum_k w_k M_k \overline{D}_k / \sum_k w_k M_k\).

## Accuracy report

The report of `aperture_losvd` checks the second moment of \(\overline{D}\) against
\(\overline{\sigma}_{\rm los}^2\) computed from the projected dispersion, without the velocity distributions. The
tier of the result is the worse of the aperture’s check and the tier of the `LosTable` ([Line-of-sight table](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/lostable)).
`aperture_losvd` issues an `AccuracyWarning` if the relative error of \(\overline{D}\) or
of the `LosTable` is above \(10^{-4}\).

The quick settings lose the most accuracy in a small aperture. Take an NFW halo of concentration 30 with a
Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) Type I anisotropy (\(\beta_{\rm c} = -0.25\), \(R_{\rm a} = 10\)):

- In a centered circle of radius 0.05 scale radii, the second moment with the quick settings differs from the
second moment with the default settings by a relative \(6.7 \times 10^{-6}\). The check of the
quick-settings result reports \(6.2 \times 10^{-6}\) (tier `"recorded"`). With the default settings the
check reports \(1.0 \times 10^{-7}\).

- In a circle of radius 1 scale radius, the second moments with the quick and with the default settings differ by
a relative \(1.5 \times 10^{-6}\). With the default settings the check reports \(6.4 \times 10^{-8}\).

For this NFW model, the quick settings build the `LosTable` in about a quarter of the time that the default
settings take.

## Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
table = pp.LosTable(model)
circle = pp.Aperture.circle(r_ape=1.0)

v = np.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 3001)
d = pp.aperture_losvd(table, circle, v)       # shape (3001,)
dv = v[1] - v[0]
d.sum() * dv                                   # one, to the accuracy of the sum on this grid
np.sqrt((v**2 * d).sum() * dv), pp.sigma_los_aperture(table, circle)

pp.aperture_losvd(table, pp.Aperture.circle(r_ape=1.0, r_off=10.0), v)   # an offset circle
```


---

# Local velocity distribution

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/pdf_v

`pianistpy.pdf_v()`, `pianistpy.LosTable`

`pdf_v(source, r, v)` returns the local velocity distribution \(p(V\,|\,R)\) at user-specified 3D radii.
\(p(V\,|\,R)\) is the probability density of the velocity \(V = |\mathbf{V}|\) of the model’s mass at the
distance \(R\) from the center. As in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), the density at a radius is written as an integral over the angle
\(\varphi\) between the velocity and the radial direction, with the angle density \(p_\varphi\), and over
the velocity magnitude, with its density \(p_V\),

\[\varrho(R) = 2\pi \int_0^\pi {\rm d}\varphi\; p_\varphi(\varphi\,|\,R)
\int_0^{V_{\rm esc}(R)} {\rm d}V\; p_V(V\,|\,R, \varphi),
\qquad V_{\rm esc}(R) = \sqrt{2P(R)},\]

and the velocity distribution is the product \(p_\varphi\,p_V\) integrated over the angle and multiplied by
\(2\pi/\varrho(R)\):

\[p(V\,|\,R) = \frac{2\pi}{\varrho(R)} \int_0^\pi p_\varphi(\varphi\,|\,R)\, p_V(V\,|\,R, \varphi)\,{\rm d}\varphi .\]

\(p(V\,|\,R)\) integrates to one over \(V \geq 0\). For an isotropic, constant-anisotropy or Type I model,
the support of \(p(V\,|\,R)\) ends at the escape velocity \(V_{\rm esc}(R)\). A Type II model also holds
unbound orbits, and the velocities of a Type II model reach \(V_{\rm esc}/\sqrt{1 - R^2/R_{\rm a}^2}\). For a Type
II model, a radius at or beyond the anisotropy radius \(R_{\rm a}\) raises `InputError`. The
radius \(R\) of
[Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758) is `r` in the package.

## Arguments and units

- `source` is a `Model` or the model’s line-of-sight table (`LosTable`).

- `r` and `v` are arrays that broadcast against each other. `r` holds radii in the model’s unit of length:
internal units by default, parsecs or an Astropy quantity in the physical system. `v` holds velocities in the
model’s unit of velocity (km/s in the physical system).

- The result has the broadcast shape of `r` and `v` and is a probability density per unit velocity of the
model’s unit system. The result is zero at negative velocities and beyond the end of the support.

For a superposition, the components are mixed by their density at the radius,
\(p = \sum_k w_k \varrho_k p_k / \sum_k w_k \varrho_k\).

## Accuracy

Each distinct radius is computed once, with three checks:

- the norm of the distribution against the density;

- the second moment of the distribution against \(\sigma_{\rm r}^2 (3 - 2\beta_\sigma)\) from [Radial velocity dispersion](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_r);

- the change of the distribution when the number of nodes of the distribution’s angle integral doubles.

The number of nodes of the angle integral doubles, at most three times, until the change of the distribution is
under `velocity_tolerance`: \(10^{-6}\) with the default settings, \(10^{-4}\) with `Settings(quick=True)`.
A distribution whose relative error is above \(10^{-4}\) is returned with an
`AccuracyWarning`. A distribution whose relative error is above \(10^{-2}\) raises
`AccuracyError`, unless the model’s settings set `write_anyway=True`.

[`pianistpy.observables.stages.velocity_distribution()`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/observables#pianistpy.observables.stages.velocity_distribution) returns the velocity distribution of a one-component model at
one radius, in internal units in every unit system. The returned object also holds the record of the distribution’s
checks, the escape velocity, the end of the distribution’s support and the share of the distribution above the escape
velocity (`unbound_fraction`, nonzero only for a Type II model).

## Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
v = np.linspace(0.0, 1.4, 1401)                           # beyond the escape velocity at each of the three radii
p = pp.pdf_v(model, np.array([[0.1], [1.0], [10.0]]), v)   # (3, 1401): radii by velocities
p.sum(axis=1) * (v[1] - v[0])                              # one at each radius, to the accuracy of the sum on this grid

physical = model.to("physical", concentration=10.0, mass_0=1e9, r_0=500.0)
pp.pdf_v(physical, 500.0, [10.0, 50.0, 100.0])             # per km/s, at 500 pc
```


---

# Line-of-sight table

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/lostable

`pianistpy.LosTable`, `pianistpy.losvd()`, `pianistpy.sigma_los()`,
`pianistpy.sigma_los_aperture()`, `pianistpy.sigma_r()`, `pianistpy.sigma_t()`, `pianistpy.pdf_v()`

`LosTable(model)` computes, once, everything the observables of a model read:

- the intrinsic dispersion profile ([Radial velocity dispersion](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_r));

- the surface density \(\Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})\) and the line-of-sight dispersion
\(\sigma_{\rm los}(R_{\rm 2D})\) over projected radius;

- the line-of-sight velocity distributions \(D(R_{\rm 2D}, V_{\rm los})\) ([Line-of-sight velocity distribution](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/losvd)), one row per projected
radius, from the center outward.

Every observable then takes the table in place of the model and reads its values from the table. Build a table when a model is asked
for more than one observable, or for one observable many times (a fit, a grid of apertures).

As in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), the dispersion inside an aperture is the surface-density weighted average of
\(\sigma_{\rm los}^2\). A centered circle of radius \(R_{\rm ape}\) gives

\[\overline{\sigma}_{\rm los}^2(R_{\rm ape}) =
\frac{\int_0^{R_{\rm ape}} \Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})\,\sigma_{\rm los}^2(R_{\rm 2D})\,R_{\rm 2D}\,{\rm d}R_{\rm 2D}}
{\int_0^{R_{\rm ape}} \Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})\,R_{\rm 2D}\,{\rm d}R_{\rm 2D}},\]

and an offset circle or a rectangle gives the same average over its own area.
`sigma_los_aperture()` computes the dispersion inside an aperture in two ways:

- Given the model, `sigma_los_aperture` computes the surface-density weighted average of
\(\sigma_{\rm los}^2\) and reads no velocity distribution.

- Given the table, `sigma_los_aperture` takes the second moment of the aperture’s velocity distribution, which is
the table’s rows averaged over the aperture with the surface density as the weight.

The results on the model and on the table agree to a relative error of \(10^{-6}\). The call on the table
takes longer than the call on the model.

## Arguments and units

`LosTable(model)` takes a `Model` of one component or a superposition
(`superpose()`). For a superposition it holds one table per component in `parts`, and reads each
with its component’s weight.

The table is computed in internal units, at the model’s own settings. `table.to("physical", ...)` recomputes
nothing. `table.to` returns the same tables presented in the units of `model.to("physical", ...)`, and the
observables read from the returned table take and return quantities in those units.

The rows are computed in parallel processes. In a script, build the table under `if __name__ == "__main__":`, as
Python’s `multiprocessing` requires. A call of `losvd()` or `aperture_losvd()` on a
model, and a `ProjectedSampler` given a model, also build a table and need the same
`if __name__ == "__main__":` guard. A notebook or an interactive session needs no `if __name__ == "__main__":`
guard. If a parallel process ends during the computation, the call raises `pianistpy.exceptions.WorkerError` at
once and states the cause. The usual cause is that the machine ran out of memory. Fewer cores
(`set_cores()`) lower the memory that the call uses.

The table holds:

- `model`, the model the table was built from;

- `profile` (the intrinsic dispersion profile), `projected` (the surface density and the line-of-sight
dispersion over projected radius), `kept` (the ranges of projected radius of the velocity quadrature) and
`table` (the line-of-sight velocity distributions), each of the first component for a superposition;

- `validation`, the table’s accuracy report;

- `parts`, one table per component.

## Where the rows run

The rows stop at the first row beyond which less than `losvd.outer_mass_share` of the model’s total projected
mass lies. The default is \(10^{-6}\). `Settings(losvd={"outer_mass_share": 0})` keeps the
rows to the model’s edge.

By default the rows start at the innermost radius of the dispersion profile. The setting
`losvd.innermost_read_radius` sets the smallest projected radius the table will be read at. The rows then start
at the last row inside the projected radius whose disk holds \(10^{-6}\) times the projected mass inside
`innermost_read_radius`. An aperture’s integral then starts at the table’s first row. Each row kept is identical
to the row at the same projected radius of a table built with `innermost_read_radius` and `outer_mass_share`
set to 0.

A read outside the rows raises `InputError`. For a read beyond the last row or inside the first
row, at a point or over an aperture, the error message gives the radius of the end row and the setting that moves
the end row (`losvd.outer_mass_share` or `losvd.innermost_read_radius`). An aperture whose part inside the
first row carries more than \(10^{-6}\) of the aperture’s weight also raises `InputError`.
The error message gives the radius of the smallest centered circle that the table computes to a relative error of
\(10^{-6}\).

## Accuracy report

The table adds rows until the interpolation between rows meets the tolerance of the model’s settings. Every row is
checked against the surface density and the line-of-sight dispersion, both computed without the row. The report `table.validation` holds six checks, each with its relative error
and the radius where it is worst:

- `norm`: each row’s integral against the surface density;

- `second_moment`: each row’s second moment against the projected dispersion;

- `unjudged`: infinite if a row where the surface density is positive could not be checked, and 0 otherwise;

- `t_converged`: infinite if the integral of a row along the line of sight did not converge, and 0 otherwise;

- `certificate`: the table’s estimate of its error between rows;

- `layer_floor`: the error floor of the integration toward zero angular momentum. The floor is nonzero only for a
central anisotropy \(\beta_{\rm c}\) between 1/2 and 1, and a floor above \(10^{-6}\) raises
`ResultError`.

The report’s tier is the band of the worst relative error among the six checks and the model’s own report
([Accuracy](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/accuracy)). Building a table whose relative error is above \(10^{-4}\) issues an
`AccuracyWarning`. A table whose relative error is above \(10^{-2}\) (tier `"refused"`)
raises `AccuracyError`, unless the model’s settings set `write_anyway=True`. An aperture call
on a table (`aperture_losvd`, `sigma_los_aperture`) warns above \(10^{-4}\) and raises above
\(10^{-2}\) in the same way for the aperture’s distribution. `table.table.r_uncertified` records the
intervals of projected radius where the table could not meet the table’s tolerance. A read inside one of the
intervals in `table.table.r_uncertified` raises `ResultError`, whose message gives the
interval.

## Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
table = pp.LosTable(model)                     # built once
table.validation.tier                          # "silent", "recorded", "warned" or "refused"
{key: check.error for key, check in table.validation.checks.items()}

circle = pp.Aperture.circle(1.0)
pp.sigma_los_aperture(model, circle), pp.sigma_los_aperture(table, circle)   # on the model and on the table
pp.sigma_los(table, [0.1, 1.0, 10.0])
pp.losvd(table, 1.0, [0.0, 0.5, 1.0])

physical = table.to("physical", concentration=10.0, mass_0=1e9, r_0=500.0)
pp.sigma_los_aperture(physical, pp.Aperture.circle(500.0))                   # km/s, 500 pc circle
```

The [Representative computing time](https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/computing-time) page gives the time of a table’s first build and
of the calls that read the table, measured on a workstation CPU, with a GPU, and on a laptop.


---

# End-to-end differentiability

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiability

[`pianistpy.inference.likelihood()`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/inference#pianistpy.inference.likelihood), [`pianistpy.df.gradient.make_inversion_table()`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/df#pianistpy.df.gradient.make_inversion_table),
[`pianistpy.df.gradient.table_jacobian()`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/df#pianistpy.df.gradient.table_jacobian), [`pianistpy.df.gradient.make_inversion_rows()`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/df#pianistpy.df.gradient.make_inversion_rows),
[`pianistpy.df.gradient.rows_jacobian()`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/df#pianistpy.df.gradient.rows_jacobian)

## What is differentiable

- **The likelihood.** The log-likelihood that [`pianistpy.inference.likelihood()`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/inference#pianistpy.inference.likelihood) returns is a JAX function of
the components’ weights and of the model’s mass and length scales, which JAX traces and differentiates in each
weight and each scale. With `free=`, the anisotropy \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) of each component listed in
`free` is also a parameter of the log-likelihood (see [Which models](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiability#which-models) below and the
[Inference](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/inference) page). With `free=`, data of the binned distributions
(`"losvd"`, `"losvd_aperture"`, `"pdf_v"`) or of the Gauss-Hermite moments (`"h3"`, `"h4"`) raise
`InputError`.

- **The observables.** `pianistpy.Differentiable` provides the observables of a one-component model as JAX
functions of the component’s anisotropy \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) ([Differentiable observables](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiable)).

- **The distribution function.** The derivative of the distribution function in the central anisotropy
\(\beta_{\rm c}\) and the anisotropy radius \(R_{\rm a}\) is available at the inversion’s energies and for
the full table (see [The distribution function](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiability#the-distribution-function) below).

The derivative of the distribution function is available for the following anisotropy models, with their parameters:

- isotropic and constant anisotropy \((\beta_{\rm c})\),

- Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) Type I (\(\beta_{\rm c}\) and \(R_{\rm a}\)),

- Osipkov-Merritt Type I and Type II \((R_{\rm a})\).

The following cases raise `InputError`:

- COM Type II. The COM Type II inversion has an interior point at the potential \(P(R_{\rm a})\), which moves
with both \(R_{\rm a}\) and \(\beta_{\rm c}\), so the derivative is not integrable at \(P(R_{\rm a})\).
The log-likelihood of `"sigma_los"` and `"sigma_los_aperture"` data still has a derivative in the anisotropy
of a free COM Type II component, computed from the Jeans equation. `Differentiable` raises
`InputError` for a COM Type II component. The distribution function of a COM Type II component
and the observables read from the distribution function (`losvd`, `aperture_losvd`, `pdf_v`) have no
derivative.

- A distribution function whose center lies on the critical branch, where the inner slope \(\gamma\) of the
density equals \(2\beta_{\rm c}\) and the form of the center changes with \(\beta_{\rm c}\).

- A component on a truncated profile that does not carry the distribution function of the model the profile was
taken from.

## Which models

The anisotropy is a parameter, through `likelihood` with `free=` and through `pp.Differentiable`, only for a
Method II model: a component whose distribution function is inverted on another model’s truncated profile. The
truncated profile is held fixed, so the profile and the potential do not change with the anisotropy, and the
derivative is complete. Other models raise `InputError`:

- A Method I truncated model. The truncated profile of a Method I model follows from the model’s own distribution
function, so the truncated profile changes with \(\beta_{\rm c}\) and \(R_{\rm a}\). Ver. 1.0.0 does not
compute the derivative of the truncated profile in the anisotropy.

- An untruncated model, or a model that is not spatially finite.

## The distribution function

The derivative of the distribution function is available in two forms:

- the rows (the distribution function on the inversion’s energy grid), through `make_inversion_rows` and
`rows_jacobian`, for a component on its own analytic profile only;

- the table, as the lookup reads it, through `make_inversion_table` and `table_jacobian`. The derivative covers
every array of the table: the rows (`log_df`, `log_df_slope`), the nodes below the table’s first energy
(`log_df_below`, `log_df_slope_below`), the closed form at the center (`central`) and the tail (`tail`).
For a Method II component, the arrays are the rows (`log_df`), the power law at the lowest energies
(`edge_law`) and the closed form at the center (`center`).

`make_inversion_rows` and `make_inversion_table` each return a JAX function of the anisotropy parameters, the
names of the parameters (`params`), and the energies or the table at the component’s own parameters. The value of
the returned function is the result of `compute_df()` at the given parameters, computed on the CPU.
The derivative of the returned function is the package’s analytic derivative (Eq. (T:7.1) of the
[Technical notes](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/notes)). The `*_jacobian` functions return the values and their derivatives
as arrays.

Both returned functions hold the energies at the component’s own parameters. The function that
`make_inversion_table` returns makes the anchor of the closed form at the center and the nodes kept again at each
new parameter value, except that a component on a truncated profile also holds the nodes kept at the component’s
own parameters. The derivative is thus the derivative of the table that `compute_df()` returns at the
given parameters, on the held energies. Where a discrete choice would change between two parameter values, the value
of the returned function differs from a new `compute_df()` call by up to the tolerance of the
inversion.

## Accuracy and the record

The derivative is exact except for the derivative of the inversion’s operator in \(\beta_{\rm c}\). The
derivative of the operator in \(\beta_{\rm c}\) has no closed form and is taken by finite differences of the
operator’s values at nearby \(\beta_{\rm c}\). `rows_jacobian` and `table_jacobian` return a record of the
finite differences:

- the kind of difference: central (a Richardson quotient) where the inversion’s form is the same on both sides of
\(\beta_{\rm c}\), or one-sided at a \(\beta_{\rm c}\) where the form changes (integer and half-integer
\(\beta_{\rm c}\));

- the step of the difference;

- the Richardson residual of the quotient and, for a one-sided difference, the spread between the derivatives from
the two sides, relative to the largest \(|\partial F/\partial\beta_{\rm c}|\) in the record of
`rows_jacobian` and absolute in the record of `table_jacobian`;

- for a component on a truncated profile, where the component’s energy grid is placed.

The Richardson residual is the accuracy of the derivative, read against the thresholds \(10^{-6}\),
\(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-2}\) of the validation reports ([Accuracy](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/accuracy)). Where the difference is central, the
residual is below \(10^{-6}\). At the isotropic value \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0\), the difference is one-sided, and
the residual is about \(10^{-5}\) of the largest derivative, between \(10^{-6}\) and \(10^{-4}\). The
record gives the residual. A gradient at \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0\) is usable at an error of about \(10^{-5}\).
For a gradient with an error below \(10^{-6}\), take a \(\beta_{\rm c}\) away from 0, where the difference
is central.

## Example

The derivative of \(\log_{10} F\) at one node of a Hernquist component’s table, by the analytic derivative and by
a central difference of the same function:

```python
import jax
import numpy as np

import pianistpy as pp
from pianistpy.df.gradient import make_inversion_table

halo = pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25))
table, params, values = make_inversion_table(halo, pp.Settings())
node = int(np.searchsorted(values["k"], 0.5))  # the first node at or above K = 0.5

def log_df(theta):
    return table(theta)["log_df"][node]

theta = np.array([0.25])  # params == ("beta_c",)
rule = float(jax.grad(log_df)(theta)[0])
h = 1e-3
difference = float(log_df(theta + h) - log_df(theta - h)) / (2 * h)
print(rule, difference)
```

The analytic derivative and the central difference agree to the error of the central difference, of order
\(h^2\) times the third derivative. The table is made once. Each
call of `table` solves the inversion again at the new parameters, on the held grid.


---

# Differentiable observables

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiable

`pianistpy.Differentiable`

## The object

`pp.Differentiable(model)` gives the observables of a model of one component as JAX functions of the component’s
anisotropy \(\theta = (\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\), the central anisotropy and the anisotropy radius, passed as
`theta`. The model is a Method II model, a distribution function inverted on the truncated profile of a Method I
model ([Truncation in phase space](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/truncation)), as in the example below. Each method takes \(\theta\) as
the first argument, returns the value of the public function of the same name on the model rebuilt at
\(\theta\), and works under `jax.jit` and `jax.grad`:

```python
d = pp.Differentiable(model)
d.sigma_r(theta, r)                    # as pp.sigma_r(model at theta, r)
d.sigma_t(theta, r)                    # as pp.sigma_t
d.sigma_los(theta, r_2d)               # as pp.sigma_los
d.sigma_los_aperture(theta, aperture)  # as pp.sigma_los_aperture
d.losvd(theta, r_2d, v)                # as pp.losvd
d.pdf_v(theta, r, v)                   # as pp.pdf_v
d.aperture_losvd(theta, aperture, v)   # as pp.aperture_losvd
```

Every radius, velocity, aperture length and \(\theta\) that a method reads, and every value that a method
returns, is in internal units whatever the model’s unit system, as is the anisotropy `theta` of `likelihood`.
`d.theta` is the model’s own anisotropy.

`Differentiable` accepts an isotropic, constant-anisotropy, Osipkov-Merritt Type I or Type II, or
Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) Type I component. For an isotropic or constant-anisotropy component,
\(R_{\rm a}\) is infinite and stays at infinity at every \(\theta\), and the gradient in \(R_{\rm a}\) is
zero. For an Osipkov-Merritt component, the gradient of `losvd`, `aperture_losvd` and `pdf_v` in
\(\beta_{\rm c}\) is NaN. An Osipkov-Merritt component has \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0\), where the form of the
inversion changes and the derivatives of the distribution function from the two sides of \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0\)
differ by more than \(10^{-6}\). For an Osipkov-Merritt component, `sigma_r`, `sigma_t`, `sigma_los` and
`sigma_los_aperture` carry the derivative in \(\beta_{\rm c}\), computed from the Jeans equation.

The constructor raises `InputError`, with a message that states the cause, for:

- a COM Type II component ([End-to-end differentiability](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiability)),

- a model of more than one component, such as a superposition (the components of a superposition are
differentiated through `likelihood`),

- a component that is not spatially finite,

- a component not on a truncated profile that carries the distribution function of the Method I model it was built from.

## What a method computes

A method’s value at \(\theta\) is the public call on the model rebuilt at \(\theta\). At the model’s own
\(\theta\), a method returns the value of the public call on the model itself, bit for bit. The derivative of a
method holds fixed the radii and velocities at which the tables at \(\theta\) are tabulated, as `likelihood`
does for a free component. Where the tabulated radii and velocities change from one \(\theta\) to another, the
value of a method changes by up to the tolerance of the tables, and the derivative omits that change.

The derivatives of `losvd`, `pdf_v` and `aperture_losvd` are taken through the derivative of the distribution
function ([End-to-end differentiability](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiability)), with the energies of the distribution function’s table held fixed. For a
component whose distribution function has no derivative in the anisotropy, such as an isotropic component,
`losvd`, `pdf_v` and `aperture_losvd` raise `InputError` with a message that states the
reason.

At a \(\theta\) where rebuilding the model raises `InputError`,
`UnphysicalModelError`, `AccuracyError` or `ResultError`, the
value is NaN and the gradient is zero. A method is not differentiable in the radii or velocities that the method
reads, and the gradient in a radius or a velocity is NaN.

## The cost

The first call of a method at a new \(\theta\) rebuilds the model at \(\theta\). The rebuild inverts the
distribution function at \(\theta\) on the component’s truncated profile, then computes the dispersion profile
and the table of the line-of-sight dispersion. A rebuild costs about as much as the public call on a model built at
\(\theta\), as does the rebuild of a free component in `likelihood`. A `Differentiable` keeps the tables of
at most eight values of \(\theta\), the model’s own \(\theta\) and the seven other values first met most
recently, so the value and the gradient at one \(\theta\) share one rebuild.

The derivatives of `losvd` and `aperture_losvd` cost far more. The derivatives of `losvd` and
`aperture_losvd` recompute and differentiate each row of the line-of-sight table that the call reads, and take
minutes to hours, with the number of rows the call reads ([Release notes](https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/release-notes)).

The values of `losvd` and `aperture_losvd`, without a derivative, cost only the rebuild at \(\theta\) and the
public call of the same name.

`Settings(check_rows=True)`, off by default, checks each row that the derivatives of `losvd` and
`aperture_losvd` read. The check requires that:

- each recomputed row equals the stored row, bit for bit;

- the row built again one velocity at a time, each at the quadrature level that gave the velocity’s value, equals the
recomputed row, bit for bit;

- the JAX computation of the row that carries the derivative in the anisotropy equals the row to \(10^{-12}\) of
the row’s largest value.

A row that fails raises a `ResultError` that identifies the row. The gradient is the same with and without the checks. On a
GPU the checks may fail a row, since a GPU’s order of summation does not promise the same bits. On the CPU, every row
passes the checks.

## Example

The example computes the derivative in \(\beta_{\rm c}\) of the line-of-sight dispersion at one projected radius
twice, by `jax.grad` and by a central difference:

```python
import jax
import numpy as np

import pianistpy as pp

truncated = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy()), pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05)
)
model = pp.solve(pp.Component(truncated.profile, pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)))
d = pp.Differentiable(model)

rule = float(jax.grad(lambda t: d.sigma_los(t, 0.3))(d.theta)[0])
h = np.array([1e-3, 0.0])
difference = float(d.sigma_los(d.theta + h, 0.3) - d.sigma_los(d.theta - h, 0.3)) / 2e-3
print(rule, difference)
```

The `jax.grad` derivative and the central difference agree to the error of the central difference. Each of the two
shifted \(\theta\) costs one rebuild.


---

# Superposition and inference

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/superposition

`pianistpy.superpose()`, [`pianistpy.inference`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/inference#module-pianistpy.inference)

## Superposition

Method II models built on the truncated density of one Method I model
([Truncation in phase space](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/truncation)) share that density. The distribution functions of those Method II models, combined with
positive weights that sum to one, form one equilibrium model in that truncated density. `superpose` returns the combined model as a
`Model`, which `Sampler`, the observables, `likelihood` and `write` take as any other model.
`Differentiable` raises `InputError` for a combined model, whose components are differentiated
through `likelihood`.

```python
members = {model_a: 0.6, model_b: 0.3, model_c: 0.1}   # Method II models on one truncated density
composite = pp.superpose(members)
pp.Sampler(composite).sample(1_000_000, seed=1)
```

`superpose` takes a mapping of two or more Method II models on one truncated density, the members, to the members’
weights.
`superpose` raises `InputError` when a weight is not positive and finite, or when the members
are built on different truncated profiles or with different settings or units. The weights are normalized to sum to
one, and a warning goes to the package’s log when the sum of the weights differs from one by more than
\(10^{-10}\).

## Inference

[`pianistpy.inference`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/inference#module-pianistpy.inference) gives the log-likelihood of a model against data as a JAX function. The function’s arguments
are the weights of the components, the mass scale and the length scale in the units of the data, and, for the
components listed in `free=`, the anisotropy \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\). Each modeled dispersion is a
ratio of two sums that are linear in the weights, so the gradient with respect to the weights is exact and needs no
new table.

```python
from pianistpy.inference import Data, likelihood

data = Data("sigma_los", values=sigma_obs, r_2d=radii, errors=sigma_err, unit_system="physical")
loglike = likelihood(composite.to("physical", concentration=..., mass_0=..., r_0=...), data)
loglike(weights)                       # a JAX scalar; jax.grad(loglike)(weights) is its gradient
```

`likelihood` computes the tables of the observables of each component once. Each later call of the returned
function takes a fraction of a millisecond, except a call at a new anisotropy of a free component, which first
rebuilds the free component’s tables. An invalid argument of the returned function, such as a negative weight, a
scale that is not positive, or a length scale that moves a data radius inside the innermost tabulated radius,
gives minus infinity, not an exception, so a Monte Carlo sampler over the weights always receives a value.
A model and data that cannot be compared raise `InputError` in `likelihood` itself, never in a
call of the returned function.

[End-to-end differentiability](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiability) states what the likelihood is differentiable in, through which observables, and at what accuracy.


---

# Units

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/units

Everything is computed in internal units, the dimensionless normalization of [Widrow (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1086/317367). In internal units,
the scale radius and the central potential of the untruncated profile are 1.

The `to` method of a distribution function, a model or a `LosTable` presents the result in model
units \((G = M_0 = r_0 = 1)\) or, through [Astropy](https://www.astropy.org/), in physical units. Both systems
need the concentration \(c\), which defines \(M_0\) as the mass of the untruncated profile inside
\(c\,r_0\). The numbers are not recomputed. Observables and particles computed from the presented result are
returned in the unit system of the presented result. Some inputs and outputs stay in internal units whatever the
model’s unit system: `Sampler`’s `r_sample` and `r_range`, the radii, the `v_range` and the returned velocities of
`Sampler.velocities`, every argument and value of `Differentiable`, and the anisotropy `theta` of
`likelihood`.
