# Validation

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation

Module `pianistpy.validation`

The accuracy bands of a result and the validation report that states them.

Every result of the package (a model, a distribution function, a sampler, a
projected table) carries a ValidationReport as its `validation`
attribute. A user reads the band of a result from `result.validation.tier`
and the measured relative errors from `result.validation.checks`.
tier_level maps one relative error \(\epsilon\) to its band:

\[\begin{split}\text{band}(\epsilon) =
\begin{cases}
\text{silent}, & \epsilon \le 10^{-6},\\
\text{recorded}, & 10^{-6} < \epsilon \le 10^{-4},\\
\text{warned}, & 10^{-4} < \epsilon \le 10^{-2},\\
\text{refused}, & \epsilon > 10^{-2}.
\end{cases}\end{split}\]

The technical notes, Section T:0.5, state how each band is reported.

class pianistpy.validation.Check(*error*, *where=None*, *reason=None*, *source=None*, *excluded=None*)

One check of a result: the relative error measured and where.

A check is either judged or not judged. A judged check has a measured
relative error and the band of that error. A check that is not judged
has the error NaN, a stated reason, and the name `"not judged"` in
place of a band; a check that is not judged does not change the band of
the result.

Parameters:

- **error** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – The relative error the check measured. NaN for a check that is not
judged.

- **where** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*, **optional*) – The position of the largest relative error, in the variable the
check runs over (a radius or an energy, in internal units).
Default: `None`, which means the check has no single position of
its largest error.

- **reason** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **optional*) – The reason the check is not judged. Default: `None`, which means
the check is judged.

- **source** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **optional*) – For a judged check that read its input from a source other than the
result’s own data: the source read, and the reason. The error and
the band are those measured on that source. Default: `None`,
which means the check read the result’s own data.

- **excluded** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **optional*) – For a judged check that leaves part of its input unjudged: the part
left out, and the reason. The error and the band are those of the
remaining input. Default: `None`, which means the check judged
its whole input.

Variables:

- **level** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – The band of the check’s error as returned by tier_level; 0 for a
check that is not judged.

- **tier** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The name of the check’s band, one of TIER_NAMES, or
`"not judged"`.

See also

[`ValidationReport`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.ValidationReport)
The checks of one result together.

[`tier_level`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.tier_level)
The band of a relative error.

Examples

```python
>>> check = Check(error=3e-5, where=12.5)
>>> check.tier
'recorded'
>>> Check(error=float("nan"), reason="the table has no outer rows").tier
'not judged'
```

property level: [int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)

The band of the check’s error as a level from 0 to 3; 0 for a check
that is not judged.

property tier: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

The name of the check’s band, or `"not judged"`.

class pianistpy.validation.ValidationReport(*keys*, *checks*, *parents_level=0*)

The validation report of one result: its checks and its band.

Each kind of result reports a fixed set of keys, one Check per key.
The band of the result is the worst band among the result’s own checks
and the worst band among the results the result was built from (its
parents). A report holds only the result’s own checks: a derived result
carries the worst level of its parents as one number, not the parents’
reports.

Parameters:

- **keys** ([*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)* of *[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The keys the kind of result reports, in the order the report lists
them.

- **checks** (*mapping** of **str to Check*) – One Check for each entry of keys.

- **parents_level** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)*, **optional*) – The worst level, from 0 to 3, among the parents of the result.
Default: `0`, which means the result has no parent above
\(10^{-6}\).

Variables:

- **level** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – The worst level among the result’s own checks and parents_level.

- **tier** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The name of the worst band, `TIER_NAMES[level]`.

Raises:

[**InputError**](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.InputError) – If the keys of checks are not the entries of keys.

See also

[`Check`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.Check)
One check of the report.

[`tier_level`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.tier_level)
The band of a relative error.

Examples

```python
>>> report = ValidationReport(
...     keys=("round_trip", "top_form"),
...     checks={"round_trip": Check(2e-7), "top_form": Check(3e-5)},
... )
>>> report.tier
'recorded'
>>> ValidationReport(report.keys, report.checks, parents_level=2).tier
'warned'
```

property level: [int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)

The worst level among the result’s own checks and its parents.

property tier: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

The name of the worst band of the result.

classmethod from_dict(*record*, *key_sets=None*)

Build a report from the dictionary that to_dict writes.

Parameters:

- **record** (*mapping*) – The report in the form to_dict returns: the entries
`"parents_tier"` and `"checks"`.

- **key_sets** (*sequence** of *[*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)* of *[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **optional*) – Every key set that a report of the record’s kind of result can
have. With key_sets given, the report takes the smallest key
set that holds every check of the record, and a key of that set
that the record lacks becomes a check that is not judged, with
the reason that the file does not hold the check. Default:
`None`, which means the report takes the record’s own checks
as its keys.

Returns:

**report** – The report the record describes.

Return type:

[ValidationReport](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.ValidationReport)

Raises:

- [**ResultError**](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.ResultError) – If key_sets is given and a check of the record belongs to no
    key set of key_sets.

- [**ResultError**](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.ResultError) – If key_sets is given and no single key set of key_sets holds
    every check of the record.

See also

[`to_dict`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.ValidationReport.to_dict)
The dictionary form of a report.

Examples

```python
>>> report = ValidationReport(("a",), {"a": Check(3e-5)})
>>> record = report.to_dict()
>>> ValidationReport.from_dict(record) == report
True
>>> wider = ValidationReport.from_dict(record, [("a", "b")])
>>> wider.checks["b"].tier
'not judged'
```

to_dict()

Return the report as a plain dictionary.

Returns:

**record** – The entries `"tier"` (the report’s band), `"parents_tier"`
(the name of the parents’ worst band) and `"checks"` (one
dictionary for each key, in the order of keys, with the
entries `"error"`, `"where"` and `"tier"`, and
`"reason"`, `"source"` or `"excluded"` where the check
states one).

Return type:

[dict](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

See also

[`from_dict`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.ValidationReport.from_dict)
The report built from the dictionary.

Examples

```python
>>> report = ValidationReport(("a",), {"a": Check(3e-5, where=1.0)})
>>> record = report.to_dict()
>>> record["tier"], record["parents_tier"]
('recorded', 'silent')
>>> record["checks"]["a"]
{'error': 3e-05, 'where': 1.0, 'tier': 'recorded'}
```

pianistpy.validation.announce(*what*, *report*, *detail*)

Report a result whose relative error is above \(10^{-6}\).

The announcement depends on the band of report. A result in the band
`"silent"` (at most \(10^{-6}\)) is not announced. A result in the
band `"recorded"` (above \(10^{-6}\), at most \(10^{-4}\)) is
written as one line to the `pianistpy` logger at level INFO, and no
warning is issued. A result in the band `"warned"` (above
\(10^{-4}\), at most \(10^{-2}\)) is written to the
`pianistpy` logger at level WARNING and issued as an
AccuracyWarning, which the standard `warnings` filter can silence or
turn into an error. A result in the band `"refused"` (above
\(10^{-2}\)) reaches announce only if its settings set
`write_anyway=True`; that result is announced as a result in the band
`"warned"` is.

Parameters:

- **what** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The result’s name as messages write it, for example
`"The sampler of 'nfw'"`.

- **report** ([*ValidationReport*](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.ValidationReport)) – The validation report of the result.

- **detail** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The checks above \(10^{-6}\), each with its relative error and
the position of its largest error.

Warns:

**AccuracyWarning** – If the band of report is `"warned"` or `"refused"`.

Return type:

None

See also

[`refuse_unless_asked`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.refuse_unless_asked)
The error for an input in the band `"refused"`.

`set_verbosity`
The lowest level of the messages printed on the screen.

Examples

```python
>>> silent = ValidationReport(("a",), {"a": Check(1e-8)})
>>> announce("The sampler of 'x'", silent, "a 1.0e-08")
```

pianistpy.validation.refuse_unless_asked(*what*, *report*, *settings*)

Raise if an input result is in the band `"refused"` and the settings
do not ask for the result anyway.

A result in the band `"refused"` (relative error above
\(10^{-2}\)) exists only if the settings that built the result set
`write_anyway=True`, or if the result was read from a file that holds
such a result. A computation that takes such a result as input proceeds
only if its own settings also set `write_anyway=True`; the new result
then carries the band `"refused"`.

Parameters:

- **what** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The input result’s name as messages write it, for example
`"The model 'nfw'"`.

- **report** ([*ValidationReport*](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.ValidationReport)) – The validation report of the input result.

- **settings** ([*Settings*](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/settings#pianistpy.settings.Settings)) – The settings of the computation that takes the input result.

Raises:

[**AccuracyError**](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.AccuracyError) – If the band of report is `"refused"` and settings does not set
    `write_anyway=True`.

Return type:

None

See also

[`announce`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.announce)
The message for a result above \(10^{-6}\).

`Settings`
The setting `write_anyway`.

Examples

```python
>>> from pianistpy import Settings
>>> report = ValidationReport(("a",), {"a": Check(0.5)})
>>> report.tier
'refused'
>>> refuse_unless_asked("The model 'x'", report, Settings(write_anyway=True))
>>> refuse_unless_asked("The model 'x'", report, Settings())
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
pianistpy.exceptions.AccuracyError: The model 'x' is beyond 0.01 (tier ...
```

pianistpy.validation.tier_level(*error*)

Return the band of a relative error as a level from 0 to 3.

The level indexes TIER_NAMES: level 0 is `"silent"`, level 1 is
`"recorded"`, level 2 is `"warned"` and level 3 is `"refused"`.

Parameters:

**error** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – Relative error \(\epsilon\), a non-negative number. A NaN error
has level 3, the level of an error above \(10^{-2}\).

Returns:

**level** – 0 if error is at most \(10^{-6}\); 1 if error is above
\(10^{-6}\) and at most \(10^{-4}\); 2 if error is above
\(10^{-4}\) and at most \(10^{-2}\); 3 if error is above
\(10^{-2}\) or is NaN.

Return type:

[int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)

See also

`TIER_NAMES`
The name of each level.

`TIER_BOUNDS`
The three relative errors that separate the levels.

[`Check`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/validation#pianistpy.validation.Check)
One measured relative error and its level.

Examples

```python
>>> [tier_level(e) for e in (1e-7, 1e-5, 1e-3, 1e-1, float("nan"))]
[0, 1, 2, 3, 3]
>>> TIER_NAMES[tier_level(3e-5)]
'recorded'
```


---

# Exceptions

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions

Module `pianistpy.exceptions`

The exception classes and warning classes of PIANISTpy.

Every error the package raises is an instance of PianistpyError. Every
warning the package issues is an instance of PianistpyWarning.

exception pianistpy.exceptions.AccuracyError(*message*, *result=None*)

Raised when a result’s relative error is above \(10^{-2}\).

AccuracyError is also raised when the resolution of the settings cannot
resolve the result. An AccuracyError raised after the result is built
carries the result. With `Settings(write_anyway=True)`, the call
returns such a result, with its validation report, and raises no
AccuracyError.

Parameters:

- **message** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The check the result fails, the relative error of the failed check,
and the position where the failed check’s relative error occurs.

- **result** ([*object*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)*, **optional*) – The result, with its validation report. The user can inspect the
attached result without computing the result a second time.
Default: `None`, which means no result is attached.

Variables:

**result** ([*object*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)* or **None*) – The result passed as result. None where the AccuracyError is
raised before the result exists.

Return type:

None

See also

[`AccuracyWarning`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.AccuracyWarning)
Issued when a result’s relative error is above \(10^{-4}\).

[`PianistpyError`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.PianistpyError)
Base class of every error raised by PIANISTpy.

Examples

```python
>>> import pianistpy as pp
>>> issubclass(pp.AccuracyError, pp.PianistpyError)
True
```

exception pianistpy.exceptions.AccuracyWarning

Issued when a result’s relative error is above \(10^{-4}\).

A result with a relative error above \(10^{-4}\) and at most
\(10^{-2}\) has the validation report tier `"warned"`. A result
with a relative error above \(10^{-2}\) also issues AccuracyWarning
when `Settings(write_anyway=True)` lets the call return the result.

See also

[`AccuracyError`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.AccuracyError)
Raised when a result’s relative error is above \(10^{-2}\).

Examples

```python
>>> import pianistpy as pp
>>> issubclass(pp.AccuracyWarning, pp.PianistpyWarning)
True
```

exception pianistpy.exceptions.InputError(**args*)

Raised when a call does not accept one of its inputs.

A call raises InputError for an input of the wrong type, an input
outside its valid range, or an input inconsistent with another input of
the same call. The message of an InputError identifies the input and the rule
the input breaks. InputError is a subclass of `ValueError`.

See also

[`PianistpyError`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.PianistpyError)
Base class of every error raised by PIANISTpy.

Examples

```python
>>> import pianistpy as pp
>>> try:
...     pp.Aperture.circle(-1.0)
... except pp.InputError as error:
...     print(type(error).__name__, isinstance(error, ValueError))
InputError True
```

Parameters:

**args** ([*object*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object))

Return type:

None

exception pianistpy.exceptions.PianistpyError(**args*)

Base class of every error raised by PIANISTpy.

Variables:

**recent** ([*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)* of *[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The most recent messages of the package at the moment the error is
raised, oldest first. The package keeps the recent messages at every
verbosity setting. A run with its messages silenced therefore still
reports, in recent, the steps the run took before the error.

Parameters:

**args** ([*object*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object))

Return type:

None

See also

[`PianistpyWarning`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.PianistpyWarning)
Base class of every warning issued by PIANISTpy.

Examples

```python
>>> import pianistpy as pp
>>> issubclass(pp.InputError, pp.PianistpyError)
True
```

exception pianistpy.exceptions.PianistpyWarning

Base class of every warning issued by PIANISTpy.

See also

[`PianistpyError`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.PianistpyError)
Base class of every error raised by PIANISTpy.

Examples

```python
>>> import pianistpy as pp
>>> issubclass(pp.PianistpyWarning, UserWarning)
True
```

exception pianistpy.exceptions.ResultError(**args*)

Raised when a result fails a check of its integrity.

Reading a file raises ResultError in three cases: the file’s format
version is unknown; the file’s data digest does not match the arrays
stored in the file; or the parent of the stored result differs from the
parent the file records. Writing a file raises ResultError when the
written file does not read back as written. A computation raises
ResultError when an intermediate result fails a check that the next
step of the computation needs, such as values that are not finite or
radii that do not increase.

See also

[`PianistpyError`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.PianistpyError)
Base class of every error raised by PIANISTpy.

Examples

```python
>>> import pianistpy as pp
>>> issubclass(pp.ResultError, pp.PianistpyError)
True
```

Parameters:

**args** ([*object*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object))

Return type:

None

exception pianistpy.exceptions.UnphysicalModelError(*message*, *result=None*)

Raised when the requested model has no valid equilibrium.

Parameters:

- **message** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The condition the model fails and the values of the quantities in
the failed condition.

- **result** ([*object*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)*, **optional*) – The distribution function computed before the error is raised. The
user can inspect the attached distribution function without
computing the distribution function a second time. Default:
`None`, which means no distribution function is attached.

Variables:

**result** ([*object*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)* or **None*) – The distribution function passed as result, or None.

Return type:

None

See also

[`PianistpyError`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.PianistpyError)
Base class of every error raised by PIANISTpy.

[`AccuracyError`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.AccuracyError)
Raised when a result’s relative error is above \(10^{-2}\).

Examples

```python
>>> import pianistpy as pp
>>> issubclass(pp.UnphysicalModelError, pp.PianistpyError)
True
```

exception pianistpy.exceptions.WorkerError(**args*)

Raised when a parallel process ends before finishing its task.

A call raises WorkerError as soon as the call finds one of its parallel
processes ended. The call does not wait for the lost task’s result. The
usual cause of a WorkerError is a lack of memory. The operating system
ends a process when the machine runs out of memory. Fewer cores lower
the memory a call uses. The number of cores is set by set_cores or by
the environment variable
`PIANISTPY_CORES`. WorkerError is a subclass of `RuntimeError`.

Under a JAX transformation such as `jax.grad`, the caller receives
`jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError` with the message of the WorkerError.

See also

[`PianistpyError`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.PianistpyError)
Base class of every error raised by PIANISTpy.

Examples

```python
>>> from pianistpy.exceptions import PianistpyError, WorkerError
>>> issubclass(WorkerError, PianistpyError), issubclass(WorkerError, RuntimeError)
(True, True)
```

Parameters:

**args** ([*object*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object))

Return type:

None


---

# Runtime options

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime

Module `pianistpy.runtime`

Options of the Python session: the messages printed, the stage times, the
number of cores, the hardware JAX runs on, and JAX’s compilation cache.

A user sets each option once for the session, by a call such as
`pp.set_verbosity("info")` or `pp.set_cores(8)`, or by an environment
variable read when the package is imported: `PIANISTPY_VERBOSITY`,
`PIANISTPY_TIMING`, `PIANISTPY_CORES`, `PIANISTPY_PLATFORM` and
`PIANISTPY_COMPILATION_CACHE`. No option changes a computed number, and no
option is part of a result’s identity. No computation of the package takes
a runtime option as an argument.

class pianistpy.runtime.Timing(*stages=<factory>*, *memory=<factory>*)

The elapsed time of each stage of one computation, and the largest
memory of the process at the end of each stage.

Parameters:

- **stages** ([*dict*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)* of **str to float**, **optional*) – Each stage’s name mapped to the seconds spent in the stage, in the
order in which the stages first ran. A stage that runs more than
once has the sum of its times. Default: an empty dictionary.

- **memory** ([*dict*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)* of **str to int**, **optional*) – Each stage’s name mapped to the largest resident memory of the
process, in bytes, at the last end of the stage (peak_memory).
The largest memory never decreases from one stage to the next, so
a stage raised the largest memory if the stage’s value exceeds the
value of the stage before. Default: an empty dictionary.

Variables:

**total** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – The sum of the stage times, in seconds.

See also

[`timing_record`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.timing_record)
Collect a Timing for a block of code.

[`set_timing`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_timing)
Print each result’s stage times.

Examples

```python
>>> timing = Timing(stages={"inversion": 1.5, "truncation": 0.25})
>>> timing.total
1.75
```

property total: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

The sum of the stage times, in seconds.

to_dict()

Return the stage times as a plain dictionary.

Returns:

**stages** – Each stage’s name mapped to the seconds spent in the stage.

Return type:

[dict](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict) of str to float

Examples

```python
>>> Timing(stages={"inversion": 1.5}).to_dict()
{'inversion': 1.5}
```

pianistpy.runtime.allowed_cores()

Return the number of cores the Python process may use.

The number is the first one available of three: the job’s number of
cores as a batch scheduler states the number in its environment
variable; the number of cores the operating system lets the process run
on; the number of cores of the machine.

Returns:

**cores** – The number of cores, at least 1.

Return type:

[int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)

See also

[`set_cores`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_cores)
Choose the number of cores the package uses.

[`get_cores`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.get_cores)
The number of cores the package uses.

Examples

```python
>>> allowed_cores() >= 1
True
```

pianistpy.runtime.card_memory()

Return the free memory and the total memory of the GPU that JAX
runs on, in bytes, as the CUDA driver states them.

The free memory counts the memory that every process holds on the GPU,
including each process’s CUDA context; JAX’s allocator statistics do
not count the contexts. The call uses the GPU’s primary context, which
JAX also uses, so the call creates no CUDA context.

Returns:

**memory** – The free memory and the total memory, in bytes; None if JAX does
not run on a GPU, if the CUDA driver library cannot be loaded, or
if the driver reports an error.

Return type:

[tuple](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple) of ([int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int), [int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) or None

See also

[`platform`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.platform)
The hardware JAX runs on.

[`peak_memory`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.peak_memory)
The largest memory of the process on the host.

Examples

```python
>>> memory = card_memory()
>>> memory is None or memory[0] <= memory[1]
True
```

pianistpy.runtime.configure_jax()

Configure JAX for the package: 64-bit floating point, the hardware,
and the compilation cache.

The package calls configure_jax once, when the package is imported.
The environment variable `PIANISTPY_PLATFORM`, if set, chooses the
hardware (set_platform). The compilation cache is turned on in the
folder of default_compilation_cache, unless
`PIANISTPY_COMPILATION_CACHE` turns the cache off.

See also

[`set_platform`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_platform)
Choose the hardware JAX runs on.

[`set_compilation_cache`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_compilation_cache)
Turn the compilation cache on or off.

Examples

```python
>>> import jax
>>> jax.config.jax_enable_x64
True
```

Return type:

None

pianistpy.runtime.cores_explicit()

Return whether the number of cores was set as an integer.

Returns:

**explicit** – True if the last call of set_cores, or `PIANISTPY_CORES`, gave
an integer; False if the value is `"auto"`, `"full"` or
`"half"`.

Return type:

[bool](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)

See also

[`set_cores`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_cores)
Choose the number of cores the package uses.

Examples

```python
>>> set_cores(2)
>>> cores_explicit()
True
>>> set_cores("auto")
>>> cores_explicit()
False
```

pianistpy.runtime.default_compilation_cache()

Return the folder that the compilation cache uses by default.

Returns:

**folder** – None if the environment variable `PIANISTPY_COMPILATION_CACHE` is
`0`, `false`, `no` or `off`, which turns the cache off; the
variable’s value, a folder’s path, if the variable has any other
value;
`~/.cache/pianistpy/jax` if the variable is unset.

Return type:

[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) or None

See also

[`set_compilation_cache`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_compilation_cache)
Turn the compilation cache on or off.

Examples

```python
>>> folder = default_compilation_cache()
>>> folder is None or isinstance(folder, str)
True
```

pianistpy.runtime.get_cores()

Return the number of cores the package uses.

Returns:

**cores** – The integer last given to set_cores; for `"full"`, the count of
allowed_cores; for `"half"`, half of that count, at least 1;
for `"auto"`, the count of allowed_cores inside a batch job and
half of that count, at least 1, elsewhere.

Return type:

[int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)

See also

[`set_cores`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_cores)
Choose the number of cores the package uses.

Examples

```python
>>> set_cores(3)
>>> get_cores()
3
>>> set_cores("auto")
```

pianistpy.runtime.log_to_file(*path*, *level='debug'*)

Write the package’s messages during a `with` block to a file.

The file receives the messages in addition to the screen; the screen
keeps the session’s verbosity.

Parameters:

- **path** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)* or **path-like*) – The file the messages are appended to. The file is created if
path does not exist.

- **level** (*{"quiet"**, **"info"**, **"debug"}**, **optional*) – The verbosity of the file, with the meanings of set_verbosity.
Default: `"debug"`, which means every message is written.

Raises:

[**InputError**](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.InputError) – If level is not `"quiet"`, `"info"` or `"debug"`.

Return type:

[*Iterator*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Iterator)[None]

See also

[`set_verbosity`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_verbosity)
Choose the messages printed on the screen.

Examples

```python
>>> import os, tempfile
>>> path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "run.log")
>>> with log_to_file(path):
...     log.debug("A message for the file.")
>>> open(path).read()
'pianistpy DEBUG: A message for the file.\n'
```

pianistpy.runtime.peak_memory()

Return the largest resident memory of the Python process, in bytes.

The value counts the memory of the Python process on the host. Memory
held on a GPU is not counted.

Returns:

**peak** – The largest resident memory since the process started, in bytes;
None if the operating system does not report the value.

Return type:

[int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int) or None

See also

[`Timing`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.Timing)
The stage times and memory of one computation.

Examples

```python
>>> peak = peak_memory()
>>> peak is None or peak > 0
True
```

pianistpy.runtime.recent_messages()

Return the package’s most recent messages, oldest first.

The package keeps its 50 most recent messages at every verbosity, so
that the messages that led to an error can be read after a run at the
verbosity `"quiet"`.

Returns:

**messages** – Each message as printed: the logger’s name, the message’s level and
the message text.

Return type:

[tuple](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple) of [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

See also

[`set_verbosity`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_verbosity)
Choose the messages printed on the screen.

Examples

```python
>>> log.debug("A message kept at every verbosity.")
>>> recent_messages()[-1]
'pianistpy DEBUG: A message kept at every verbosity.'
```

pianistpy.runtime.platform()

Return the hardware JAX runs on.

A call of platform makes JAX choose its hardware if no computation
has chosen the hardware yet.

Returns:

**name** – JAX’s name of the hardware: `"cpu"`, `"gpu"`, or another name
that JAX reports.

Return type:

[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

See also

[`set_platform`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_platform)
Choose the hardware JAX runs on.

Examples

```python
>>> isinstance(platform(), str)
True
```

pianistpy.runtime.set_compilation_cache(*cache=True*, *max_size=None*)

Turn JAX’s persistent compilation cache on or off.

With the cache on, a later Python session reuses the code that an
earlier session compiled, which shortens every session after the first.
The cache changes no computed number. When the package is imported,
the cache is on, in the folder of default_compilation_cache, with no
bound on the folder’s size, unless `PIANISTPY_COMPILATION_CACHE`
turns the cache off.

A bound on the folder’s size slows every compilation: with a bound,
JAX locks the folder at every read and every write, and scans every
entry of the folder at every write. On a shared or network file
system, keep the folder unbounded.

Parameters:

- **cache** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)* or *[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)* or **path-like**, **optional*) – True for the folder of default_compilation_cache, or for
`~/.cache/pianistpy/jax` if the environment variable turns the
cache off; a path for another folder; False to turn the cache off.
Default: `True`.

- **max_size** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)* or **None**, **optional*) – The largest size of the folder, in bytes; above max_size, JAX
removes the oldest entries. Default: `None`, which means the
folder has no bound.

Returns:

**folder** – The folder the cache uses; None if the cache is off.

Return type:

[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) or None

See also

[`default_compilation_cache`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.default_compilation_cache)
The folder the cache uses by default.

Examples

```python
>>> on = default_compilation_cache() is not None
>>> set_compilation_cache(on) == default_compilation_cache()
True
```

pianistpy.runtime.set_cores(*value*)

Set the number of cores the package uses for parallel computations.

The number of cores changes no computed number: a result is the same,
bit for bit, for every value. Each parallel process of the package runs
one thread, so the number of cores is also the largest number of
parallel processes. The environment variable `PIANISTPY_CORES` sets
the value when the package is imported; with the variable unset, the
value is `"auto"`.

Parameters:

**value** (*{"auto"**, **"full"**, **"half"}** or *[*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – `"auto"` uses every core allowed_cores counts inside a batch job
and half of those cores, at least 1, elsewhere. `"full"` uses
every core allowed_cores counts. `"half"` uses half of those
cores, at least 1. A positive integer, or a string of digits, uses
that number of cores.

Raises:

[**InputError**](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.InputError) – If value is none of `"auto"`, `"full"`, `"half"` and a
    positive integer.

Return type:

None

See also

[`get_cores`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.get_cores)
The number of cores the package uses.

[`allowed_cores`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.allowed_cores)
The number of cores the process may use.

Examples

```python
>>> set_cores(2)
>>> get_cores()
2
>>> set_cores("auto")
```

pianistpy.runtime.set_platform(*name*)

Choose the hardware JAX runs on, before the session’s first
computation.

Every function of the package runs on the CPU alone (`"cpu"`), and
the CPU alone gives the same numbers on every machine. On a machine
with a GPU, results computed on the GPU and results computed on the CPU
differ at the level of rounding; each result file records the hardware
that computed the result.

JAX chooses its hardware at the first computation of the Python process
and keeps the choice for the rest of the process. A call of
set_platform after the first computation does not change the
hardware. To choose the hardware before the package is imported, set
the environment variable `PIANISTPY_PLATFORM`.

Parameters:

**name** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – `"auto"` leaves JAX’s own order: a usable GPU first, the CPU
otherwise. `"cpu"` runs on the CPU alone. `"gpu"` runs on a
CUDA GPU first and on the CPU second. Any other string is passed to
JAX as JAX’s platform list, for example `"rocm,cpu"`.

Raises:

[**InputError**](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.InputError) – If name is not a non-empty string.

Return type:

None

See also

[`platform`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.platform)
The hardware JAX runs on.

Examples

```python
>>> set_platform("")
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
pianistpy.exceptions.InputError: ...
```

pianistpy.runtime.set_timing(*enabled*)

Turn the printing of each computation’s stage times on or off.

The package measures the stage times of every computation and keeps
the times with the result, whether the printing is on or off. The
printing does not depend on the verbosity. The environment variable
`PIANISTPY_TIMING` turns the printing on when the package is imported
if the variable is `1`, `true`, `yes` or `on`.

Parameters:

**enabled** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – Whether the stage times are printed at the end of each computation.

Return type:

None

See also

[`timing_enabled`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.timing_enabled)
Whether the stage times are printed.

[`Timing`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.Timing)
The stage times of one computation.

Examples

```python
>>> set_timing(True)
>>> timing_enabled()
True
>>> set_timing(False)
```

pianistpy.runtime.set_verbosity(*level*)

Set which of the package’s messages are printed on the screen.

The verbosity holds for the rest of the session. The verbosity changes
no computed number. The environment variable `PIANISTPY_VERBOSITY`
sets the verbosity when the package is imported; with the variable
unset, the verbosity is `"quiet"`.

Parameters:

**level** (*{"quiet"**, **"info"**, **"debug"}*) – `"quiet"` prints warnings and errors only. `"info"` also prints
one line when each stage of a computation starts, and the messages
of results with relative error above \(10^{-6}\) and at most
\(10^{-4}\). `"debug"` also prints the details of each stage.

Raises:

[**InputError**](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.InputError) – If level is not `"quiet"`, `"info"` or `"debug"`.

Return type:

None

See also

[`log_to_file`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.log_to_file)
Write the messages of a block to a file.

[`recent_messages`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.recent_messages)
The most recent messages at every verbosity.

Examples

```python
>>> set_verbosity("info")
>>> set_verbosity("quiet")
```

pianistpy.runtime.timed(*stage*)

Time one stage of a computation in a `with` block.

The stage’s start is written to the log at level INFO and the stage’s
time at level DEBUG. Inside a timing_record block, the stage’s time
and the process’s largest memory are added to the record.

Parameters:

**stage** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The stage’s name.

Return type:

[*Iterator*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Iterator)[None]

See also

[`timing_record`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.timing_record)
Collect the stage times of a block.

Examples

```python
>>> with timed("example"):
...     pass
```

pianistpy.runtime.timing_enabled()

Return whether the stage times are printed at the end of each
computation.

Returns:

**enabled** – The value last given to set_timing.

Return type:

[bool](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)

See also

[`set_timing`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.set_timing)
Turn the printing of stage times on or off.

Examples

```python
>>> isinstance(timing_enabled(), bool)
True
```

pianistpy.runtime.timing_record()

Collect the stage times of the computation in a `with` block.

With the printing of stage times on (set_timing), the times are
printed when the block ends.

Yields:

**timing** (*Timing*) – The record to which each timed stage inside the block adds its
time and memory.

Return type:

[*Iterator*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Iterator)[[*Timing*](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.Timing)]

See also

[`timed`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.timed)
Time one stage.

[`Timing`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/runtime#pianistpy.runtime.Timing)
The stage times of one computation.

Examples

```python
>>> with timing_record() as record:
...     with timed("example"):
...         pass
>>> list(record.stages)
['example']
```

# Numerics

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/numerics

Module `pianistpy.numerics`

Gauss-Legendre quadrature and cubic Hermite interpolation.

A user calls gauss_legendre or gauss_legendre_unit for the nodes
\(x_j\) and weights \(w_j\) of the \(n\)-point Gauss-Legendre
rule, which integrates a polynomial of degree up to \(2n - 1\) exactly:

\[\int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,{\rm d}x \approx \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j f(x_j).\]

A user calls hermite for the piecewise cubic interpolant that takes given
values and slopes at given nodes, and hermite_inverse for the points where
an increasing piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant takes given values.

pianistpy.numerics.gauss_legendre(*n_nodes*)

Return the nodes and weights of the Gauss-Legendre rule on `[-1, 1]`.

The nodes and weights of each node count are computed once per Python
session and then reused. The arrays are read-only, so that no caller can
change the nodes or weights that another caller receives.

Parameters:

**n_nodes** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – Number of nodes \(n\). n_nodes must be 1 or larger.

Returns:

- **nodes** (*array, shape (n_nodes,)*) – Nodes \(x_j\) in increasing order, read-only.

- **weights** (*array, shape (n_nodes,)*) – Weights \(w_j\), read-only. The weights sum to 2.

Raises:

[**InputError**](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.InputError) – If n_nodes is smaller than 1.

Return type:

[tuple](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[*Any*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any), [*Any*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]

See also

[`gauss_legendre_unit`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/numerics#pianistpy.numerics.gauss_legendre_unit)
The Gauss-Legendre rule mapped to `[0, 1]`.

Notes

The \(n\)-point rule integrates every polynomial of degree up to
\(2n - 1\) exactly:

\[\int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,{\rm d}x \approx \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j f(x_j).\]

Examples

The 2-point rule integrates \(x^2\) over `[-1, 1]` to 2/3:

```python
>>> from pianistpy.numerics import gauss_legendre
>>> nodes, weights = gauss_legendre(2)
>>> float(weights.sum())
2.0
>>> round(float(weights @ nodes**2), 15)
0.666666666666667
```

pianistpy.numerics.gauss_legendre_unit(*n_nodes*)

Return the nodes and weights of the Gauss-Legendre rule on `[0, 1]`.

The nodes and weights are those of gauss_legendre mapped from
`[-1, 1]` to `[0, 1]`. The nodes and weights of each node count are
computed once per Python session and then reused, as read-only arrays.

Parameters:

**n_nodes** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – Number of nodes \(n\). n_nodes must be 1 or larger.

Returns:

- **nodes** (*array, shape (n_nodes,)*) – Nodes \(t_j = (x_j + 1)/2\) in increasing order, read-only, with
\(x_j\) the nodes of gauss_legendre.

- **weights** (*array, shape (n_nodes,)*) – Weights \(w_j/2\), read-only, with \(w_j\) the weights of
gauss_legendre. The weights sum to 1.

Raises:

[**InputError**](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/exceptions#pianistpy.exceptions.InputError) – If n_nodes is smaller than 1.

Return type:

[tuple](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[*Any*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any), [*Any*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]

See also

[`gauss_legendre`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/numerics#pianistpy.numerics.gauss_legendre)
The Gauss-Legendre rule on `[-1, 1]`.

Notes

The \(n\)-point rule integrates every polynomial of degree up to
\(2n - 1\) exactly:

\[\int_{0}^{1} f(t)\,{\rm d}t \approx \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{w_j}{2}\,
f(t_j).\]

Examples

The 1-point rule on `[0, 1]` has its node at 1/2 and its weight 1:

```python
>>> from pianistpy.numerics import gauss_legendre_unit
>>> nodes, weights = gauss_legendre_unit(1)
>>> nodes.tolist(), weights.tolist()
([0.5], [1.0])
```

pianistpy.numerics.hermite(*x*, *x_nodes*, *f_nodes*, *df_dx_nodes*)

Return the cubic Hermite interpolant and its derivative at given points.

Between two neighboring nodes, the interpolant is the cubic polynomial
that takes the given values and the given slopes at both nodes. Below
the first node and above the last node, the interpolant is the straight
line through the end node with the slope given at the end node. Between
the first and the last node, the interpolant reproduces every cubic
polynomial exactly.

Parameters:

- **x** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)* or **array-like*) – Points \(x\) at which the interpolant is evaluated, in the unit
of x_nodes.

- **x_nodes** (*array**, **shape** (**n**,**)*) – Nodes \(x_i\), strictly increasing, with \(n \ge 2\).

- **f_nodes** (*array**, **shape** (**n**,**)*) – Values \(f_i\) of the interpolant at the nodes, in the unit of
\(f\).

- **df_dx_nodes** (*array**, **shape** (**n**,**)*) – Slopes \(f'_i\) of the interpolant at the nodes, in the unit of
f_nodes per unit of x_nodes.

Returns:

- **f** (*array*) – The interpolant at x, with the shape of x.

- **df_dx** (*array*) – The derivative of the interpolant in \(x\) at x, with the
shape of x.

Return type:

[tuple](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[*Any*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any), [*Any*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]

See also

[`hermite_inverse`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/numerics#pianistpy.numerics.hermite_inverse)
The points where an increasing interpolant takes given values.

Notes

On the interval \(x_i \le x \le x_{i+1}\), with
\(h = x_{i+1} - x_i\) and \(t = (x - x_i)/h\), the interpolant
is

\[f(x) = (2t^3 - 3t^2 + 1) f_i + (t^3 - 2t^2 + t)\,h f'_i
+ (-2t^3 + 3t^2) f_{i+1} + (t^3 - t^2)\,h f'_{i+1}.\]

Examples

The cubic \(x^3\) is reproduced exactly from its values and slopes
at the two nodes 0 and 2:

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from pianistpy.numerics import hermite
>>> x_nodes = np.array([0.0, 2.0])
>>> f, df_dx = hermite(1.0, x_nodes, x_nodes**3, 3.0 * x_nodes**2)
>>> float(f), float(df_dx)
(1.0, 3.0)
```

pianistpy.numerics.hermite_inverse(*f*, *x_nodes*, *f_nodes*, *df_dx_nodes*)

Return the points where an increasing cubic Hermite interpolant takes values f.

The interpolant is the cubic Hermite interpolant that hermite
evaluates. Each point is found between the two neighboring nodes whose
values enclose the given value, or on the straight line beyond an end
node for a value outside the values at the nodes. For a value between
the values at two neighboring nodes, the returned point lies between
the two nodes, or outside the two nodes by less than \(10^{-12}\)
plus \(2^{-60}\) times the distance between the two nodes, in the
unit of x_nodes.

Parameters:

- **f** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)* or **array-like*) – Values of the interpolant for which the points are sought, in the
unit of f_nodes.

- **x_nodes** (*array**, **shape** (**n**,**)*) – Nodes, strictly increasing, with n of 2 or more.

- **f_nodes** (*array**, **shape** (**n**,**)*) – Values of the interpolant at the nodes, increasing.

- **df_dx_nodes** (*array**, **shape** (**n**,**)*) – Slopes of the interpolant at the nodes, in the unit of f_nodes
per unit of x_nodes. The slopes at the first and the last node
must be positive.

Returns:

- **x** (*array*) – Points at which the interpolant equals f, with the shape of f,
in the unit of x_nodes.

- **residual** (*float*) – Largest absolute difference between the interpolant at x and f,
in the unit of f_nodes.

Return type:

[tuple](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[*Any*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any), [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]

See also

[`hermite`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/numerics#pianistpy.numerics.hermite)
The interpolant and its derivative.

Examples

The interpolant of the line \(f = 2x\) takes the value 1.5 at
\(x = 0.75\):

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from pianistpy.numerics import hermite_inverse
>>> x_nodes = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0])
>>> x, residual = hermite_inverse(1.5, x_nodes, 2.0 * x_nodes, np.full(3, 2.0))
>>> float(x), residual
(0.75, 0.0)
```


---

# Numerical settings

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/settings

Every numerical setting of the package is a field of `pianistpy.Settings`. The tables below list each
field, its value under the default settings and under the quick settings ([Accuracy](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/accuracy)),
and what the field controls. The fields fall in five groups, one table each: `inversion`, `truncation`,
`sampling`, `observables` and `losvd`.

An override of a field, such as `pp.Settings(inversion={"n_nodes": 256})`, raises
`InputError` when the group or the field’s name is unknown. An override also
raises `InputError` when the value has the wrong type, or when the value is not positive for a
field that must be positive.

## inversion

Field

Default

Quick

What it controls

`n_nodes`

500

same

The number of Gauss-Legendre nodes of the integral that inverts the density into the distribution function.

`n_grid_rows`

1000

same

The number of energies in the middle zone of the inversion’s energy grid, where the energies are spaced linearly.

`n_grid_tail_rows`

3000

same

The number of energies in each of the two end zones of the inversion’s energy grid, where the energies are spaced logarithmically toward the grid’s floor and toward the grid’s top.

`grid_tail_extent`

0.03

same

The width of each end zone of the inversion’s energy grid, as a fraction of the central potential.

`table_nodes_per_decade`

50

same

The number of energies per decade below the floor of the inversion’s energy grid, down to the floor of the distribution function’s table.

`n_floor_nodes`

240

same

The number of Gauss-Legendre nodes, in ln P, of the integral that completes the distribution function below the table’s floor; a third of the nodes, and at least 40 nodes, lie near the floor.

## truncation

Field

Default

Quick

What it controls

`n_source_nodes`

500

same

The number of Gauss-Legendre nodes in each of the two intervals of the quadrature that computes the auxiliary density on the source grid.

`n_source_rows`

12000

same

The number of potential values of the source grid.

`n_source_tail_rows`

3000

same

The number of potential values in each logarithmic tail of the source grid, toward the grid’s floor and toward the grid’s top; each tail holds at most a third of the source grid’s potential values.

`source_tail_extent`

0.03

same

The largest width of each tail of the source grid, as a fraction of the grid’s top; the width used is at most a hundredth of the grid’s top.

`source_tail_floor`

1.20401e-08

same

The smallest start of the source grid’s lower tail and the smallest width of the source grid’s upper tail, as fractions of the grid’s top.

`quadrature_split`

0.9

same

The fraction of the potential at which the first interval of the source quadrature ends and the second interval begins.

`quadrature_stretch`

2

same

The power k of the map Q = P - u^k on the second interval of the source quadrature, where the exponent of the quadrature’s kernel is not negative.

`ode_rtol`

1e-11

same

The relative tolerance of the integration of Poisson’s equation.

`ode_atol`

1e-11

same

The absolute tolerance of the integration of Poisson’s equation.

`n_rows_inner`

500

same

The number of radii of the Poisson solve’s grid inside the inner zone.

`n_rows_outer`

59500

same

The number of radii of the Poisson solve’s grid outside the inner zone.

`log10_r_min`

-9

same

The base-10 logarithm of the innermost radius of the Poisson solve, in internal length units.

`log10_r_max`

12

same

The base-10 logarithm of the outermost radius of the Poisson solve, in internal length units. A computation raises the outermost radius until the potential at the outermost radius is below half the floor, and the result records the value used.

`continuation_start`

0.01

same

The fraction of the central potential below which the outermost radii of a truncated model are solved again on a grid geometric in R_t - r, where R_t is the truncation radius.

`continuation_rows_per_decade`

1200

same

The number of radii per decade of R_t - r in the solve toward the truncation radius R_t.

`continuation_floor_fraction`

0.02

same

The potential at the outermost radius of the solve toward the truncation radius, as a fraction of the floor.

`profile_bin_decades`

0.1

same

The width, in decades of the potential, of each bin in which the profile’s radii are counted.

`profile_rows_per_decade`

1000

same

The smallest number of radii per decade of the potential, and per decade of the depth, that the profile keeps at the profile’s two ends; the profile’s fills supply the other radii.

## sampling

Field

Default

Quick

What it controls

`n_rows`

512

same

The number of potential values of the velocity table at the start of the table’s refinement; the number doubles until the table’s own error across potential values is below row_error_goal or until the number reaches n_rows_max.

`n_rows_max`

4075

same

The largest number of potential values of the velocity table; the table’s refinement stops at n_rows_max potential values.

`n_nodes`

2048

512

The number of nodes at each potential value of the velocity table.

`n_velocity_intervals`

200

same

The number of intervals in the scaled velocity over which the velocity distribution is integrated at each potential value of the velocity table.

`n_gauss_legendre`

16

8

The number of Gauss-Legendre nodes of each panel of the velocity integrals.

`panels_per_decade`

8

same

The number of panels per decade of the local variable where the velocity integrals refine toward the two ends of the velocity range at one potential value and inside each interval.

`velocity_low_refined`

1e-09

same

The smallest scaled velocity that the velocity integrals refine in panels; below that velocity, the density follows the density’s power law in the velocity and is integrated in closed form.

`edge_refined`

1e-12

same

The distance from the edge of the velocity range, relative to the edge, down to which the velocity integrals refine in panels; closer to the edge, the distribution function’s form below the distribution function’s table is integrated in closed form.

`radius_edge_refined`

1e-10

same

The smallest fraction of the mass beyond a radius that the radius table of a model with a sharp edge resolves in nodes; for smaller fractions, the mass follows the mass’s power law in the distance from the edge.

`n_radius_nodes`

2048

same

The number of nodes of the radius table.

`n_angle_nodes`

1024

same

The number of nodes of each half of the angle table, spaced uniformly in the logarithm of the cumulative probability from the half’s end.

`draw_block`

262144

same

The number of particles drawn at once. A draw runs over blocks of draw_block particles, so the draw’s working memory, above the memory of the drawn particles, is the memory of one block: about 0.75 kB per particle, or about 0.2 GB for \(2^{18}\) particles. The drawn particles do not depend on draw_block.

`row_error_goal`

1e-06

0.0001

The error across the potential values of the velocity table at which the table’s refinement stops: the number of potential values doubles until the table’s own error is below row_error_goal or until the number reaches n_rows_max.

`tail_mass_min`

1e-18

same

The smallest cumulative probability tabulated at either end of a table. The smallest nonzero value of a uniform random double is \(2^{-53}\), which is above tail_mass_min, so a draw never reads beyond the tabulated range.

## observables

Field

Default

Quick

What it controls

`n_radii`

10000

500

The number of projected radii of the projection table before the table’s check between projected radii adds projected radii; the projected radii are spaced logarithmically from the innermost radius of the profile to the edge.

`profile_tolerance`

1e-07

1e-06

The relative error of sigma_r at which radii stop being added to the radial dispersion’s profile: sigma_r at the midpoint of every interval between the profile’s radii is read within profile_tolerance. The default value, \(10^{-7}\), is a tenth of \(10^{-6}\): the profile’s share of the error of the quantities projected from the profile.

`n_profile_start`

100

same

The number of radii, spaced logarithmically from the innermost radius of the profile to the edge, with which the radial dispersion’s profile starts before radii are added to meet profile_tolerance.

`n_jeans_nodes`

500

same

The number of Gauss-Legendre nodes of the Jeans integral of the radial dispersion at one radius, as the superposition of components computes the radial dispersion. The observables’ profile does not use n_jeans_nodes: the profile sums panels between the profile’s radii and doubles each panel’s nodes until sigma_r changes by less than profile_tolerance.

`n_projection_nodes`

`rows_route`

kernel

The computation of the angle rule of the line-of-sight velocity distributions: “kernel” computes the angle rule with JAX, and “numpy” computes the angle rule with NumPy, as a reference.

`n_velocity_angle_nodes`

`velocity_tolerance`

1e-06

0.0001

The bound on the change of the local velocity distribution (pdf_v) when the nodes of the distribution’s angle rule double: the nodes double, at most three times, until the change is below velocity_tolerance.

The value 0 keeps the table out to the model’s edge.

Settings levels: `default`, `quick`. A field is overridden by its group and its name, for example `pp.Settings(inversion={'n_nodes': 800})`. A result computed with an overridden field records that its settings are custom, and lists the fields that differ from the settings level.

# Code and paper notations

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/symbols

The package’s identifiers follow the notation of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758). A quantity with a symbol in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758) or in the
Technical notes is called `<family>_<symbol>`. The family prefix gives the kind of quantity, and the rest of the
name is the symbol or the symbol’s subscript in lower case. A truncated quantity (hatted in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758)) takes the
suffix `_trunc`, as in `p_trunc`, `df_trunc`, `rho_trunc` and `mass_trunc`. The untruncated quantity
keeps the name without the suffix. Every docstring gives the
symbol beside the name the first time the docstring describes the quantity.

Family

Prefix

Names

Paper

density and its parameters

`rho_`

`rho`, `rho_aux`, `rho_alpha`, `rho_beta`, `rho_gamma`, `rho_norm`

\(\varrho\), \(\varrho_{\rm aux}\), \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\), \(C\)

anisotropy

`beta_`

`beta_c`, `beta_sigma`

\(\beta_{\rm c}\), \(\beta_\sigma\)

radii

`r_`

`r`, `r_a`, `r_t`, `r_2d`, `r_off`, `r_ape`

\(R\), \(R_{\rm a}\), \(R_{\rm t}\), \(R_{\rm 2D}\), \(R_{\rm off}\), \(R_{\rm ape}\)

relative potential

`p_`

`p`, `p_0`

\(P\), \(P_0\)

energy-like variables

`k_`, `q_`

`k`, `k_t`, `q`, `q_min`, `q_0`

\(\mathcal{K}\), \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\), \(\mathcal{Q}\), \(\mathcal{Q}_{\rm min}\), \(\mathcal{Q}_0\)

distribution function

`df_`

`df`, `df_k`

\(F\), \(F_\mathcal{K}\)

mass

`mass_`

`mass`, `mass_t`, `mass_0`

\(\mathcal{M}\), \(M_{\rm t}\), \(M_0\)

order of the inversion

`order_`

`order_m`, `order_n`

\((m, n)\)

velocities and dispersions

`v_`, `sigma_`

`v_r`, `v_t`, `v_los`, `v_esc`, `sigma_r`, `sigma_t`, `sigma_los`

\(V_{\rm r}\), \(V_{\rm t}\), \(V_{\rm los}\), \(V_{\rm esc}\), \(\sigma_{\rm r}\), \(\sigma_{\rm t}\), \(\sigma_{\rm los}\)

probability densities

`pdf_`

`pdf_v`

\(p(V \,|\, R)\)

Where the letter of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758) cannot serve as a name, a fixed word replaces the letter. The normalization \(C\) of the
density is `rho_norm`, since `rho_c` would read as a central density. The concentration \(c\) is
`concentration`. The letter `c` alone is never a name. As a subscript, `c` means central (`beta_c`).

Example

`r_grid`, `df_grid`

boolean

`is_`, `has_` prefix

`is_physical`, `has_edge`

The three unit systems are `internal`, `model` and `physical` ([Units](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/units)).

# Accuracy tables

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/accuracy

The accuracy tables below record the relative error of extensive “roundtrip” tests over a grid of systematically
varying input density profiles and anisotropy models. In each test, the package first
numerically computes the distribution function inverted from the input density profile \(\varrho\); the density
profile \(\varrho_{\rm inv}\) numerically evaluated from that distribution function is then compared against
the analytical input (the truth). Each cell reports the relative error
\(|(\varrho_{\rm inv} - \varrho)/\varrho|\) over \(10^{-8} < R < 10^{8}\), with \(R\) in units of the
profile’s scale radius. The column heads give the anisotropy models: OM is
Osipkov-Merritt and COM is Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt, of Type I or Type II ([Velocity anisotropy](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/anisotropy)). A cell
shows one of three outcomes:

- the error’s **maximum** (bold) and **median** (gray), and the result’s **tier** ([Accuracy](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/accuracy)); a
cell without a tier is silent. The tier comes from every check of the result, so a tier can be higher than the
cell’s error alone gives.

- **error** and the exception’s class, where the package raises an exception instead of returning a result:
`UnphysicalModelError` where no physical equilibrium exists for the model’s parameters,
`InputError` where the parameters are outside what the package supports, and
`AccuracyError` where the package cannot compute the model to the required accuracy. The
exception’s full message is in the cell’s tooltip and in the CSV.

- **excluded**, where the model violates the Cusp Slope–Central Anisotropy theorem
([An & Evans 2006b](https://doi.org/10.1086/501040)), which requires the inner slope of the density
profile, \(\gamma\), to be at least twice the central velocity anisotropy, \(\beta_{\rm c}\) (i.e.,
\(\gamma \ge 2\beta_{\rm c}\)). The model is still
computed and recorded in the CSV.

The distribution function of an untruncated Type II model is defined only at energies above
\(P(R_{\rm a})\), the relative potential at the anisotropy radius \(R_{\rm a}\). The cell of such a model
gives the tier that the package reports at energies above \(P(R_{\rm a})\), with the note “support above
\(P(R_{\rm a})\)”. Below \(P(R_{\rm a})\), the density \(\varrho_{\rm inv}\) does not measure the
distribution function’s accuracy, so the cell gives no error values.

A † marks a cell whose outcome differs from the outcome that the CSV’s `expected outcome` column states for the
model. The tables use the default settings level. The
downloadable files below hold every radial range the grid reads and the radius of each maximum, for the default
and the quick settings level. The counts of each release are on [Accuracy by release](https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/accuracy).

The grid of ver. 1.0.0 with the default settings level; the files that hold it, with the quick level’s grid, are listed under [The downloadable files](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/accuracy#the-downloadable-files) below.

## Limiting cases

Anisotropies and truncations at the edges of the supported range (columns): the limit of the Cusp Slope-Central Anisotropy theorem ([An & Evans 2006b](https://doi.org/10.1086/501040)), the degenerate and steep constant anisotropies, and a small anisotropy radius inside a deep truncation. The rows include an outer slope of 2.5, which the package refuses.

\({\beta_{\rm c} = \gamma/2}\)
\({\beta_{\rm c} = -1/2 + 10^{-7}}\)
\({\beta_{\rm c} = -1}\)
\({\beta_{\rm c} = -1.5}\)
\({\beta_{\rm c} = +0.75}\)
OM I \({R_{\rm a} = 0.3}\) \({\mathcal{K}_{\rm t} = 0.01}\)
\({\beta_{\rm c} = -1/2}\) \({\mathcal{K}_{\rm t} = 0.3}\)

## The downloadable files

The grid of ver. 1.0.0 is published as three files, each of which opens with a comment block that repeats the definitions below (`#` lines, which `pandas.read_csv(path, comment='#')` skips):

- [`grid_default.csv`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/_downloads/6f15053f3a7f4c7d100c986afa508c4e/grid_default.csv): the grid with the default settings level. One row is one model of the grid.

- [`grid_quick.csv`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/_downloads/2e7555df8c0babbc2a009c85f6173c54/grid_quick.csv): the same grid with the quick settings level, in the same columns.

- [`members.csv`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/_downloads/962e66e37a969157210bdebc01173211/members.csv): the list of the grid’s models with the place of each in the tables above and the outcome the grid expects of it. One row is one model.

The columns of the grid files, in their order:

`model`
the model’s key in the grid: its table (T1 the main grid, T2 anisotropy radius, T3 truncation energy, T4 limiting cases, the sections of the Accuracy tables page), its profile, its anisotropy model and its truncation

`settings level`
the settings level of the run: “default” or “quick” (the two tested levels of pianistpy.Settings)

`truncation method`
1 where the distribution function is inverted from the model’s own density (Method I, with or without a truncation); 2 where the model is a Method II model, the distribution function inverted from the truncated density of a Method I model

`anisotropy model`
the velocity anisotropy model: “iso” (isotropic), “constant” (constant anisotropy \(\beta_{\rm c}\)), “OM_I” and “OM_II” (Osipkov-Merritt of Type I and Type II), “COM_I” and “COM_II” (Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt of Type I and Type II)

`alpha`
the transition sharpness of the double power law

`beta`
the outer slope of the double power law

`gamma`
the inner slope of the double power law

`beta_c`
the central velocity anisotropy; 0 for the isotropic and the Osipkov-Merritt models

`r_a`
the anisotropy radius in scale radii; blank for the isotropic and the constant-anisotropy models

`k_t`
the truncation energy as a fraction of the central potential; blank for an untruncated model

`source model`
for a Method II model, the Method I model whose truncated density it is built on (its profile, anisotropy model and truncation energy); blank otherwise

`expected outcome`
what the grid expects of the model: “value” (a result is served), “value: not physical” (a result is served for a model that is not a physical equilibrium), “value: the Method I model’s DF within \(10^{-6}\), read by the package’s rule” (a Method II model whose distribution function equals its Method I model’s), or a refusal with the error the package raises (its kind, then the opening words of its message)

`physical`
whether the model is a physical equilibrium by the grid’s own criteria: True, False, or blank where the model is refused before the criteria apply; a result can be served for a model that is not physical

`outcome`
what the package did: “value” (the model was computed and the error of the density computed back from its distribution function measured); “refused: the package’s tier (checks)” (the model was computed and its validation report is in the tier refused, with the checks beyond \(10^{-2}\) listed); “refusal: <error>: <message>” (the package raised that error; no model exists)

`outcome as expected`
True where the outcome is the expected outcome, False where it is not (the Accuracy tables page marks such a cell)

`tier`
the tier of the model’s validation report: silent, every check at most \(10^{-6}\); recorded, at most \(10^{-4}\); warned, at most \(10^{-2}\); refused, beyond \(10^{-2}\); blank where the model is refused before a report exists

`tier of the distribution function`
the tier of the distribution function’s own report, read as the model’s tier (the model’s tier is at least this one, since a model’s report carries its distribution function’s checks)

`lowest energy of the support`
for a Type II model without a truncation, the energy \(P(R_{\rm a})\), as a fraction of the central potential, above which its distribution function is defined; the errors are read over that support only; blank otherwise

`median relative error, 1e-4 < R < 1e4`
the median over the radii \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{4}\) (\(R\) in scale radii) of the relative error of the density computed back from the distribution function against the model’s density; blank where no result exists

`maximum relative error, 1e-4 < R < 1e4`
the maximum of the same relative error over the radii \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{4}\)

`radius of the maximum, 1e-4 < R < 1e4`
the radius, in scale radii, at which the maximum over \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{4}\) is taken

`number of radii, 1e-4 < R < 1e4`
the number of radii over which the error is read in \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{4}\)

`radii with a non-finite error, 1e-4 < R < 1e4`
the number of those radii at which the computed density is not finite; 0 where every radius is finite

`median relative error, 1e-4 < R < 1e5`
the median over the radii \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{5}\) (\(R\) in scale radii) of the relative error of the density computed back from the distribution function against the model’s density; blank where no result exists

`maximum relative error, 1e-4 < R < 1e5`
the maximum of the same relative error over the radii \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{5}\)

`radius of the maximum, 1e-4 < R < 1e5`
the radius, in scale radii, at which the maximum over \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{5}\) is taken

`number of radii, 1e-4 < R < 1e5`
the number of radii over which the error is read in \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{5}\)

`radii with a non-finite error, 1e-4 < R < 1e5`
the number of those radii at which the computed density is not finite; 0 where every radius is finite

`median relative error, 1e-8 < R < 1e8`
the median over the radii \(10^{-8} < R < 10^{8}\) (\(R\) in scale radii) of the relative error of the density computed back from the distribution function against the model’s density; blank where no result exists

`maximum relative error, 1e-8 < R < 1e8`
the maximum of the same relative error over the radii \(10^{-8} < R < 10^{8}\)

`radius of the maximum, 1e-8 < R < 1e8`
the radius, in scale radii, at which the maximum over \(10^{-8} < R < 10^{8}\) is taken

`number of radii, 1e-8 < R < 1e8`
the number of radii over which the error is read in \(10^{-8} < R < 10^{8}\)

`radii with a non-finite error, 1e-8 < R < 1e8`
the number of those radii at which the computed density is not finite; 0 where every radius is finite

`refusal of the distribution function`
the package’s message where it refused to compute the model’s distribution function; blank where it did not

`refusal of the truncation`
the package’s message where it refused a truncation of the model: for a truncated model, its own truncation; for an untruncated model, the grid’s probe that asks the package to truncate it (a profile whose total mass diverges, outer slope at most 3, and a Type II model whose support ends at the anisotropy’s domain edge are refused by design); blank where nothing was refused

`refusal of the density check`
the package’s message where the density could not be computed back from the distribution function (a distribution function that is negative somewhere has no logarithm); blank otherwise

The columns of the model list, in their order:

`model`
the model’s key, as in the grid files

`table`
the table of the Accuracy tables page the model is in: 1 the main grid, 2 anisotropy radius, 3 truncation energy, 4 limiting cases (the page’s sections)

`row`
the key of the model’s row in that table, as the page labels it

`column`
the key of the model’s column in that table, as the page labels it

`alpha`
the transition sharpness of the double power law

`beta`
the outer slope of the double power law

`gamma`
the inner slope of the double power law

`anisotropy model`
the velocity anisotropy model, as in the grid files

`beta_c`
the central velocity anisotropy

`r_a`
the anisotropy radius in scale radii; blank where the model has none

`truncation method`
1 or 2, as in the grid files

`k_t`
the truncation energy as a fraction of the central potential; blank for an untruncated model

`source model`
for a Method II model, the Method I model it is built on; blank otherwise

`expected outcome`
what the grid expects of the model, as in the grid files


---

# Technical notes

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/notes

The Technical notes detail the analytical and numerical treatments implemented in PIANISTpy, building upon the high-level overviews provided in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758). The Technical notes follow and refer to the notations, equations, and results of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758). The Technical notes are organized by the objects of the pipeline, from upstream to downstream, and each object-specific section first treats the analytical theory (whenever applicable) and then the accompanying numerical implementations. [Section T:0](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/principles#tn-sec-principles) states the conventions and notations used; we then discuss the input potential-density models ([Section T:1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-model)), the distribution function ([Section T:2](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-df)), the truncation ([Section T:3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation#tn-sec-truncation)), the linear superposition of components ([Section T:4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sup#tn-sec-sup)), the particle sampling ([Section T:5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sampling#tn-sec-sampling)), the velocity profiles and projections ([Section T:6](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables#tn-sec-observables)), and the JAX-based gradients ([Section T:7](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients#tn-sec-gradients)). [Section T:8](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/verification#tn-sec-verification) documents the accuracy and validation tests and related information.

This document was last updated on October 21, 2026. Section, equation and table numbers of the Technical notes carry the prefix T: (Section T:2.3, Eq. (T:2.4), Table T:2.1). The [Functions by subpackage](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/api/index) page gives the form in which the docstrings cite the Technical notes.

# T:0 Principles and conventions

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/principles

## T:0.1 Notation

We adopt the notation of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758). The relative potential is \(P\), with the central value \(P_0\); the energy-like variable is \(\mathcal{K}\); the distribution function (DF) is \(F(\mathcal{K}, L) = F_\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{K})\,L^{-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\); the density is the double power law of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (5) with exponents \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\); and \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) is the auxiliary density, which for the (C)OM models is given by [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B23). Three derived quantities are used throughout these notes. The first is the order of the inversion,

\begin{equation}
  \nu \equiv \tfrac{3}{2} - \beta_\mathrm{c} = m + n, \qquad m \equiv \lfloor \nu \rfloor, \qquad 0 \leq n < 1 ,
  \tag{T:0.1}
\end{equation}
and the other two are the exponent of the inner expansion and the depth below the center,

\begin{equation}
  \delta \equiv \frac{\alpha}{2-\gamma}, \qquad u \equiv P_0 - \mathcal{K} .
  \tag{T:0.2}
\end{equation}
Internally, every model is expressed in the units of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), in which the scale radius and the central potential of the untruncated profile are both unity; a truncated model therefore has \(P_0 = 1 - \mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\). The depth \(u\) is carried as a variable of its own wherever the difference \(P_0 - \mathcal{K}\) would lose significant digits.

## T:0.2 Thresholds derived from the inputs

Every threshold that judges a result is one of the three levels of [Section T:0.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/principles#tn-sec-tiers) or a stated fraction of \(10^{-6}\), and it is derived from the problem at hand wherever the problem gives one; the method’s remaining fixed numbers, such as the floor and the gap of the energy grid ([Section T:0.4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/principles#tn-sec-host)), are its own and change with no settings level. For example, the depth at which a table ends is the depth at which the exact derivatives leave the range of a double ([Section T:2.5.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-top)); the radius out to which the inner series is trusted is the radius at which its next term reaches the tolerance ([Section T:1.2.2](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-series)). A settings level changes only node counts and tolerances; of the runtime options, verbosity, timing and cores change no number, and the device can, since the order of summation on a GPU is not the CPU’s ([Section T:7.3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients#tn-sec-tangent-rows)). Whatever cannot be computed is refused by an error that states the reason; a refused truncation carries the DF it started from, and a model refused after it is built carries the model, as the error’s result. Nothing is silently approximated.

## T:0.3 Closed forms, symbolic derivatives and arbitrary precision

Wherever a quantity has a closed form, we use that closed form, and we form its derivatives symbolically rather than by finite differences. The derivatives of the auxiliary density with respect to the potential are built by computer algebra from the closed-form density, enclosed mass, and anisotropy factor ([Section T:1.2.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-derivatives)).
