They are evaluated in double precision where that evaluation is stable, and in arbitrary precision where it suffers from cancellation: at small and at large radii, at high orders far out, and within a band around \(R_\mathrm{a}\) for a Type II model. The coefficients of the central series of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) are exact ([Section T:2.2.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-center)); the amplitude of the central term of the DF is a closed form; and the enclosed mass is the incomplete Beta function, evaluated in arbitrary precision where its closed form fails. Every exact form is checked against an arbitrary-precision reference in the test suite ([Section T:8](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/verification#tn-sec-verification)).

## T:0.4 Limits of double precision and of the energy grid

Two limits of double precision are read from the host rather than assumed, and the energy grid has fixed ends of its own. The energy grid has a floor at \(q_0 = 10^{-10}\) in units of \(P_0\), and it ends at a gap of \(10^{-9}\) below \(P_0\), which is the depth at which energies are still separable from the center; no node lies above this gap, and the closed form of the center carries the DF beyond the last node ([Section T:2.5.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-top)). The top of a table may end deeper still, at the deepest of three depths: the depth at which the exact derivatives needed by the inversion exceed the largest double, the depth at the smallest radius whose square the host can represent (\(2^{-537}\) with subnormals), and the depth at which the closed form of the center exceeds \(10^{300}\). All three are computed from the model and the host alone. Near the center, the depth is formed without subtraction, from the inner series ([Section T:1.2.2](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-series)) and, in the lookup, from node differences that are exact by Sterbenz’s lemma ([Section T:2.5.4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-lookup)).

## T:0.5 Accuracy tiers, settings levels, and devices

Every product is judged against three levels of relative error: \(10^{-6}\), \(10^{-4}\), and \(10^{-2}\). A check at most \(10^{-6}\) is silent. A check above \(10^{-6}\) and at most \(10^{-4}\) is recorded: its tier stays attached to the result and one line is written to the log. A check above \(10^{-4}\) is returned with a warning that stays attached to the result and to everything computed from it. A check beyond \(10^{-2}\) refuses the result, unless the settings explicitly ask for it. The four tiers are silent, recorded, warned, and refused. Every result carries a report with a fixed set of checks ([Section T:8.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/verification#tn-sec-reports)); a derived result holds its own checks together with the worst tier of the results it was computed from, never a copy of their reports. With the default settings, a component of a product that feeds a projected quantity is held to a fraction of \(10^{-6}\), \(10^{-7}\) or \(10^{-8}\) as stated where it is used, which is its share of the error budget of what is computed from it.

Two settings levels are tested, the default settings and the quick settings for exploration. Both report the same checks, the test suite runs both, and the quick settings change only node counts and tolerances. The CPU-only mode gives the same numbers on every machine, and every result file records the versions and the backend of the session that wrote it. A stage whose wall time scales with a sequential count (the steps of a solve, or rows computed one at a time) is latency-bound on a GPU, and it therefore stays on the CPU on every device; a stage whose wall time scales with a batch (the velocity table, the particle draw) runs on a GPU when one is present. The rows of the line-of-sight tables are computed in a pool of CPU processes, each process taking one row at a time. This classification rests on measured scaling, with no margin constant.


---

# T:1 The potential–density pair and the auxiliary density

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model

## T:1.1 The potential–radius relation as P → P₀ and P → 0

The potential of the double power law is given in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (A3), and its inner and outer expansions in Eq. (A11) and Eq. (A13). Two consequences of those expansions are used below.

*Near the center*, \(P_0 - P \propto R^{2-\gamma}\,[1 + \mathcal{O}(R^{\alpha})]\). Since \(R^{\alpha} \propto (P_0-P)^{\delta}\), any function of \(R\) that is a series in \(R^{\alpha}\) is also a series in \((P_0 - P)^{\delta}\):

\begin{equation}
  R^{\alpha} \propto (P_0 - P)^{\delta}\left[1 + \mathcal{O}\!\left((P_0-P)^{\delta}\right)\right] .
  \tag{T:1.1}
\end{equation}
The coefficients of such a series are exact, and no fit is needed. The depth \(P_0 - P\) is itself a series in \(R^{\alpha}\) with known coefficients, [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (A11). Inverting that series order by order gives \(R = t\,[1 + S(t)]\), with \(t \propto (P_0-P)^{1/(2-\gamma)}\) and \(S\) a series in \(t^{\alpha}\). Substituting this inverse into the density and into the anisotropy factor of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) yields the coefficient of every power \(s\) of \(P_0 - P\) as \(C\,c_u^{-s}\), with \(c_u = C/[(2-\gamma)(3-\gamma)]\), times a finite sum of products of generalized binomial coefficients, of the depth’s relative coefficients \((2-\gamma)(3-\gamma)\binom{e}{k}/[(2-\gamma+k\alpha)(3-\gamma+k\alpha)]\), \(e = (\gamma-\beta)/\alpha\), and, for the OM and COM factors, of powers of \(\pm R_\mathrm{a}^{-2}\). The package forms these coefficients in closed form by a power-series algebra, keeping every term up to the power \(3\max(\alpha, 2)\) of \(t\) beyond the leading power, that is, up to \((P_0-P)^{3\max(\alpha,2)/(2-\gamma)}\) beyond the leading power of \(P_0 - P\).

*At large radii*, the potential of an untruncated profile behaves as

\begin{equation}
  P \propto \begin{cases} R^{-1} & (\beta > 3),\\
   R^{-1}\ln R & (\beta = 3),\\
   R^{-(\beta-2)} & (2 < \beta < 3). \end{cases}
  \tag{T:1.2}
\end{equation}

## T:1.2 Derivatives of the auxiliary density

### T:1.2.1 Exact derivatives with respect to the potential

The inversion with the order pair \((j, n')\) of [Eq. (T:2.16)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-unified-pair) requires \(\mathrm{d}^k\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d}P^k\) up to \(k = j+1\) (\(k = j = m\) at \(n = 0\)), that is up to \(m+1\), or \(m+2\) for a replaced pair; Method I reads one order higher as well, as the slope of its source and as the source of the slope of the DF. In Method I the profile is analytical and these derivatives are exact. The operator

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} P} = -\frac{R^2}{M(R)}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} R},
  \tag{T:1.3}
\end{equation}
with the closed-form enclosed mass \(M(R)\) of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (A7), is applied symbolically to the closed-form auxiliary density \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}(R) = \varrho(R)\,h(R)\), where \(h = R^{2\beta_\mathrm{c}}(1 \pm R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2)^{s}\) is the inverse of the anisotropy factor (\(s = 1\) for OM, \(s = 1 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\) for COM, and \(s = 0\) otherwise). The result is evaluated at \(R(P)\), which we obtain by bisection in \(\ln R\) on the monotonic \(P(R)\) and, near the center, on the subtraction-free depth. The potential \(P(R)\) does not enter the derivatives’ expressions, which hold \(M(R)\) only; its closed form, [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (A3), enters only through the radius \(R(P)\) at which they are evaluated. A single expression of \(h\) serves every closed-form evaluation of the factor in the package: the Method I sources, the Method II sources, the edge law, the density of the Poisson solve, and the parameter derivatives of [Section T:7](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients#tn-sec-gradients); the inner series of [Section T:1.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-pair) and its parameter derivatives expand the same factor as a binomial series in \(R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2\), and the central deficit of [Section T:3.4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation#tn-sec-fills) writes the factor’s logarithmic step and slope out by hand. In Method II the input is a tabulated pair, and the derivatives are integrals of the Method I model’s DF ([Section T:2.6](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-tabulated)).

Our first design for the tabulated case was a spline of \(\ln{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}}\) in \(P\) with knots placed by the equidistribution principle ([de Boor 1978](https://link.springer.com/book/9780387953663)). Its derivatives of second and higher order carried the conditioning of the spline, which grows as the square of the ratio of its largest to its smallest knot spacing, into the inversion. The exact and integral forms replaced it.

### T:1.2.2 Inner series expansions and their range of validity

Near the center, the density is its closed form, and the enclosed mass and the depth are the series of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (A12) and Eq. (A11), carried to four terms in \(R^{\alpha}\) and summed term by term with no subtraction from the central value; the potential is \(P_0\) less that depth. The series is trusted out to the largest radius at which its next term, relative to the depth, stays within \(10^{-7}\). This bound follows from the parameters of the profile alone, and no fixed depth is assumed. The Poisson solve of a truncated model starts from the same series, and its inner rows are filled from the series out to that join ([Section T:3.4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation#tn-sec-fills)).

## T:1.3 Interpolation of the tabulated truncated profile

The self-consistent profile of a truncated model is a table of rows (radius, potential, density, and enclosed mass), and a single object owns its reading: every stage and every reader evaluates the profile through the four functions of that object and holds no interpolant of its own. The potential and the mass are cubic Hermite interpolants in the logarithms, with the exact slopes that the rows state, \(\mathrm{d}\ln P/\mathrm{d}\ln r = -M/(rP)\) and \(\mathrm{d}\ln M/\mathrm{d}\ln r = r^3\varrho/M\) (the Poisson equation and the mass integral). The density is a cubic spline of \(\ln\varrho\) in \(\ln r\), since the rows state no density slope. The radius at a given potential is the guarded inverse of the potential interpolant. A spatially finite profile carries its edge as its last row, where the density is zero and the radius is \(R_\mathrm{t}\). On the last interval the potential takes the Kepler form \(M_\mathrm{t}(1/r - 1/R_\mathrm{t})\) and the density follows the edge law \(\varrho_L\,(P/P_L)^{q}\), with the exponent \(q\) stated by the profile; beyond \(R_\mathrm{t}\) the potential continues as \(M_\mathrm{t}(1/r - 1/R_\mathrm{t})\) and the density is zero; the package serves no reading there. Inside the first row, the interpolants continue as the power laws of the end rows. Nothing outside the domain is clipped: a radius that lies beyond the edge by a rounding error is treated as the edge, and anything further out is refused with the reason stated.


---

# T:2 The distribution function

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df

## T:2.1 The two forms of the inversion and the forward relation

[Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758) gives the inversion in two forms: with the derivative outside the integral, Eq. (B22), and with the derivative inside the integral together with a surface term at \(P = 0\), Eq. (B9). The second form follows from the first by one integration by parts and is simpler to evaluate. The integration by parts requires that

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}^m\varrho_\mathrm{aux}}{\mathrm{d} P^m}\ \text{continuous on}\ [0, \mathcal{K}] \qquad\text{and}\qquad \int_0^{\mathcal{K}}\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}^{m+1}\varrho_\mathrm{aux}}{\mathrm{d} P^{m+1}}\right|(\mathcal{K}-P)^{-n}\,\mathrm{d} P < \infty .
  \tag{T:2.1}
\end{equation}
Neither condition is guaranteed. The first can fail at the outer end, \(P = 0\) ([Section T:2.2.6](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-outer)), and at the anisotropy radius of a Type II model ([Section T:2.2.8](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-ra)).

For half-integer \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) we have \(n = 0\), and the general form reduces to a derivative with no integral,

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{K}) = \frac{2^{\beta_\mathrm{c}}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}^m\varrho_\mathrm{aux}}{\mathrm{d} P^m}\right|_{P=\mathcal{K}} .
  \tag{T:2.2}
\end{equation}
The forward relation is a Volterra equation whose lower limit lies at \(P = 0\), that is, at the outer edge of the model (\(R = \infty\) for an untruncated model, \(R = R_\mathrm{t}\) for a truncated one):

\begin{equation}
  \varrho_\mathrm{aux}(P) = \frac{2\pi^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}{\Gamma(3/2-\beta_\mathrm{c})} \int_0^{P} F_\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{K})\,\left[2(P - \mathcal{K})\right]^{1/2-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K} .
  \tag{T:2.3}
\end{equation}

## T:2.2 Asymptotic behavior of the DF

### T:2.2.1 The limit P → P₀: the contribution of one power-law term

Consider a single term \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \supset A_s\,(P_0 - P)^{s}\) of the expansion of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) about the center. Its \((m+1)\)-th derivative is \((-1)^{m+1} A_s\,[\Gamma(s+1)/\Gamma(s-m)]\,(P_0-P)^{s-m-1}\). With \(t = \mathcal{K} - P\), the integral of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B9) becomes \(\int_0^{\mathcal{K}} t^{-n} (u+t)^{s-m-1}\,\mathrm{d} t\), whose behavior as \(u \to 0\) follows from the Mellin-type integral

\begin{equation}
  \int_0^{\infty} t^{a-1}(u+t)^{-b}\,\mathrm{d} t = u^{a-b}\,\frac{\Gamma(a)\,\Gamma(b-a)}{\Gamma(b)},
  \tag{T:2.4}
\end{equation}
with \(a = 1-n\) and \(b = m+1-s\). The finite upper limit adds only a part that is analytic at \(u = 0\). Using \(\Gamma(s-m)\,\Gamma(m+1-s) = \pi/\sin[\pi(s-m)]\) and \(\Gamma(-s)\,\Gamma(1+s) = -\pi/\sin(\pi s)\), the term contributes

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K}^{\rm sing}(\mathcal{K}) = \frac{2^{\beta_\mathrm{c}}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\; A_s\,\frac{\Gamma(\nu - s)}{\Gamma(-s)}\; u^{\,s-\nu},
  \tag{T:2.5}
\end{equation}
plus a part that is analytic in \(u\). Three properties of [Eq. (T:2.5)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-singular) decide what follows.

- For \(s\) a non-negative integer, \(1/\Gamma(-s) = 0\), and the term has no singular part.

- For \(s = \nu + k\) with \(k\) a non-negative integer and \(\nu\) not an integer, \(\Gamma(\nu - s)\) has a pole, and the power is replaced by a logarithm,

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K}^{\rm sing}(\mathcal{K}) = \frac{2^{\beta_\mathrm{c}}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\,\frac{(-1)^{k}\,A_s}{k!\;\Gamma(-s)}\;u^{k}\,(-\ln u) ,
  \tag{T:2.6}
\end{equation}
which for \(k = 0\) reduces to \(-\,2^{\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,A_\nu\,\ln u\,/\,[(2\pi)^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})\,\Gamma(-\nu)]\).

- Otherwise the term is a power law \(u^{\,s-\nu}\), whose sign is that of \(A_s\,\Gamma(\nu-s)/\Gamma(-s)\).

Since the inversion is linear, every power in the expansion of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) contributes its own term of the form [Eq. (T:2.5)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-singular) or [Eq. (T:2.6)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-log), and the singular part of \(F_\mathcal{K}\) at the center is the sum of these terms in order of increasing \(s\). Only the non-negative integer powers drop out; a negative integer \(s\) is singular like any other. The coefficients \(A_s\) follow from the expansion of [Section T:1.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-pair). A ratio of two Gamma functions is formed as the exponential of a difference of log-Gamma values together with its sign, never as a direct quotient, so that a steep center whose Gamma values overflow still has a finite amplitude.

### T:2.2.2 The central DF for γ > 2β_c

The leading term of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) is \(A\,(P_0-P)^{s_0}\) with \(s_0 = (2\beta_\mathrm{c} - \gamma)/(2-\gamma) < 0\). [Eq. (T:2.5)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-singular) reproduces the exponent \(\kappa\) of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B36) and supplies its amplitude,

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K} \simeq \frac{2^{\beta_\mathrm{c}}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\,A\,\frac{\Gamma(\nu - s_0)}{\Gamma(-s_0)}\,u^{\kappa},
  \tag{T:2.7}
\end{equation}
which is positive. For the isotropic Hernquist profile in units \(G = M = a = 1\), \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \simeq (2\pi u)^{-1}\) and \(F \simeq 3\,u^{-5/2}/(16\sqrt{2}\,\pi^2)\), which is the leading term of its known closed form.

As \(\gamma \to 2\beta_\mathrm{c}\), the amplitude vanishes linearly, \(\Gamma(\nu - s_0)/\Gamma(-s_0) = -s_0\,\Gamma(\nu) + \mathcal{O}(s_0^2)\), while the exponent tends to \(-\nu\). The regular and the critical branch therefore join in amplitude but not in exponent.

### T:2.2.3 The central DF in the boundary case γ = 2β_c

By [Eq. (T:1.1)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-eq-inner-map), \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} = C_1 + C_2\,(P_0-P)^{\delta} + \dots\): for constant anisotropy it is a series in \((P_0-P)^{\delta}\); for OM (\(\gamma = 0\)) the factor \(1 \pm R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2\) adds the powers \((P_0-P)^{1 + j\delta}\), \(j \geq 0\), of which the integer power drops out and the others lie above \(\delta\). The constant term has \(s = 0\) and no singular part. The next term has \(s = \delta\) and the exponent \(\kappa' = \delta - \nu\) of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B37). [Table T:2.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-tab-critical) lists the cases; its last four rows assume that \(\delta\) is not an integer.

Table T:2.1. The central DF in the critical case \(\gamma = 2\beta_\mathrm{c}\), for constant anisotropy and OM models.

Condition

Central behavior

Leading form

\(\delta\) a positive integer

finite

analytic in \(u\)

\(\kappa' < 0\)

power-law divergence

[Eq. (T:2.5)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-singular) with \(s = \delta\), \(A_s = C_2\)

\(\kappa' = 0\)

logarithmic divergence

[Eq. (T:2.6)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-log) with \(A_\nu = C_2\)

\(\kappa' > 0\), \(n \neq 0\)

finite

\(F_\mathcal{K}(P_0) + c_1 u + \dots + A\,u^{\kappa'}\), with \(c_1 u + \dots\) analytic in \(u\) and \(A\,u^{\kappa'}\) of [Eq. (T:2.5)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-singular) (\(s = \delta\), \(A_s = C_2\)), replaced by [Eq. (T:2.6)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-log) when \(\kappa'\) is an integer

\(\kappa' > 0\), \(n = 0\)

vanishing

\(\propto u^{\kappa'}\)

In the row \(\kappa' > 0\), \(n \neq 0\), the constant \(F_\mathcal{K}(P_0)\) is the non-local integral of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B9) at \(\mathcal{K} = P_0\); it is finite and may have either sign, and \(F_\mathcal{K} - F_\mathcal{K}(P_0) = \mathcal{O}(u^{\min(\kappa', 1)})\), with a factor \(\ln u\) at \(\kappa' = 1\).

- *Sign.* With \(C_2 < 0\), the divergence is toward negative values for \(1 < \delta < \nu\), and also for \(\kappa' = 0\) with \(\beta_\mathrm{c} < 1/2\). Such models are unphysical even though they satisfy [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (12).

- *The finite case at* \(\kappa' = 0\)*.* This case requires \(\delta = \nu\) to be an integer. Within \(0 \leq \gamma < 2\) it occurs only for \(\alpha = 1\), \(\gamma = 1\), \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 1/2\), which includes the NFW and Hernquist profiles.

- *The local case.* For \(n = 0\) the inversion is the derivative of [Eq. (T:2.2)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-local), and the non-local constant \(F_\mathcal{K}(P_0)\) is absent.

### T:2.2.4 The central DF of COM models

For COM models, the factor \((1 \pm R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2)^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) contributes a series in \(R^2 \propto (P_0-P)^{2/(2-\gamma)}\). The expansion of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) then contains the powers

\begin{equation}
  s_{kj} = k\,\delta + \frac{2j}{2-\gamma}, \qquad k, j \geq 0,
  \tag{T:2.8}
\end{equation}
and the leading singular term is the smallest \(s_{kj}\) that is not an integer. The result of [Section T:2.2.3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-critical) is modified when \(2/(2-\gamma)\) is not an integer and, in addition, either \(2/(2-\gamma) \leq \delta\) or \(\delta\) is an integer. At \(2/(2-\gamma) = \delta\) (that is, \(\alpha = 2\)) the exponent is unchanged and only the amplitude is modified: \(C_2 \to C_2\,[1 \mp 2(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})/((\beta-\gamma)\,R_\mathrm{a}^2)]\), with \(-\) for Type I and \(+\) for Type II. Since \(2/(2-\gamma)\) is an integer at \(\gamma = 0\) and at \(\gamma = 1\), OM models (which are critical only at \(\gamma = 0\)) and all \(\gamma = 1\) profiles are unaffected.

Where the modification applies, the exponent is \(2/(2-\gamma) - \nu\), which is negative for \(0 < \gamma < (5-\sqrt{17})/2 \simeq 0.438\). A center that is finite under constant anisotropy is then divergent under COM Type I. For example, \((\alpha, \gamma, \beta_\mathrm{c}) = (1.8, 0.2, 0.1)\) has \(\delta = 1\) and a finite center under constant anisotropy, but \(F_\mathcal{K} \propto u^{-13/45}\) under COM Type I.

### T:2.2.5 The closed-form DF of the NFW profile at β_c = 1/2

With \(\varrho = 1/[R(1+R)^2]\) and \(P = \ln(1+R)/R\), [Eq. (T:2.2)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-local) gives

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K} = \frac{1}{2\pi^2}\frac{\mathrm{d}(R\varrho)}{\mathrm{d} P} = \frac{1}{\pi^2}\,\frac{R^2}{(1+R)^3\left[\ln(1+R) - R/(1+R)\right]},
  \tag{T:2.9}
\end{equation}
evaluated at \(R(\mathcal{K})\). Its expansion about the center contains integer powers only,

\begin{equation}
  \pi^2 F_\mathcal{K} = 2 - \frac{20}{3}u + \frac{28}{3}u^2 - \frac{1024}{135}u^3 + \mathcal{O}(u^4),
  \tag{T:2.10}
\end{equation}
so the central DF is finite, \(F_\mathcal{K}(P_0) = 2/\pi^2\).

### T:2.2.6 The limit P → 0

Let \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \propto P^{\,y}\) as \(P \to 0\), where \(y\) is not a non-negative integer smaller than \(m\). Then \(\mathrm{d}^m\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d} P^m \propto P^{\,y-m}\), and the surface term of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B9)

\begin{equation}
  \text{vanishes for}\ y > m, \qquad \text{is finite for}\ y = m, \qquad \text{diverges for}\ y < m .
  \tag{T:2.11}
\end{equation}
Where \(y\) is a non-negative integer smaller than \(m\), the \(m\)-th derivative of the leading term vanishes and the next term of the expansion decides. For integer \(\alpha\) and integer \(\beta > 3\), a (C)OM Type I \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) is analytic in \(P\) at \(P = 0\), and the surface term is finite.

For an untruncated profile with \(\beta > 3\), [Eq. (T:1.2)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-eq-outer-map) gives

\begin{equation}
  y = \beta - 2\beta_\mathrm{c} \ \ \text{(constant anisotropy)}, \qquad y = \beta - 2 \ \ \text{[(C)OM Type~I]}.
  \tag{T:2.12}
\end{equation}
[Table T:2.2](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-tab-surface) lists the consequences. The bound \(\beta > m+2\) is sharp.

Table T:2.2. The surface term at \(P = 0\) for untruncated profiles with \(\beta > 3\).

Model

\(m\)

Surface term vanishes

constant anisotropy

\(\lfloor 3/2 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\rfloor\)

always

(C)OM Type I, \(\beta_\mathrm{c} > 1/2\)

0

always

(C)OM Type I, \(-1/2 < \beta_\mathrm{c} \leq 1/2\)

1

always

(C)OM Type I, \(\beta_\mathrm{c} \leq -1/2\)

\(\geq 2\)

for \(\beta > m + 2\)

At \(\beta = 3\) the constant-anisotropy surface term still vanishes. For (C)OM Type I, \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \propto P/\ln(1/P)\), so the term vanishes only as \(1/\ln(1/P)\) for \(m = 1\) and diverges for \(m \geq 2\). For \(2 < \beta < 3\), a (C)OM Type I model has \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \propto P\), so the term is finite and non-zero for \(m = 1\) and diverges for \(m \geq 2\). A constant-anisotropy model has \(y = (\beta - 2\beta_\mathrm{c})/(\beta - 2) > m\), and its term vanishes. PIANISTpy does not compute DFs for \(2 < \beta < 3\).

### T:2.2.7 The low-energy tail of the DF and its contribution to the density

For an untruncated (C)OM Type I model with \(\beta > 3\), [Eq. (T:2.12)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-y) and [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B25) give a power-law tail,

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{K}) \simeq A\,\mathcal{K}^{-a} \quad (\mathcal{K} \to 0), \qquad a = \nu - (\beta - 2) = \tfrac{7}{2} - \beta_\mathrm{c} - \beta ,
  \tag{T:2.13}
\end{equation}
which diverges for \(a > 0\); a profile with an outer slope of exactly 3 carries a logarithmic factor beside the power. By [Eq. (T:2.3)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-volterra), the part of the tail below an energy \(q\) contributes to the auxiliary density at \(P > q\) the amount

\begin{equation}
  \varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{\rm tail}(P) = \frac{2\pi^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}{\Gamma(3/2-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\; 2^{\,\nu-1} A\, P^{\,\nu-a}\; B\!\left(\frac{q}{P};\, 1-a,\, \nu\right),
  \tag{T:2.14}
\end{equation}
where \(B(x; p, r) = \int_0^x t^{p-1}(1-t)^{r-1}\,\mathrm{d} t\) is the incomplete Beta function. The integral converges for \(a < 1\). For \(a \geq 1\) the density integral diverges at \(\mathcal{K} = 0\), and the untruncated model does not exist; a truncated model does exist, since the truncated DF of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B27) vanishes at its lower end.

### T:2.2.8 Behavior of the inversion at the anisotropy radius of a Type II model

For Type II models, \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \propto w^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) as \(w \equiv 1 - R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2 \to 0\), and \(w\) is linear in \(P - P(R_\mathrm{a})\) there. Hence

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}^m\varrho_\mathrm{aux}}{\mathrm{d} P^m} \propto |P - P(R_\mathrm{a})|^{\,1-\beta_\mathrm{c}-m} = |P - P(R_\mathrm{a})|^{\,n - 1/2},
  \tag{T:2.15}
\end{equation}
which diverges at \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) for \(n < 1/2\). The divergence is approached from inside \(R_\mathrm{a}\) and does not depend on how \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) is continued beyond it ([Section T:3.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation#tn-sec-typeii)). For OM Type II, \(n = 1/2\) and the factor is a polynomial, so the conditions of [Eq. (T:2.1)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-conditions) hold. For COM Type II with integer \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\), \(n = 1/2\) as well. Where \(1 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\) is odd, the continued factor \(\mathrm{sign}(w)\,|w|^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) equals \(w^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\), a polynomial, and the conditions hold. Where \(1 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\) is even (\(\beta_\mathrm{c} = -1, -3, \dots\)), the continuation makes \(\mathrm{d}^m\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d} P^m\) jump at \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\), so the first condition of [Eq. (T:2.1)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-conditions) fails there. Unlike the divergence for \(n < 1/2\), this failure is set by the continuation. A truncated model with \(R_\mathrm{t} < R_\mathrm{a}\) does not contain the point. At \(R_\mathrm{t} = R_\mathrm{a}\) the point is the model’s edge, and the code admits only \(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t} > P(R_\mathrm{a})\), that is, \(R_\mathrm{t} < R_\mathrm{a}\).

## T:2.3 Evaluating the inversion at each tabulated energy

### T:2.3.1 Choice of the derivative order and of the inversion form

The form of the inversion is fixed from the model parameters alone, before any integral is evaluated.

- *Order pair.* From \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) the code forms the pair \((m, n)\) of [Eq. (T:0.1)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/principles#tn-eq-order). For \(n > 1/2\) it replaces the pair by

\begin{equation}
  (j, n') = (m+1,\; n-1),
  \tag{T:2.16}
\end{equation}
so that the kernel exponent always satisfies \(|n'| \leq 1/2\); otherwise \((j, n') = (m, n)\). With the higher order, the surface term can diverge as \(P \to 0\) ([Section T:2.2.6](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-outer)) and cancel against the integral, so a replaced pair is evaluated in the general form, [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B22), on every row.

- *Half-integer* \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\)*.* For \(n = 0\) the closed form of [Eq. (T:2.2)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-local) is used, and no quadrature is performed.

- *Interior point.* For an untruncated COM Type II model, the point \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) and the exponent of [Eq. (T:2.15)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-ra-exponent) are known in closed form. Rows with \(\mathcal{K} \leq P(R_\mathrm{a})\) take the form that items 1, 4 and 5 fix; rows above it take the general form, with the lower integral of [Eq. (T:2.18)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-split) split at \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) and evaluated on either side by a Gauss-Jacobi rule in \(\ln P\) that carries the exponent as its weight ([Section T:2.3.3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-split)). For odd integer \(1-\beta_\mathrm{c}\) the factor is a polynomial, and there is no such point.

- *An unbounded outer end.* Where \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}\) is unbounded at \(P = 0\), the rows above a stated energy use the general form.

- *All other rows* use the form with the surface term.

Applying the same operator one derivative higher gives \(\mathrm{d} F_\mathcal{K}/\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K}\) on the same rows, so the table carries an exact slope column.

### T:2.3.2 The lowest tabulated energy

The table of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) and its derivatives starts at a floor \(q_0 > 0\), not at \(P = 0\). Splitting the integral of the general form at \(q_0\) and integrating its upper part by parts gives, with no assumption about the behavior at \(P = 0\),

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K}}\int_0^{\mathcal{K}}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n}}\,\mathrm{d} P = \int_{q_0}^{\mathcal{K}}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j+1)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n}}\,\mathrm{d} P + \frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(q_0)}{(\mathcal{K}-q_0)^{n}} - n\int_0^{q_0}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n+1}}\,\mathrm{d} P ,
  \tag{T:2.17}
\end{equation}
where \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)} \equiv {\mathrm{d}}^j\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d} P^j\). The first two terms need only the table. The third term is the contribution of the stretch below the floor. In Method I it is evaluated in the floor pair \((m, n)\) from the exact derivatives of [Section T:1.2.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-derivatives), over \([P_\mathrm{min}, q_0]\) with \(P_\mathrm{min} = 10^{-42}\): on Gauss-Legendre nodes in \(\ln P\) up to \(q_0/10\) and on Gauss-Legendre nodes in \(w = (q_0 - P)^{1-n}\) above it, integrated once by parts (or, where \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(m)}\) is unbounded at \(P = 0\), as written), with \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(m)}(P_\mathrm{min})\) standing for the stretch below \(P_\mathrm{min}\); so the floor of the table is not the floor of the model. A half-integer \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) needs no completion, and a model whose outer end is bounded and whose tail exponent is at least 1 has none. In Method II it is the closed form of [Section T:2.6](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-tabulated). The floor is \(q_0 = 10^{-10}\) in units of the central potential. An untruncated table’s rows start at the first grid energy at or above \(2\,q_0\), and the nodes below the written floor ([Section T:2.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-num-beyond)) are written with them; where the model has no such nodes, the rows start at \(q_0\).

### T:2.3.3 Splitting the integral of the general form

Rows that use the general form ([Section T:2.3.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-df-form)) split the integral at an interior point \(c < \mathcal{K}\). Below \(c\) the derivative is taken under the integral sign; above \(c\) the integral is integrated by parts:

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K}}\int_{q_0}^{\mathcal{K}}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n}}\,\mathrm{d} P = -n\int_{q_0}^{c}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n+1}}\,\mathrm{d} P + \frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(c)}{(\mathcal{K}-c)^{n}} + \int_{c}^{\mathcal{K}}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j+1)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n}}\,\mathrm{d} P .
  \tag{T:2.18}
\end{equation}
The right-hand side requires \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}\) only on \([q_0, c]\), where it is bounded except at an interior point, and \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j+1)}\) only above \(c\). For a replaced pair, [Eq. (T:2.16)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-unified-pair), this avoids \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(m+1)}\) at the floor, which the form with the surface term would require and which can diverge as \(P \to 0\). For rows above the interior point of a COM Type II model, \(c\) lies above \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\), and the lower integral is evaluated on the two sides of that point with a rule that carries as its weight the exponent \(1-\beta_\mathrm{c}-j\) of \(\mathrm{d}^j\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d}P^j\) at \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\), which is [Eq. (T:2.15)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-ra-exponent) at the order \(j\) in use: \(n - 1/2\) for a pair that is not replaced and \(n - 3/2\) for a replaced one.

### T:2.3.4 Quadrature of the inversion integral

Each row is integrated on three sub-intervals: from the floor to one tenth of the split point, on Gauss-Legendre nodes in \(\ln P\); from there to the split point, on Gauss-Legendre nodes in \(P\); and from the split point to \(\mathcal{K}\), where the kernel is singular. The split point is \(c = 0.9\,\mathcal{K}\) on the rows of \(F_\mathcal{K}\) that use the surface form, and the largest grid energy at or below \(0.9\,\mathcal{K}\) on the rows of \(\mathrm{d}F_\mathcal{K}/\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K}\), on every row of a replaced pair and on the rows of an unbounded outer end. On the rows above the interior point of a COM Type II model, \(c = \max(0.9\,\mathcal{K}, [P(R_\mathrm{a}) + \mathcal{K}]/2)\), moved down to the largest grid energy at or below it where that energy lies at least halfway from \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) to \(c\), and the stretch below \(c\) is the two Gauss-Jacobi pieces of [Section T:2.3.3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-split) in place of the first two sub-intervals. On the last sub-interval the integration variable is \(v\), with

\begin{equation}
  P = P_0 - (P_0 - \mathcal{K})\,e^{y}, \qquad y = v^{k}, \qquad k = \frac{1}{1-n} .
  \tag{T:2.19}
\end{equation}
Near the upper limit, \(\mathcal{K} - P \simeq (P_0 - \mathcal{K})\,y\), so that

\begin{equation}
  (\mathcal{K} - P)^{-n}\,\mathrm{d} P \;\propto\; y^{-n}\,\mathrm{d} y = k\,v^{\,k(1-n)-1}\,\mathrm{d} v = k\,\mathrm{d} v ,
  \tag{T:2.20}
\end{equation}
and the kernel singularity is removed for every exponent that the order pair allows. Away from the upper limit, \(\ln(P_0 - P)\) is a power of \(v\), so Gauss-Legendre nodes in \(v\) are graded logarithmically in \(P_0 - P\), which resolves an integrand that steepens as a power of \(P_0 - P\) toward the center.

## T:2.4 The energy grid

The DF is tabulated on a grid of energies in five zones, from the floor to the gap below the central potential: zone A, logarithmic in \(\mathcal{K}\) from the floor; zone AB, a buffer; zone B, linear (where it starts below \(0.01\,P_0\), logarithmic at 120 nodes per decade up to \(0.05\,P_0\) and linear above); zone BC, a buffer; and zone C, logarithmic in \(P_0 - \mathcal{K}\), cut at the gap, whose node is added. An untruncated COM Type II model with an interior point ([Section T:2.3.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-df-form)) adds nodes around \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\): a band of half-width \(P(R_\mathrm{a})/2\) at a fifth of the local spacing, and pairs at \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\,(1 \pm 10^{-k/4})\), \(k = 0, \dots, 24\), within twice the local spacing. A buffer carries the step geometrically from the spacing on one side to the spacing on the other. Its number of steps is the one whose total comes closest to the width of the buffer, and the steps are rescaled to sum to that width exactly, so that no jump in spacing enters the rows. The linear zone and the two logarithmic zones take their row counts from the settings, and the logarithmic zones extend over a stated fraction of the central potential. An OM Type I model places zones A and AB around the potential of its anisotropy radius; an OM Type II or COM model places them around the feature that a pilot inversion on a coarse grid finds: the least value of its DF below a stated energy, among the nodes where the DF exceeds \(10^{-3}\) of its median positive value, refined by a parabola through that node and its two neighbors in that set (where the DF crosses zero, this is the least value above that threshold, not the crossing). Where no such feature lies between \(10^{3}\,q_0\) and that energy, the standard zones are used. The upper end is never moved. The grid starts at the floor \(q_0\); the energies below it are those of the completion below the floor ([Section T:2.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-num-beyond)), where the rule below the table takes over ([Section T:2.5.4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-lookup)). Energies that coincide in double precision are merged into one node, so the grid is strictly increasing.

## T:2.5 The distribution function outside the tabulated energies

### T:2.5.1 The highest tabulated energy

The inversion’s rows reach the last energy of the grid, a gap of \(10^{-9}\) below \(P_0\), unless the exact derivatives required by the inversion cannot be formed that deep, or the host floor or the DF’s ceiling stops them first (below). Each term \(C_s u^{s}\) of the central series of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) gives \(\mathrm{d}^N\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d} P^N = (-1)^N C_s\, s(s-1)\cdots(s-N+1)\,u^{s-N}\), which exceeds the largest double below \(u = (|C_s\,s\cdots(s-N+1)|/\mathrm{DBL\_MAX})^{1/(N-s)}\) for \(s < N\). The largest such depth over the terms and over the orders that the form needs is the top limit of the table, and it is zero where no term grows. The rows end at the shallowest of three depths: that depth, the depth at the smallest radius whose square the host represents ([Section T:0.4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/principles#tn-sec-host)), and, where the center’s closed form is a power \(A\,u^{\kappa}\) with \(\kappa < 0\) and \(A > 0\) on the regular or the critical divergent branch of an isotropic, constant-anisotropy or Type I model, the depth at which that form reaches the package’s ceiling \(10^{300}\) on the DF; the closed form of the center owns the energies above. Where no closed form covers the top, a row above the ceiling is refused with an error that states the ceiling and the first such row. Where the leading exponent of the series vanishes (\(\gamma = 2\beta_\mathrm{c}\) at the center), there is no closed form to join to, and a model whose host floor alone would cut its table is refused with the reason stated.

### T:2.5.2 Between the highest tabulated energy and P₀

The table of \(F_\mathcal{K}\) ends at a top node, a small depth \(u_{\rm top}\) below the center. Between that node and the center, the DF is continued by its central form, [Section T:2.2.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-center) to [Section T:2.2.4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-com-center), which is computed from the model alone and stored with the table. The stored form consists of the leading singular term \(S_1(u)\) and the next one, \(S_2(u)\), each a power or a logarithm with the coefficient of [Eq. (T:2.5)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-singular) or [Eq. (T:2.6)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-log). The coefficients of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) that they need come from the exact expansion of [Section T:1.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-pair), carried to the second power that is not a non-negative integer. No exponent is fitted to the table, and the amplitude is the closed form wherever the center states one.

What remains of \(F_\mathcal{K}\) once the two singular terms are removed is the sum of a part analytic in \(u\) and the higher singular terms, each smaller than \(S_1\) by the factor \(u^{\kappa_i - \kappa_1}\), with \(\kappa_i\) the exponent of the \(i\)-th singular term; held at its value at the top node, it errs relative to \(F_\mathcal{K}\) by an amount of order \(u_{\rm top}\) (the analytic part, relative to the value at the center) or \(u_{\rm top}^{\kappa_3 - \kappa_1}\) (the third singular term), whichever is larger. It is therefore held at its value at the top node,

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K}(u) = S_1(u) + S_2(u) + \left[F_\mathcal{K}(u_{\rm top}) - S_1(u_{\rm top}) - S_2(u_{\rm top})\right], \qquad u < u_{\rm top} .
  \tag{T:2.21}
\end{equation}
Two cases depart from [Eq. (T:2.21)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-top). Where the leading power is positive and the inversion is local (the last row of [Table T:2.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-tab-critical)), \(F_\mathcal{K}\) vanishes at the center, and the bracket is multiplied by \(u/u_{\rm top}\) so that the continuation vanishes with it. Where the center is analytic, there is no singular term, and \(F_\mathcal{K}\) is held at its top value. For a divergent power, the expression is evaluated in logarithms relative to \(S_1\), so that a DF whose central values exceed the range of double precision is continued without overflow.

For an isotropic, constant-anisotropy or Type I model whose center is a divergent power (the regular and the critical divergent branches), the table ends at an anchor wherever the potential at the innermost radius of the settings, \(R = 10^{-9}\) by default (`log10_r_min`), lies more than \(10^{-10}\) below \(P_0\): the anchor is the last node at or below that potential, and at least one node below the grid’s top. Above the anchor the DF is \(A\,u^{\kappa} + B + D\,u\), with \(A\) the closed-form amplitude and \(\kappa\) the singular exponent, never fitted; \(B\) and \(D\) are fitted to the rows with \(u_\mathrm{anchor} \leq u \leq W u_\mathrm{anchor}\), \(W\) doubling from 2 until the amplitudes of the three-term fit (\(A\), \(B\), \(D\)) and of the four-term fit (with \(E\,u^2\)) agree to \(10^{-7}\), and they are kept only where the three-term fit is positive on every energy above the anchor (else \(B\) joins the form to the anchor and \(D = 0\)). A Type II model and a component on a tabulated pair carry no anchor, and the other branches carry one only where a band at the top is excluded (below); without an anchor, the DF is continued by [Eq. (T:2.21)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-top) from the last row. A band of rows at the top that is not positive is excluded only where the form holds there, as judged by the local slope \(\mathrm{d}\ln F/\mathrm{d}\ln u\) against \(\kappa\).

A truncated Method I model has \(\hat{F}_\mathcal{K}(\hat{\mathcal{K}}) = F_\mathcal{K}(\hat{\mathcal{K}} + \mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}) - F_\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t})\), which differs from the untruncated DF by a constant. Its singular terms and their coefficients are those of the untruncated model, with \(u\) measured from the truncated central potential.

The stored form is tested against the table that it continues. Across the top decade of the table, \(u_{\rm top} \leq u \leq 10\,u_{\rm top}\), the table less its singular terms may change only by the variation of the analytic part. A change above \(10^{-6}\) is reported with the product; a change above \(10^{-2}\) means that the stored form belongs to a different model, and the product is refused.

### T:2.5.3 Below the lowest tabulated energy

Below its first energy, the DF follows a stated rule that is recorded with the table: the tail \(A\,\mathcal{K}^{-a}[\ln(E_0/\mathcal{K})]^{-b}\) of [Eq. (T:2.13)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-tail-exponent) for an untruncated model whose exponent \(a\) is positive, with \(E_0 = P_0\) and with \(A\) and \(b\) chosen so that the tail joins the lowest node below the written floor in value and in logarithmic slope (\(b = 0\), and the join in value only, where those nodes carry no slope, or where there are none, at the written floor); the Taylor form \(F_1\mathcal{K} + F_2\mathcal{K}^2/2\) of a truncated Method I model at its edge, together with the energy up to which it holds; the edge law \(\mathcal{K}^{p}(C_0 + C_1\mathcal{K})\) of a Method II model ([Section T:2.6.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-edge-law)); or zero. The integral of the rule from zero up to an energy below the table is the same set of numbers in closed form, so a density integral never truncates the DF at its table.

### T:2.5.4 Interpolation between tabulated energies

Inside the table, the base-10 logarithm of the DF is the cubic Hermite interpolant in \(\ln{\mathcal{K}}\) through the nodes with the exact slope column. Where a table carries no exact slopes (a DF from a function, [Section T:2.7](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-from-function), and a component on a tabulated pair, [Section T:2.6](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-tabulated)), the slopes are those of the not-a-knot spline through the nodes. The lookup has two entry points, by the energy and by the depth \(u = P_0 - \mathcal{K}\), and a caller asks by whichever argument it holds exactly. For example, a velocity draw near the top holds the depth \(u = (P_0 - \Psi) + \Psi x^2\) exactly, whereas the energy \(\Psi(1 - x^2)\) formed in doubles loses it. In the entry by \(u\), the cell position is formed from \(u_i - u\) with \(u_i = P_0 - \mathcal{K}_i\), which is exact for \(\mathcal{K}_i \geq P_0/2\), and the form above the table is read at \(u\) itself. The nodes and every number of the forms are arrays, so that under JAX the table is a traced argument, and two tables with the same node bucket and the same kinds of forms share one compiled function.

### T:2.5.5 Checks stored with the table

A table is written together with its checks: the stated slope column against the table’s own \(F\), the stated center against the top decade of the table, and the joins of the forms below the floor with the bottom row. A reader refuses a table whose slope column or stated center fails beyond \(10^{-2}\), or whose forms below the floor miss the bottom row beyond \(10^{-6}\). The sign report states where the DF is negative and the smallest truncation above which it is not ([Section T:3.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation#tn-sec-gate)). The validity certificate is a closed form: from the model, the central exponent and the closed-form amplitude, it states whether the columns of the table are representable in double precision, judged at the table’s own top row (the anchor, or the shallowest of the gap, the top limit, the host floor and the DF’s ceiling); a component on a tabulated pair carries none.

## T:2.6 Method II: inversion of a truncated potential–density pair

Method II is not a second pipeline. A component whose profile is the truncated profile of another model runs through the same stages; the source of the derivatives differs, and so do four steps: no slope column is made, a defective band at the top is refused rather than repaired, the stretch below the floor has the closed form below, and at \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 1/2\) on a Method I model with \(\gamma = \alpha = 1\) the top rows are a closed-form band. The integral of the Method I model’s DF is its augmented density, the density itself for an isotropic Method I model and \(h_\mathrm{I}\,\hat\varrho\), \(h_\mathrm{I} = 1 + R^2/R_{\mathrm{a},\mathrm{I}}^2\), for an OM Type I Method I model:

\begin{equation}
  h_\mathrm{I}\,\hat\varrho(P) = 4\pi\sqrt{2}\int_0^{P} F(\mathcal{K})\,(P - \mathcal{K})^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K} ,
  \tag{T:2.22}
\end{equation}
so its derivatives with respect to \(P\) are integrals of the DF and of its derivatives against \((P - \mathcal{K})^{-1/2}\), with the boundary term \(F_1 P^{-1/2}\) at order three, evaluated from the Method I model’s table, its exact slope column, and its Taylor edge; the second derivative of the DF at order three is the derivative of the monotone cubic through the slope column, the only spline that is differentiated. The auxiliary density of the Method II model is \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} = h(R)\,\hat\varrho\) with the Method II model’s own factor, and its derivatives follow by the Leibniz rule with \(\mathrm{d} R/\mathrm{d} P\) taken from the rows. Orders up to three are served, the third only where the Method I model states its Taylor edge. An isotropic or OM Type I Method I model is served, and a Method II model of Type II must have its \(R_\mathrm{a}\) beyond the Method I model’s edge.

The grid is the five-zone grid of [Section T:2.4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-grid) on the first potential of the Method I model, compact, with no extension below the floor, since the support of the Method II model ends at the Method I model’s edge. The stretch below the floor has a closed form. For each power \(P^{q}\) of the two-term edge expansion of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) ([Section T:2.6.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-edge-law)), with \(a = q - m_f\), \(b = 1 - n_f\), and \(x = q_0/\mathcal{K}\),

\begin{equation}
  C(n_f)\,a_q\,\frac{\Gamma(q+1)}{\Gamma(a+1)}\;\mathcal{K}^{\,a-n_f}\,x^{a}\left[{}_2F_1(a, n_f;\, a+1;\, x) - 1\right]
  \tag{T:2.23}
\end{equation}
is the exact contribution of \([0, q_0]\) to the row at \(\mathcal{K}\), relative to the boundary form that the kernel carries, and the boundary term is the sources’ own value of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(m_f)}\) at the floor node: the Method I model’s derivatives there (in closed form from its Taylor edge where the node lies below the switch), its density from its rows, and the Method II model’s factor, by the Leibniz rule.

At \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 1/2\) on a Method I model with \(\gamma = \alpha = 1\), the inversion is a derivative whose two terms are both of order \(1/u\) toward the center, so the rows there carry the Method I model’s accuracy multiplied by \(C/[2(\beta - 1)\,u]\), with \(\hat\varrho \simeq C/R\) at the center (\(1/(4u)\) for NFW, \(1/(3u)\) for Hernquist). Above an anchor, the rows are the closed form \(F = A\sum_{k \leq 4} a_k u^{k}\) with \(A = 1/(2\pi^2)\) ([Section T:2.2.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-nfw-half)), which is exact in the truncation through the Method I model’s central deficit. The anchor is the smaller of the series’ own range at \(10^{-6}\) and the top zone of the grid, and the median relative deviation of the computed rows from the form over the outermost decade inside it, on at least ten rows, must be within \(10^{-6}\); otherwise the anchor steps inward one decade at a time until it is, and where no decade is, the rows stand as computed and the record says so.

### T:2.6.1 The Method II DF at the truncation boundary

A density that ends as \(P^{q}\) at its edge has a DF of central anisotropy \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) if and only if \(\beta_\mathrm{c} > 1/2 - q\), and the DF then behaves as \(\mathcal{K}^{\,q - 3/2 + \beta_\mathrm{c}}\) there. This statement holds for every profile and every anisotropy model of the package, and a Method II model that violates it is refused before any stage runs, with the admissible range stated. Below the Method I model’s switch energy, the Method I model’s DF is its Taylor form \(F_1\mathcal{K} + F_2\mathcal{K}^2/2\), so the Method I model’s augmented density near the edge is \(4\pi\sqrt{2}\,[\tfrac{4}{15}F_1 P^{5/2} + \tfrac{8}{105}F_2 P^{7/2}]\) to the order kept. The Method II model’s augmented density, with \(h = h_\mathrm{t} + H_1 P\), \(H_1 = h'(R_\mathrm{t})\,R'(P)\), and \(R' = -R_\mathrm{t}^2/M_\mathrm{t}\), is then

\begin{equation}
  \varrho_{\rm aug}(P) = a_{5/2}\,P^{5/2} + a_{7/2}\,P^{7/2} + \mathcal{O}(P^{9/2}) .
  \tag{T:2.24}
\end{equation}
Each power inverts to a power, so the Method II model’s DF below its switch is the edge law \(\mathcal{K}^{p}(C_0 + C_1\mathcal{K})\) with \(p = 1 + \beta_\mathrm{c}\), and the same coefficients give the floor terms of [Eq. (T:2.23)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-method2-floor-tail).

## T:2.7 A distribution function supplied as input

A DF obtained elsewhere, from a fitting function or from the output of another code, is checked in the same way. Its values on the energy grid that the inversion would place for the component enter at the point where the rows of the inversion would enter, and everything downstream is unchanged: the forms beyond the table, the sign report, the checks and the result’s record, which carries no inversion record and no rows. Such a table has no exact slope column, which its report states, and a value that is not finite is refused, with the first such energy stated. Truncation needs the rows of the inversion, which such a table does not carry, and it is refused with the reason stated.


---

# T:3 Truncation

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation

The two truncation methods are defined in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Section 3.1.

## T:3.1 Type II models beyond the anisotropy radius

*The model is not defined for* \(R > R_\mathrm{a}\)*.* In the Type II variable \(Q_+\), the tangential velocity enters with the factor \(1 - R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2\). For \(R > R_\mathrm{a}\) this factor is negative, the velocity integral diverges, and no DF of this form yields a density. An untruncated profile that extends beyond \(R_\mathrm{a}\) therefore has no Type II DF, whereas a truncated model with \(R_\mathrm{t} < R_\mathrm{a}\) is well defined.

*Method I nevertheless needs* \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) *there.* The inversion solves the Volterra equation [Eq. (T:2.3)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-volterra), whose lower limit lies at \(R = \infty\). The values of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) on \(P > P(R_\mathrm{a})\) determine \(F_\mathcal{K}\) there only in combination with \(F_\mathcal{K}\) on \(P < P(R_\mathrm{a})\). Method I constructs the truncated DF from the untruncated one by the shift of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B27), and the contribution of the stretch \(0 < P < P(R_\mathrm{a})\) to \(F_\mathcal{K}\) depends on \(\mathcal{K}\), so it does not cancel in that difference. A value of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) must therefore be supplied on that stretch.

*The continuation.* For OM Type II, the factor \(1 - R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2\) is a polynomial and is used as it stands. For COM Type II the factor \(w^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) is not real for \(w < 0\) where \(1 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\) is not an integer; PIANISTpy adopts, for every COM Type II model, the continuation

\begin{equation}
  w^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}} \;\to\; \mathrm{sign}(w)\,|w|^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}},
  \tag{T:3.1}
\end{equation}
which equals \(w^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) where \(1 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\) is an odd integer and differs from it in sign beyond \(R_\mathrm{a}\) where it is an even integer, is odd in \(w\), and reduces to the OM form at \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 0\). The continuation is requested through an explicit argument in the symbolic form of the Method I inversion alone; every other reading of the factor at or beyond \(R_\mathrm{a}\) is refused with the reason stated. The adopted convention is recorded in the product file.

*The support.* An untruncated Type II model is defined only inside \(R_\mathrm{a}\), so its DF is returned over \(\mathcal{K} > P(R_\mathrm{a})\) only. The table keeps its fixed grid, the rows at and below \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) hold no value, and the record states the first row of the support. The values that the inversion forms below \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) belong to the continuation rather than to the model, whatever their sign; they are used by the inversion above \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\), which depends on them non-locally; the table does not carry them, and they are kept only among the inversion’s rows as made, which the truncation reads. The gates on the sign and on the last minimum of \(F_\mathcal{K}\) are evaluated on the support, and the lowest admissible truncation value is \(\max(\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_{\min}, P(R_\mathrm{a}))\), below which the truncated DF would read the continuation; it is necessary but not sufficient for \(R_\mathrm{t} < R_\mathrm{a}\), which the truncated solve decides ([Section T:3.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation#tn-sec-gate)). The anisotropy object declares the edge of its domain (\(R_\mathrm{a}\) for Type II, none otherwise); the support and the gates read that edge and not the Type. The same bound holds for a Method II model whose anisotropy is of Type II: a model whose \(R_\mathrm{a}\) does not lie beyond the Method I model’s edge is refused before the inversion.

*What the convention can and cannot change.* Every DF of the form \(\hat F(\hat{\mathcal{K}})\,L^{-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) in the Type II variable has the COM Type II anisotropy profile, and the truncated density is computed from \(\hat F\). The convention therefore affects neither the anisotropy profile nor the self-consistency of a Method I model. What it selects is which truncated density the model has, and under Method I that density is an output. For that density the DF is unique. The effect of the convention on the truncated density exceeds \(10^{-6}\) ([Section T:0.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/principles#tn-sec-tiers)).

Method II inverts the truncated pair, which lies within \(R_\mathrm{a}\), and never evaluates the continuation. A user who needs a Type II model with a prescribed density should therefore use Method II.

## T:3.2 The truncated DF and its density

From the table that the inversion leaves, the truncation energy, and the settings, the truncated DF \(F(\mathcal{K} + \mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}) - F(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t})\) is formed on the source grid, together with its Taylor form at the edge and the edge integral that joins the form to the table. The auxiliary density

\begin{equation}
  \varrho_\mathrm{aux}(P) = C(\beta_\mathrm{c})\int_0^{P} \hat F(\mathcal{K})\,\left[2(P - \mathcal{K})\right]^{1/2-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K}
  \tag{T:3.2}
\end{equation}
with \(C(\beta_\mathrm{c}) = 2\pi^{3/2}\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})/\Gamma(3/2-\beta_\mathrm{c})\) as in [Eq. (T:2.3)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-volterra), is what the Poisson solve takes as its source (the table holds the integral, and the solve applies \(C\)); the density of a component is \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) times the factor \(g(R)\) of its anisotropy, which the solve applies. The source grid runs from the floor to the gap below the truncated central potential, with logarithmic tails toward both ends over a stated fraction of the top. The integral at each potential is taken on two intervals: Gauss-Legendre nodes in \(\ln{\mathcal{K}}\) from the floor to a split at a stated fraction of \(P\), and above the split the map \(\mathcal{K} = P - v^{k}\): with \(k = 1/(3/2 - \beta_\mathrm{c})\) where \(1/2 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\) is negative, which removes the kernel’s singularity at \(\mathcal{K} = P\), and with a stated \(k\) (2) otherwise, which makes the kernel’s end-point factor \(v^{2 - 2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\), a polynomial for OM and isotropic models. The lookup at a grid node returns the node’s value, to the rounding of its logarithm; at the bottom no clip by an absolute epsilon enters (the clip is the table’s first node), and below the floor, where the solve ends, the source is set to zero.

### T:3.2.1 The low-energy tail of the DF in the density integral

The source quadrature runs for truncated models only: an untruncated model takes the closed forms of its source profile ([Section T:3.7](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation#tn-sec-trust)), and a truncated DF vanishes at its lower end, so no tail term enters.

## T:3.3 Solving the truncated Poisson equation

The truncated Poisson equation, [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B28), is integrated outward in \(s = \ln r\) as a first-order system in \([\Phi,\; W = r\,\mathrm{d}\Phi/\mathrm{d} r,\; u = P_0 - \Phi]\), under a relative tolerance of \(10^{-11}\) and no absolute tolerance (the edge continuation in \(\ln\Phi\), also relative-only), starting from the series of the cusp ([Section T:1.2.2](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-series)). The right-hand side is the density of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B29), read from the source table of [Section T:3.2](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation#tn-sec-num-truncation). The solve ends at the event where \(\Phi\) reaches the floor, which is the edge of a spatially finite model, or else at the outer radius; the last rows of a truncated model are re-solved on a grid geometric in \(R_\mathrm{t} - r\), and the row at the floor is the crossing of the event. A request whose solve reaches no edge within its radius is refused with the reason stated. The solve is a serial integration, and it runs on the CPU on every device ([Section T:0.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/principles#tn-sec-tiers)).

## T:3.4 Completing the truncated profile toward the center and the truncation radius

The rows of the solve are sparse where the potential approaches the floor and where it approaches the center, so both ends are filled to the row density of the profile: at least a stated number of rows per decade of the potential and of the depth, in bins of a stated width, over the profile’s own span. The inner end is the inner series of [Section T:1.2.2](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-series), lowered by the central deficit where the model carries one, out to the depth to which the series is trusted (on a lowered model, moved inward to where the series and the rows of the solve agree); between that join and the threshold of the fill, the solve’s own interpolant is used. The outer end takes the radius by a log-log interpolation of the solve’s rows in the potential and the density likewise down to a fixed anchor, \(3.6\times10^{-7}P_0\), below which the density follows the power law of the two rows above the anchor and, below the Taylor switch, the closed form of the edge. The profile keeps every filled row that is finite, with positive density and the potential at or above the floor, the inner series rows inside the solve’s first radius included; a spatially finite model ends with one edge row at \(\Phi = 0\), at the radius where the Kepler exterior of its last row reaches zero; a profile that reaches no edge is read to its last row.

## T:3.5 The lowest admissible truncation value

The truncated DF of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B27) is non-negative and non-decreasing when the untruncated DF is non-decreasing above the truncation energy; the code asks in addition that the untruncated DF be non-negative there. From the computed untruncated DF on its support, the code takes the energy of its highest negative row and the end of its last decrease (by a relative amount above \(10^{-5}\)), and it accepts a truncation energy at or above the larger of the two and, for a Type II model, strictly above \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) ([Section T:3.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation#tn-sec-typeii)). The bound at \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) is necessary but not sufficient: only the truncated solve places the edge, and a solve whose edge lies at or beyond \(R_\mathrm{a}\) is refused afterward with an error of its own, TYPE II EDGE. A truncation that no model can carry is refused before any stage runs: a cusp shallower than \(2\beta_\mathrm{c}(0)\) at the center, where the DF is negative there for every truncation ([An & Evans 2006b](https://doi.org/10.1086/501040)); a degenerate central series whose table the host floor alone would cut ([Section T:2.5.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-top-limit)); and a central DF that tends to a negative value, to minus infinity or to zero from below.

## T:3.6 Finding the truncation value for a target mass or truncation radius

Under Method I the untruncated DF does not depend on the truncation, so it is inverted once, and every evaluation of a target costs one truncated solve. The search runs on \(x = \ln{\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}}\) for a target \(v = M_\mathrm{t}\) or \(v = R_\mathrm{t}\), in four stages: deeper truncation from a probe until the model is admissible; a bracket by secant steps in \((\ln{\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}}, \ln v)\) toward the target, by at most a factor of 16 per step, until one admissible model lies on each side; where a step lands outside the admissible set, its boundary, namely the \(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\) at which \(R_\mathrm{t}\) reaches its limit, found by regula falsi on \(1/R_\mathrm{t}\) at the cap, and at \(R_\mathrm{a}\), where no model beyond it is finite, by secant steps on \(1/R_\mathrm{t}\) with bisection in \(\ln\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\); and finally the Illinois form of regula falsi on \((\ln{\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}}, \ln(v/\text{target}))\) until \(|v/\text{target} - 1|\) is within \(10^{-6}\). A value of \(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\) is admissible when its solve succeeds, the model is spatially finite, \(R_\mathrm{t}\) is within the cap and, for Type II, inside \(R_\mathrm{a}\), and \(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\) lies at or above the gates and at or below \(0.9\) of the central potential; on the admissible set both targets decrease with \(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\). When no admissible model reaches the target, the request is refused with the reason stated and the value reached at the limit that binds; the solve takes no fallback.

## T:3.7 The closed-form profile of an untruncated model

An untruncated model solves no Poisson equation: its rows are the closed forms of the source profile’s density, potential and mass, geometric in \(R\) at the stated rows per decade from the innermost radius to where \(P\) falls below the floor, with rows added at the centers of the row-count bins of the potential and of the depth, and its depth near the center is the inner series. It carries no integration constant, so its radius of trust is infinite at every tier, recorded as such, and its table is not cut. Truncated products are not cut either.

## T:3.8 Checks of the self-consistency of a model

Each check is read on the rows of the profile through the profile object of [Section T:1.3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-profile-object), so a model from a run and a model from a file are checked alike. The Poisson residual is Poisson’s equation in integral form on every interval between consecutive rows, including the edge row, \(\Phi(r_a) - \Phi(r_b) = \int M/r^2\,\mathrm{d} r\) and \(M(r_b) - M(r_a) = \int \varrho\,r^2\,\mathrm{d} r\), each relative to the larger of its two rows, widened on the floor event’s row by the root finder’s tolerance of the event over the solve’s relative tolerance. The round trip compares the density that the model’s own DF gives at a row, \(\varrho = g(R)\,C(\beta_\mathrm{c})\int_0^{\Phi} F(Q)\,[2(\Phi - Q)]^{1/2-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,\mathrm{d} Q\), with \(g\) the anisotropy’s factor of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B44), with \(F\) read through the lookup, against the density of the row. It is evaluated at the rows nearest to each half-decade of radius and at every row from the last of those to the edge, so that the check reads what a dense read would read. The row density is the count of rows per bin that the fills keep; it is silent where every bin is full and refused at any shortfall.


---

# T:4 Linear superposition of Method II DFs

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sup

Distribution functions inverted from one and the same truncated density, that is, Method II models of one Method I model, combined with positive weights that sum to one, form a single equilibrium model in that density. Members on different truncated profiles are refused, and every component keeps its own energy grid, checked on its own nodes. The anisotropy profile of the superposition is given in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B74). In terms of the radial dispersions \(\sigma_{r,i}^2\) and the anisotropy profiles \(\beta_i\) of the members, with weights \(c_i > 0\) and \(\sum_i c_i = 1\), it reads

\begin{equation}
  \beta_{\rm sup}(R) = \frac{\sum_i c_i\,\beta_i(R)\,\sigma_{r,i}^2(R)}{\sum_i c_i\,\sigma_{r,i}^2(R)} .
  \tag{T:4.1}
\end{equation}
The range of anisotropy profiles that a superposition can reach is set by three limits.

- *Outer value.* At the truncation radius,

\begin{equation}
  \beta_{\rm sup}(R_\mathrm{t}) = \sum_i c_i\,\beta_i(R_\mathrm{t}),
  \tag{T:4.2}
\end{equation}
which is a single linear constraint on the weights. In practice this is the limit that binds.

- *Central value.* For a density with central slope \(\gamma\), and with \(\beta_{\mathrm{c},i}\) the central anisotropy of member \(i\) (zero for the isotropic and OM members), \(\beta_{\rm sup}(0)\) is the largest \(\beta_{\mathrm{c},i}\) among the members in use if one of them is at least \(\gamma - 1\); if all are below \(\gamma - 1\), \(\beta_{\rm sup}(0) = (\gamma - 1) - \left[\sum_i c_i/(\gamma - 1 - \beta_{\mathrm{c},i})\right]^{-1}\), which for \(\gamma = 1\) is the weighted harmonic mean \(\left(\sum_i c_i/\beta_{\mathrm{c},i}\right)^{-1}\) of the central values.

- *Transition.* The Type I (C)OM profiles change from \(10\) to \(90\) percent of their range between \(R_\mathrm{a}/3\) and \(3R_\mathrm{a}\), about one decade in radius; the Type II profiles fall without bound toward \(R_\mathrm{a}\). A target profile that changes over a wider range is approached by mixing members with different anisotropy radii.

The composite dispersions are computed from [Eq. (T:4.1)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sup#tn-eq-betasup) and the Jeans integral of [Section T:6.1.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables#tn-sec-jeans-section) without any sampling. Downstream of this section, a superposition is treated as one model: each of its particles takes a component at random with probabilities equal to the weights and follows the enclosed mass of the mixture ([Section T:5.3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sampling#tn-sec-draw)), its projected observables are formed one component at a time and mixed by the weights ([Section T:6.9](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables#tn-sec-mixing)), and the second moments its likelihood compares with the data are linear in the normalized weights, so a new set of weights is evaluated from the members’ tabulated moments without recomputing any member ([Section T:7.4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients#tn-sec-likelihood)).


---

# T:5 Particle sampling

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sampling

## T:5.1 The velocity distribution at a given radius factorizes

At radius \(R\), let \(V\) be the velocity and \(\varphi\) the angle between the velocity and the radial direction, so that \(L = R\,V\sin\varphi\). For the (C)OM models, the argument of the DF is

\begin{equation}
  Q_\mp = P - \tfrac{1}{2}\,f\,V^2, \qquad f(R, \varphi) \equiv 1 \pm \frac{R^2}{R_\mathrm{a}^2}\sin^2\varphi ,
  \tag{T:5.1}
\end{equation}
with the upper sign for Type I and the lower sign for Type II; \(f = 1\) for constant anisotropy. The probability density of \((V, \varphi)\) at \(R\), which follows from [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eqs. (B38) to (B40), is \(\propto V^{2-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\sin^{1-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\!\varphi\;F_\mathcal{K}(P - \tfrac12 f V^2)\). In the variable

\begin{equation}
  x \equiv V\sqrt{\frac{f}{2P}} \in [0, 1]
  \tag{T:5.2}
\end{equation}
it becomes a product,

\begin{equation}
  p(x, \varphi\,|\,R) \propto \underbrace{\sin^{1-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\!\varphi\; f^{-\nu}}_{p(\varphi|R)} \;\times\; \underbrace{x^{2-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,F_\mathcal{K}\!\left[P\,(1-x^2)\right]}_{p(x|P)} .
  \tag{T:5.3}
\end{equation}
Three consequences follow.

- The angle and the scaled velocity are independent, and each can be drawn from a one-dimensional distribution.

- The distribution of \(x\) depends on the radius only through \(P(R)\) and is the same for every \(\varphi\); the velocity is \(V = x\sqrt{2P/f}\).

- The distribution of the angle is known in closed form. For Type I with \(\beta_\mathrm{c} < 1/2\), the density of the angle peaks where \(\xi\sin^2\varphi = (1 - 2\beta_\mathrm{c})/2\), with \(\xi = R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2\), that is where \(f = 3/2 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\), at \(\sin\varphi_{\rm c} = (R_\mathrm{a}/R)\,[(1 - 2\beta_\mathrm{c})/2]^{1/2}\), which lies inside \((0, \pi/2)\) for \(R > R_\mathrm{a}\,[(1 - 2\beta_\mathrm{c})/2]^{1/2}\); the orbits become radial over an angular scale that shrinks as \(R_\mathrm{a}/R\).

## T:5.2 Tabulated inverse CDFs

### T:5.2.1 The velocity table

By [Eq. (T:5.3)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sampling#tn-eq-factorized), the scaled velocity \(x\) has a distribution that depends on \(P\) alone. One table therefore serves the whole model. Its rows are indexed by the potential, uniform in \(\ln[P/(P_0 - P)]\) from the profile’s lowest positive potential to the profile’s largest potential below \(P_0\), with one guard row beyond each end, and no grid in radius or in angle is needed; where the DF’s support ends at the DF table’s lowest energy \(\mathcal{K}_0\), the lowest row is raised to \(10^3\,\mathcal{K}_0\) if that potential lies higher, and the table is refused if more than \(10^{-6}\) of the model’s mass lies below the lowest row. Each row stores the inverse of the cumulative distribution \(\mathcal{U}(x)\) in logit variables,

\begin{equation}
  s = \ln\frac{x}{x_{\rm e} - x} \quad\text{against}\quad \lambda_{\mathcal{U}} = \ln\frac{\mathcal{U}}{1-\mathcal{U}} ,
  \tag{T:5.4}
\end{equation}
where \(x_{\rm e} \leq 1\) is the edge of the support of \(x\) on that row. Both ends of the distribution are power laws, so \(s\) is close to linear in \(\lambda_{\mathcal{U}}\) toward either end, and one table per row covers the whole range of \(\mathcal{U}\). The table carries its exact slope,

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d} s}{\mathrm{d}\lambda_{\mathcal{U}}} = \frac{x_{\rm e}\,\mathcal{U}\,(1-\mathcal{U})}{p(x|P)\,x\,(x_{\rm e}-x)} ,
  \tag{T:5.5}
\end{equation}
with \(p(x|P)\) normalized on the row, and it is read by cubic Hermite interpolation. Between two rows, \(s\) is interpolated by a cubic Hermite in the row variable, with the exact slope across rows at fixed \(\mathcal{U}\) stored as a third channel. A particle at radius \(R\) and angle \(\varphi\) takes \(x\) at \(P(R)\) and the velocity \(V = x\sqrt{2P/f}\) of [Eq. (T:5.2)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sampling#tn-eq-x); nothing is inverted when a particle is drawn.

A row is built from the mass of the density on the panels of a velocity grid, refined at both ends by Gauss-Legendre panels in the logarithm of \(x\) and of \(x_{\rm e} - x\), with the closed form of the power law below the lowest refined velocity, and, beyond the closest refined distance from the edge, the closed form of the DF below its table where the DF continues to zero energy, or one Gauss-Legendre panel where the DF’s support ends at the DF’s lowest tabulated energy. The cumulative masses from each end at the edges of the panels are the construction nodes; their cubic Hermite is inverted at the nodes of the table, and each table node between the first and the last construction node is polished by a safeguarded Newton iteration on the true residual, at most 60 passes, until the node’s residual in \(\lambda_{\mathcal{U}}\) is below \(10^{-13}\), the node’s step is at the rounding of \(s\), or two successive passes fail to reduce the node’s residual. The rows are refined by halving the row spacing, every row inside the profile’s range kept and the two guard rows rebuilt at the new spacing, until the table’s own error across rows falls below \(10^{-6}\) (\(10^{-4}\) with the quick settings) or the row count reaches its cap; the report carries that error, and a table beyond \(10^{-2}\) is refused. Our first design was a two-dimensional grid of the cumulative distribution in \((\ln R, V/V_\mathrm{esc})\), read by bilinear interpolation. The factorization of [Eq. (T:5.3)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sampling#tn-eq-factorized) removes the radius from the table, and the logit variables resolve both ends of each row.

### T:5.2.2 The radius and the velocity angle

The radius is drawn from the inverse of the enclosed-mass fraction \(\mathcal{U} = M(R)/M(R_{\rm e})\), tabulated in the same logit variables with \(R\) in place of \(x\) and the outer radius of the sampling, \(R_{\rm e}\), in place of \(x_{\rm e}\). Its slope follows from \(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{U}/\mathrm{d} R = 4\pi R^2\varrho/M(R_{\rm e})\), exact at the profile’s radii; between those radii \(\ln(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{U}/\mathrm{d} R)\) is interpolated linearly in \(s\), and beyond the first and the last radius the slope is the slope at the end radius. The mass fraction is exact at the profile’s radii when the edge is the truncation radius or a profile radius; at a sharp edge between two profile radii, \(M(R_{\rm e})\) is interpolated linearly in \(\ln M\) against \(\ln R\). The variables are power laws at both ends whether the edge is smooth (the truncation radius) or sharp (a radius given by the user); at a sharp edge the last interval is refined at halved distances from the edge. The angle of an anisotropic model needs no table in radius. By [Eq. (T:5.3)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sampling#tn-eq-factorized), \(p(\varphi|R) \propto \sin^{1-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\!\varphi\,f^{-\nu}\), and the substitution

\begin{equation}
