  \sin^2\varphi = \frac{y}{1 \pm \xi\,(1-y)}, \qquad \xi \equiv \frac{R^2}{R_\mathrm{a}^2},
  \tag{T:5.6}
\end{equation}
with the upper sign for Type I and the lower sign for Type II, turns it into a Beta distribution of \(y\) with parameters \((1-\beta_\mathrm{c},\,1/2)\) at every radius. One inverse table of that variate serves the whole model, each half tabulated against the logarithm of the probability at its own end, with the slope \(u/[y\,p(y)]\) in closed form. The angle is drawn in \([0, \pi/2]\), and the sign of the radial velocity is drawn independently; the direction of the tangential component is a Gram-Schmidt projection of an independent isotropic Gaussian draw onto the plane perpendicular to the radius.

## T:5.3 Drawing particles by inverse-CDF sampling

Every variable is drawn by inversion, and nothing is rejected. The random numbers of particle \(i\) depend only on the seed and \(i\): the key of particle \(i\) is folded from the seed and the component index 0 and then from \(i\), and each variable takes its own channel of that key. The random numbers of particle \(i\) are the same on every machine and backend; on one machine and backend, the first \(n\) particles of a larger draw, made in blocks of any size, are the same particles to the bit, and another backend gives the same particles up to the rounding of the arithmetic. The potential at a particle is the profile’s own ([Section T:1.3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-profile-object)), never a linear interpolation on a table. A draw is made in blocks of a stated size, so that its working memory is that of one block, whatever the total count. A particle of a superposed model ([Section T:4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sup#tn-sec-sup)) takes its component from a separate channel of the particle’s key, with probabilities equal to the weights, and is drawn from that component’s tables; because the members share one density, the particle’s radius follows the enclosed mass of the mixture.

A draw bounded to a range of radii takes the uniform variate between the radius table’s own mass fractions at the two radii, so that every particle lands in the range and the particles carry the mass of the range. A velocity drawn in a user-specified range at a radius takes the variate between the table’s own values at the ends of the range, for a constant anisotropy, where the range does not couple to the angle. A projected pair sampler draws \((R_{\rm 2D}, V_{\rm los})\) on an annulus and in a user-specified range of velocity from the cumulative surface density and the line-of-sight tables ([Section T:6.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables#tn-sec-losvd-table)), exactly conditioned.

## T:5.4 Checks of the drawn particles and of the written files

Every particle must lie inside the phase-space support of the DF of its component. The bound is checked on the draw’s own variables, the scaled velocity and its distance from the edge of the support, which hold it exactly; the velocity is then checked against the bound from which it was built, \(V^2 + \sigma\,\xi\,V_t^2 \leq 2P\) with \(\xi = (R/R_\mathrm{a})^2\) and \(\sigma = +1\) for Type I and \(\sigma = -1\) for Type II (\(\xi = 0\) for a constant anisotropy), to within the rounding floor \(\epsilon\,(1 + \xi)\), where \(\epsilon\) is the spacing of doubles at 1. If any particle fails either check, the draw raises `AccuracyError`; no particle is discarded or redrawn, and `write_anyway` does not override the check. Each of the package’s four writers reads its file back and compares the file with what the writer wrote, bit for bit after the cast to the file’s type (for the text layout, against the value as printed with 14 digits after the decimal point); a writer added with `register_particle_writer` is not checked.


---

# T:6 Velocity distributions and dispersion profiles

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables

An observable is a function of a model, and a request builds only the stages it needs: a second moment builds the dispersion profile and the projected table, over all their rows, and no table of velocity distributions. Two routes exist: the second moments follow from the density and the potential, and, on a model that is not spatially finite, from the DF below the table’s lowest potential, whereas the velocity distributions follow from the DF. The second route reads the first’s surface density and projected dispersion only to place its first and last rows, to decide which breaks of its velocity panels it keeps, and to check its rows, so the two routes check each other. The prepared table of a model holds both routes and reads from them.

## T:6.1 3D velocity dispersion profiles

### T:6.1.1 The radial velocity dispersion from the Jeans equation

For each component, the radial dispersion follows from the Jeans equation in the form

\begin{equation}
  \varrho_\mathrm{aux}\,\sigma_r^2\,(R) = \int_0^{P(R)} \varrho_\mathrm{aux}\,\mathrm{d} P ,
  \tag{T:6.1}
\end{equation}
with the member’s own \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\); the part of the integral below the lowest potential of the table is taken over the DF, and it is zero for a spatially finite model. The profile is tabulated in radius on rows from the first row of the profile to its last. Rows are added at the midpoints, in \(\ln R\), of the intervals whose reading misses the profile tolerance in \(\sigma_r\) there, round by round, until every interval reads within it, or until three rounds running make no progress or \(40\) rounds have run, when the profile’s certificate records the intervals left above the tolerance. Before the rows are placed, the integral is taken over Gauss-Legendre panels between the profile’s own table potentials, and the nodes of each panel, from eight, are doubled until \(\sigma_r\) at the midpoints of the starting rows moves by less than the profile tolerance, at most six times; a rule that has not converged by then is recorded in the certificate, and the rows are placed against it. The superposition’s own moments take the same integral at each radius on one panel of a stated number of Gauss-Legendre nodes in \(\ln(1 - \mathcal{K}/P_0)\), which resolves the center; the two routes agree to the accuracy of that fixed rule, which no certificate tests (\(6.5\times10^{-8}\) at the innermost row at the default of \(500\) nodes, measured on a \(64\)-member subset), not to rounding. The tangential dispersion of both tangential components together is \(\sigma_t^2 = 2(1 - \beta_\sigma)\,\sigma_r^2\), with \(\beta_\sigma\) the anisotropy of the model in closed form.

## T:6.2 Surface density and line-of-sight velocity dispersion

The surface density and the line-of-sight dispersion, [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eqs. (B47) and (B46), come from a single line-of-sight rule with a single density, on two panels in the depth along the line of sight, at projected radii spaced logarithmically from the innermost row to a fixed fraction of the last row. Rows are added until the table reads itself between rows to within the certificate’s tolerance, \(10^{-8}\): at the midpoint of every interval the value read is compared with a row computed there, and a midpoint that misses becomes a row; the rows also stop when two rounds running do not halve the worst miss, and the certificate then records the end as stalled. On a spatially finite model, the surface density is read as \(\Sigma = (R_\mathrm{t}^2 - R^2)^{1/2} h\), the factor exact and \(\ln h\) a cubic in \(x = \ln[R/(1 - R/R_\mathrm{t})]\), which goes as \(\ln R\) far inside and as \(\ln R_\mathrm{t} - \ln(1 - R/R_\mathrm{t})\) toward the edge, so that a power law of \(h\) in \(R_\mathrm{t} - R\) is a straight line in \(x\); the squared dispersion is read in \(\ln R\). A projected radius inside the innermost row or beyond the last is refused, with the row and what places it stated; a negative squared dispersion, from the rule at a row or read between rows, is refused as well.

## T:6.3 Aperture-averaged velocity dispersions

The dispersion inside an aperture is the surface-density weighted average of \(\sigma_{\rm los}^2\), [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B50). For an axisymmetric integrand every aperture reduces to a one-dimensional integral, \(\int f(R)\,\mathrm{arc}(R)\,R\,\mathrm{d} R\), where \(\mathrm{arc}(R)\) is the angular measure of the circle of radius \(R\) that lies inside the aperture. A centered circle takes a Gauss-Legendre rule in \(\ln R\) from the first row of the table, with at least a stated number of nodes and more per decade of its span. An offset circle has a full-circle core and a band of its own, the band under an end-point map in \(R - R_{\rm off}\) where it is narrow. A rectangle takes one panel between consecutive breaks of its arc, each with at least a stated number of Gauss-Legendre nodes and more per decade of its span. Above \(R_\mathrm{t}/\sqrt{2}\), where the factors \(R\) and \(v\) of the measure \(R\,\mathrm{d} R = -v\,\mathrm{d} v\) are equal, a panel is taken in \(v = (R_\mathrm{t}^2 - R^2)^{1/2}\), in which the integrand carries the edge factor \(v\) as a smooth factor; the narrow band of an offset circle is the exception and stays one panel in \(R - R_{\rm off}\). An aperture that encloses no tabulated surface density, or whose disk inside the first row carries more than a stated share of its weight, is refused with the reason stated. That disk is estimated from the slope \(s = -\mathrm{d}\ln\Sigma/\mathrm{d}\ln R\) between the first two rows, as the power law \(\Sigma_0 (R/R_0)^{-s}\) continued inward, which holds \(\Sigma_0 R_0^2/(2 - s)\); the estimate is finite only for \(s < 2\), and a slope at or above 2 is refused.

## T:6.4 The line-of-sight velocity distribution

The distribution \(D(R_{\rm 2D}, V)\) of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B53) is computed row by row at projected radii. On the plane \(V_{\rm los} = V\) at depth \(u\) along the line of sight, the level sets of \(Q\) are ellipses centered on the maximum of \(Q\), so the integral over the velocity plane is

\begin{equation}
  \iint F\,\mathrm{d} V_{\perp 1}\,\mathrm{d} V_{\perp 2} = \frac{R/R_{\rm 2D}}{\sqrt{Aq}}\int_0^{Q_c} F_\mathcal{K}(Q_c - s)\,\Lambda(s)\,\mathrm{d} s ,
  \tag{T:6.2}
\end{equation}
with \(Q_c\) the maximum, \(q = 1 + (R/R_\mathrm{a})^2\) for Type I, \(1 - (R/R_\mathrm{a})^2\) for Type II and \(1\) without \(R_\mathrm{a}\), and \(A = 1 + q u^2/R_{\rm 2D}^2\), so that \(Aq\,(R_{\rm 2D}/R)^2\) is the product of the coefficients of the ellipse’s axes, and \(\Lambda(s)\) the integral of \((L^2)^{-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) around the level set. Where the DF carries no \(L\) factor, \(\Lambda = 2\pi\), and the \(s\) integral is the cumulative DF \(G(Q_c)\), read from a table of three branches. With the \(L\) factor, \(\Lambda = 2R^{-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\int_0^{\pi}[(c_1 - c_2\cos\phi)^2 + c_3\sin^2\phi]^{-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,\mathrm{d}\phi\), with \(c_1 = VR/(R_{\rm 2D}A)\), \(c_2 = (u/R_{\rm 2D})(2s/A)^{1/2}\) and \(c_3 = 2s/q\); the integral over \([0, \pi]\) is taken by a split rule dense toward \(\phi = 0\) on \([0, \pi/2]\) and toward \(\phi = \pi\) on \([\pi/2, \pi]\), with the width \(\lambda\) of the base’s quadratic minimum at that end (\(\pi\) where that end is no local minimum), \(\phi = \lambda\sinh(\mu x)\) on \([0, \pi/2]\) with \(\mu = \mathrm{arsinh}(\pi/2\lambda)\), at a count of Gauss-Legendre nodes per half chosen for each node from a stated list as the least whose convergence rate, read from a table of the distances of the zeros of the base, reaches \(10^{-8}\), a node beyond the list or off the table taking the largest, as a JAX kernel; at \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = \pm 1/2\) it is a complete elliptic integral in closed form. The \(s\) integral is taken on Gauss-Legendre panels graded toward \(s = Q_c\), where \(K = Q_c - s = 0\); the last panel is mapped by the power of the DF’s rule below its table, so that the integral of that rule’s power law is exact. The point of zero angular momentum \(s_0\), where the non-analytic part of \(\Lambda\) behaves as \(|s - s_0|^{1-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) (times \(\ln|s - s_0|\) at a non-negative integer power), is the split between the two pieces of the \(s\) rule, and each side takes graded layers toward it whose count, beyond the layers that bring the panel next to it within the pair’s own scale, follows from \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) alone: the least count that integrates the end-point power to \(10^{-8}\); where that power is negative (\(1/2 < \beta_\mathrm{c} < 1\)) the layers are self-similar, the count is the one at which the error stops falling, and that error, the floor, is recorded and refused above \(10^{-6}\). For \(0 < \beta_\mathrm{c} < 1\) the first panel above the split is mapped as \(s - s_0 \propto w^{1/(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\), which carries the point \(V = 0\), where \(\Lambda \propto s^{-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\); for \(\beta_\mathrm{c} < 0\) not an integer that point takes the least count that integrates \(s^{-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) to \(10^{-8}\). The depth integral is taken in \(t = \mathrm{arsinh}(u/R_{\rm 2D})\) on Gauss-Legendre panels of each interval of the support along the line of sight, split where the point of zero angular momentum enters the \(s\) range, with layers toward each interval’s lower end; the panels are doubled, at most a stated number of times, until the row changes by less than \(10^{-6}\) both in its weighted \(L^1\) norm and pointwise, and a row that does not converge is kept and reported.

A row is taken on panels in \(V\) between 0 and \(V_{\rm end}\), the largest velocity with a support along the line of sight, with breaks at the velocities where its layout changes: the velocity of the radial orbit, \(V_{\rm rad}\) (on the families with an \(L\) factor), the velocity \(V_k = [2P(R_{\rm 2D})/q(R_{\rm 2D})]^{1/2}\) above which \(Q_c < 0\) at \(u = 0\), the velocity \(V_{\rm edge}\) at the end of a line of sight that ends with \(P > 0\), and the velocity \(V_c = [2(P_0 - P(R_{\rm 2D}))]^{1/2}\) where the DF’s top turns the distribution over too sharply for a sub-panel. \(V_{\rm rad}\) is kept as a break only where \(2D(V_{\rm rad})(V_{\rm end} - V_{\rm rad})\), a share of the row’s norm, or of its second moment with the weight \(V_{\rm end}^2\), exceeds \(10^{-8}\), and \(V_k\) only where the same estimate for each of \([V_k, V_{\rm end}]\) and \([0, V_k]\) does, or where \(V_k\) falls among the nodes of the panel it would be merged into (decided once on the base rows and, for \(V_k\), on samples beyond the last toward \(R_{\rm t}\), with each change bisected in \(\ln R_{\rm 2D}\)); any break whose panel the row’s nodes cannot resolve in doubles is merged. Every panel takes sub-panels graded toward zero velocity and toward each break at a stated ratio, and with the innermost sub-panel kept above the spacing of doubles at the break. Every row is normalized to one and checked against two quantities computed without it: its integral against the surface density, and its second moment against the projected dispersion ([Section T:6.2](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables#tn-sec-projection)).

A general-purpose integrator applied to the same integral, as in AGAMA ([Vasiliev 2019](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/sty2672)), stops by default at a relative tolerance of \(10^{-3}\) for the moments and of \(10^{-2}\) for the distribution. The rows here are rules built on each end-point behavior of the integrand, the depth rule and the angle count adaptive within stated caps, the end point at \(L = 0\) for \(1/2 < \beta_\mathrm{c} < 1\) integrated to a recorded floor no larger than \(10^{-6}\), and each row is held to \(10^{-6}\) in its own convergence test and against the surface density and the projected dispersion, with a row that does not converge reported.

## T:6.5 Tabulating the line-of-sight velocity distribution over projected radius

The base rows are placed at a stated number per decade of projected radius. The base rows run from the first row of the profile to \(0.9999\) of the radius where the rows end (the last row of the profile, or the radius where the potential reaches the DF’s floor where the DF is zero below it). By default the table keeps the rows of that grid, with the rows added toward each R-break and toward the end, out to the first row at or beyond the radius outside which \(10^{-6}\) of the total projected mass lies; the rows beyond it are not computed, and a read beyond the last kept row, including a read at a single point, is refused, the refusal stating the radius of that row and the setting that moves it. A table whose rows reach the end is read up to the end. The inner end is kept at full depth by default. A user who will read the table only outside a stated projected radius may give that radius, and the rows then start where the projected mass inside the first row falls below \(10^{-6}\) times the projected mass inside the stated radius; a read inside the first row is refused in the same words. Rows are added toward each R-break (each radius where the layout of the panels changes and each radius where a break merged by the lattice crosses one of its nodes), toward the end, and into any stretch between R-breaks that holds fewer than six rows; a row that its nodes cannot resolve is dropped. Rows are then added at the middle of each interval between two neighboring rows of one stretch (in the stencil’s variable) where the stencil of a stated number of rows and the stencil of two rows fewer differ by more than \(10^{-8}\) in the second moment or \(10^{-7}\) of the row’s largest value pointwise, round by round, until no interval fails, a round no longer halves the worst, or no failing interval can take a row; the same estimate is taken in the gap between each true end of a stretch and its nearest row. An interval that cannot be closed is recorded with its reason, and a request inside it is refused with that reason stated. An interval of a stretch of fewer than four rows is not checked; the table counts it and reads it with the rows the stretch holds. The certificate of the table is its last estimate of its reading between rows, the worst over the intervals in units of their tolerances; the report states it times the larger tolerance, \(10^{-7}\), a bound on both estimates. The estimate in the end gaps is recorded beside it. The rows are computed in a pool of processes, as many as the cores set, each process computing one row at a time. The report of the table ([Section T:8.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/verification#tn-sec-reports)) carries the worst norm and second moment over the rows, the rows that could not be judged, the rows whose depth rule did not converge, the certificate, and the floor of the layers at the point of zero angular momentum where \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) lies between \(1/2\) and \(1\).

## T:6.6 The aperture-averaged line-of-sight velocity distribution

The distribution inside an aperture is the surface-density weighted average of the rows over the aperture, [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eqs. (B58) and (B59). No row is computed for it. The rows are read at the radii of the aperture’s rule ([Section T:6.3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables#tn-sec-aperture)), with every break of a row followed as a function of radius, and each radius is scanned once. The result is formed on its own panels in \(V\), with breaks at zero, at the smallest and the largest value of each row break over the aperture, and at the top; a velocity that meets a break curve inside the aperture takes the radii where the curve equals it as breaks of its radial rule. The output rule refines itself, bisecting each sub-panel wider than half the widest, until its norm and its second moment agree with those of the rows’ own rule (each row integrated on its own nodes) to one hundredth of \(10^{-6}\), until its widest sub-panel is no wider than the narrowest it began with, or until a round moves them by less than that; the end is recorded. At any velocity, the distribution is the polynomial of its panel through the panel’s own nodes, namely the Legendre series of the antiderivative of the quadrature, so that it integrates exactly as the quadrature does. Its second moment is checked against the dispersion of the aperture from the projected tables, which reads no distribution.

## T:6.7 Gauss–Hermite moments

With \(y = (V - V_*)/\sigma_*\), where \(V_*\) and \(\sigma_*\) are the mean and the dispersion of the distribution itself, the moments of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B63) are

\begin{equation}
  h_n = 2\sqrt{\pi}\int D(V)\,H_n(y)\,\frac{e^{-y^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\mathrm{d} V , \qquad H_3 = \frac{2y^3 - 3y}{\sqrt{3}}, \quad H_4 = \frac{4y^4 - 12y^2 + 3}{2\sqrt{6}} ,
  \tag{T:6.3}
\end{equation}
with the Gauss-Hermite polynomials of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Eq. (B61). They are taken on the velocity nodes and weights of a row or of an aperture distribution, mirrored to both signs and normalized to unit integral. For one distribution the standardized moments by direct sums are computed beside them; to first order, \(s_3 = 4\sqrt{3}\,h_3\) and \(s_4 = 3 + 8\sqrt{6}\,h_4\). The moments tabulated over radius and those over apertures are \(V_*\), \(\sigma_*\), \(h_3\) and \(h_4\). Moments at projected radii are tabulated once over radius and read between rows; moments over apertures are taken on the distribution of each aperture.

## T:6.8 The local velocity distribution

With \(t = \cos\eta\), where \(\eta\) is the angle between the velocity and the radius, \(\xi = (R/R_\mathrm{a})^2\), and \(s\) the sign of the anisotropy (\(+1\) for Type I, \(-1\) for Type II, and \(0\) without \(R_\mathrm{a}\)),

\begin{equation}
  p(V\,|\,R) = \frac{4\pi}{\varrho(R)}\,R^{-2b}\,V^{2-2b}\int_0^{1}(1 - t^2)^{-b}\,F_\mathcal{K}(Q)\,\mathrm{d} t , \qquad Q = P(R) - \frac{V^2}{2}(1 + s\xi) + \frac{s\xi V^2}{2}\,t^2 ,
  \tag{T:6.4}
\end{equation}
where \(b\) is \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) for the constant and COM classes and 0 otherwise. Since \(Q = c_0 + c_2 t^2\), with \(c_0\) and \(c_2\) independent of \(t\), is monotonic in \(t\) on \([0, 1]\), the support of the DF in \(t\) is a single interval, \([t_*, 1]\) for Type I and \([0, t_*]\) for Type II, and the integral is taken over that interval, so the edge of the support is an end of the interval of integration and never an interior point of it. The interval is split where \(Q\) crosses the first energy of the table, and for \(b > 0\) the piece that ends at \(t = 1\) is integrated in \(w\), with \(1 - t = w^{p}\) and \(p = 1/(1 - b)\), so that \((1 - t)^{-b}\,\mathrm{d} t = p\,\mathrm{d} w\). A Type II model holds unbound orbits, of negative relative energy \(P(R) - V^2/2 < 0\), and its velocities reach \(V_{\rm esc}/\sqrt{1 - R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2}\); the share beyond the escape velocity is reported, and it was measured at \(9.3\times10^{-5}\), \(1.9\times10^{-3}\) and \(5.4\times10^{-2}\) at \(R/R_\mathrm{a} = 0.1\), \(0.21\) and \(0.5\), about a fifth of \((R/R_\mathrm{a})^2\). Each radius is computed with three checks: the norm against the density, the second moment against \(\sigma_r^2(3 - 2\beta_\sigma)\), and the change of the distribution on its velocity nodes, relative to its largest value and away from the velocity at which the support starts to cut the directions, when the nodes of its angle rule are doubled: starting from a stated number of nodes, the rule is doubled until that change falls below the tolerance, at most three times, and the distribution is kept on the coarser rule of the last pair compared.

## T:6.9 Velocity distributions and dispersions of a linear superposition

A superposed model ([Section T:4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sup#tn-sec-sup)) is projected one component at a time, each on its own tables, and the components are then combined with their weights. The members share one surface density, so the projected second moment is linear in the weights,

\begin{equation}
  \sigma_{\rm los}^2(R_{\rm 2D}) = \sum_i c_i\,\sigma_{{\rm los},i}^2(R_{\rm 2D}) ,
  \tag{T:6.5}
\end{equation}
and the same holds for the intrinsic second moments. With the projected moments of each member tabulated once, the composite profile for a new set of weights costs two weighted sums over the members, of \(\Sigma_i\sigma_{{\rm los},i}^2\) and of \(\Sigma_i\), and their ratio, which is what the likelihood of [Section T:7.4](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients#tn-sec-likelihood) evaluates. A distribution at a projected radius mixes by the surface densities, \(D = \sum_i c_i\Sigma_i D_i/\sum_i c_i\Sigma_i\); a distribution in an aperture mixes by the projected masses inside it; and the local velocity distribution mixes by the densities at that radius.


---

# T:7 Gradients

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients

## T:7.1 Derivatives of the DF with respect to the anisotropy parameters

The rows of the inversion are \(F = T_b[g](q)\) on a fixed grid \(q\), where \(T_b\) is the operator of [Section T:2.3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-num-forms) with its completion below the floor, applied to the source \(g\), namely the rows of \(\mathrm{d}^N\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d} P^N\). At a fixed central anisotropy \(b = \beta_\mathrm{c}\), the operator is linear in its source, so that

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial F}{\partial {R_\mathrm{a}}} = T_b\!\left[\partial_{R_\mathrm{a}} g\right], \qquad \frac{\partial F}{\partial {\beta_\mathrm{c}}} = T_b\!\left[\partial_{b}\, g\right] + E_b[g] ,
  \tag{T:7.1}
\end{equation}
where \(\partial_\theta g\) denotes the mixed derivatives at fixed \(P\), formed symbolically in the same way as the derivatives of [Section T:1.2.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model#tn-sec-derivatives), and \(E_b\) is the derivative of the operator itself with respect to \(b\) at fixed \(g\), through its prefactor and the exponent of its kernel. \(E_b\) has no closed form and is taken from the values of the operator at nearby \(b\): a central Richardson quotient over a step and its half inside the region of one form, or the one-sided third-order combinations of both sides and their mean at a corner where the form changes on one side (half-integer \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\), or the switch of the pair). The step balances the measured accuracy of the kernel against the truncation term of the quotient. The quotient’s record states the Richardson residual of the quotient and, at a corner, the spread between its two sides, both relative to the scale of the column.

The table that the lookup reads is a function of the rows and of closed forms in \(\theta\), so its derivative is the chain rule through each piece, with every discrete choice of the forward pass held fixed: the grid, the anchor, the range of the fit, and the nodes below the written floor. The contribution of the rows is [Eq. (T:7.1)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients#tn-eq-gradient-rule) along the rows. The form above the anchor is its least-squares fit linearized in the rows, with the exponent \(\kappa(b)\) and the amplitude \(A(b)\) of the center in closed form on the regular branch. The nodes below the floor are the integral, which is linear in its source, with the source’s cubic in \((\ln P, \ln|g|)\) linearized; in \(b\), the exponent and the prefactor of the floor pair are differenced in the same way as \(E_b\). The tail contributes through its amplitude, exponent, and scale from the first node below the floor. On a Method II model the Method I model is held fixed, and the sources of the Method II model are the Leibniz sum of [Section T:2.6](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-tabulated), whose derivative is the same sum with \(\partial h/\partial\theta\) in closed form; the leaves are the rows, the edge law, and the stated form of the center, each with its derivative written out. The derivative is that of the solve with its choices fixed; between two parameters at which a choice changes, the solve at the second differs from the held one by its own tolerance.

## T:7.2 Anisotropy models and parameters with derivatives, and the refused cases

The rule of the DF’s table ([Section T:7.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients#tn-sec-gradient-rule)) serves constant anisotropy and an isotropic component (\(\beta_\mathrm{c}\)), Cuddeford Type I (\(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) and \(R_\mathrm{a}\)), and Osipkov-Merritt Type I and II (\(R_\mathrm{a}\)). The tangent rows of the second moments ([Section T:7.3](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients#tn-sec-tangent-rows)) are served in \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) for every family and in \(R_\mathrm{a}\) for every family that has it, Cuddeford Type II included, an Osipkov-Merritt model being varied in \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) as the Cuddeford model of its type at \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 0\). The velocity distributions are served in the parameters of the DF’s path: \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) of a constant member, \(R_\mathrm{a}\) of an Osipkov-Merritt member, both of a Cuddeford Type I member; the column of a parameter that path does not take is not a number, and an isotropic member’s velocity distributions are refused with the reason stated. A member without \(R_\mathrm{a}\) holds it at its own, infinite, value with a zero gradient. The rule of the DF’s table refuses three cases, each with the reason stated. The first is Cuddeford Type II, whose source, the derivative of order \(j\) of the auxiliary density, behaves as \(|P - P(R_\mathrm{a})|^{s}\) with \(s = 1 - \beta_\mathrm{c} - j\) ([Eq. (T:2.15)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-eq-ra-exponent)), with an interior point that moves with \(R_\mathrm{a}\) and an exponent that moves with \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\); the derivative of that factor with respect to \(R_\mathrm{a}\) is not integrable at the interior point for \(s < 0\) and is a point mass there at \(s = 0\), so the mixed rows do not carry the derivative, and the family is refused for both parameters. The second is a center on its critical branch, where the branch itself changes with \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\). The third is a component on a truncated profile that carries no DF of the model it was cut from. The velocity distributions, which read the DF’s table and its derivative, refuse the same cases, and besides them an isotropic member’s \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) and a row at \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = \pm 1/2\), whose angle integral is taken in closed form. The second moments read no DF: their tangent rows serve a center on its critical branch and Cuddeford Type II as well; the JAX functions of the observables refuse a Cuddeford Type II component for all the observables, the second moments included, while the likelihood serves it as a free component. The derivative of the observables of a model with respect to \((\beta_\mathrm{c}, R_\mathrm{a})\) is the full derivative for a Method II model, whose profile is held fixed. A truncated Method I model is refused with the reason stated, since its profile is that of its own DF and moves with the anisotropy, so that neither the Jeans path at a fixed profile nor the DF’s path at a fixed potential carries the full derivative; an untruncated model is refused on both paths, since its edge terms read its DF.

## T:7.3 Derivatives of the velocity dispersions and distributions

Each observable is served as a JAX function of \(\theta = (\beta_\mathrm{c}, R_\mathrm{a})\) with a custom derivative. Its value is the public call on the model rebuilt at \(\theta\) on the host, and its derivative is given by the tangent rows of the observable in \(\theta\) on the tables’ own rows, with their placement frozen. The tangent rows of the radial dispersion are the derivative of the Jeans rule [Eq. (T:6.1)](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables#tn-eq-jeans) on the same rows and nodes on the fixed profile, with the limit of the edge reading unmoved. The tangent rows of the projection are the derivative of the line-of-sight rule on the same nodes, through the derivative of the profile’s reading, with the surface density held, and zero where the surface density is zero. A negative squared dispersion is refused with the reason stated, never clipped, so no row of the forward is clipped and no tangent row is set to zero for that reason. The derivative of the squared dispersion over an aperture is the aperture’s integral of the tangent rows of the squared dispersion, on the nodes and weights of the plain call (the integral is linear in the rows); the derivative of the dispersion over the aperture is that over twice its value, and zero where the value is zero. The velocity distributions take their derivatives in two parts. The first is through the derivative of the DF’s table ([Section T:7.1](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients#tn-sec-gradient-rule)): the lookup is differentiated by JAX on its own expressions, and the transpose carries a cotangent on \(F\), and on its integral \(G\) where a row reads it, at the energies back to the numbers of the table through the three maps between them (the padded nodes, the spline slopes where a table has no exact ones, and the derived numbers of the forms), with the energies held fixed, and contracts it with the table’s derivative in \(\theta\). The second is the explicit part at a fixed table: the derivative, by JAX on a twin of the velocity plane or of the angle integral with the forward’s discrete choices held, of the distribution’s own dependence on \(\theta\) through the anisotropy’s factor, the augmented energy and the edges of the integration. For its transpose, each row of the line-of-sight tables that a nonzero cotangent reaches is computed once more by its own rule, with every read of \(F\) and \(G\) collected at the level from which the value of its velocity came. With the setting that checks the rows, which is off by default, the row so computed is held to the forward’s row bit for bit, and so is the row formed again level by level, and a row that differs is refused with the reason stated; the order of summation on a GPU does not promise that equality, so on a GPU the check can refuse a row that the CPU serves. Without the check, no row is compared and every row is served on either backend. At a \(\theta\) where the model is refused, the value is not a number and its gradient is zero.

## T:7.4 The likelihood

The log-likelihood of a model against data is a JAX function of the weights of the components and of the mass and length scales of the model, traceable and differentiable in both, and with the anisotropy of the free components as parameters through the tangent rows above. The observables predicted by a model are read on the host once, as tables over projected radius; a projected radius in the units of the data is \(R = L\,l\,x\) and a velocity is \(v = V(m/l)^{1/2}u\), with \(x\) and \(u\) in internal units, \(L\) and \(V\) the factors of the model’s units, and \(m\) and \(l\) the scales relative to the model’s own. For a superposed model, the composite profile for a new set of weights is one matrix-vector product over the members’ tabulated moments ([Section T:6.9](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables#tn-sec-mixing)); the second moments that the likelihood compares with the data are linear in the normalized weights, while the likelihood itself is not, and the gradient of the log-likelihood in the weights is exact because JAX differentiates the whole function. A refused input inside the traced function (a negative weight, a radius outside the table) gives minus infinity with a zero gradient, never an exception, so that a sampler over the parameters always sees a value. A binned distribution and the Gauss-Hermite moments in apertures are computed at the model’s own length scale: a length scale other than the model’s own gives minus infinity, and the gradient in the length scale is not a number for a binned distribution and zero for the moments in apertures.


---

# T:8 Verification

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/verification

## T:8.1 The checks of each validation report

Every result carries a validation report with a fixed set of keys for its kind, one check per key, holding an error (relative unless the key’s line below states an absolute error), or a flag that is zero when the check passes and infinite when the check fails, and, where applicable, the radius or energy at which the check is worst. The report is not a log: nothing is appended to it, and a derived result holds its own checks together with the worst tier of the results it was computed from. The checks are the following, one line per kind of result.

- *DF, untruncated* ([Section T:2.5.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-df-checks)): `top_form`, the relative residual of the table’s top decade against the center’s stated form; `slope_column`, the largest relative error in \(F\) between neighboring nodes that the stated slope column makes beyond the uncertainty of its finite differences; `below_floor_join`, the relative mismatch of \(F\) where the nodes below the floor meet the table’s first row (zero where the table has no nodes below its floor); `validity`, a flag, zero where float64 holds the table’s columns at the table’s top and infinite where float64 does not; `high_k_slope_mismatch`, the absolute difference between the table’s exponent \(\mathrm{d}\ln F/\mathrm{d}\ln u\) at the table’s top and the exponent of the center’s form; `round_trip`, the largest relative difference between the density computed from the DF and the profile’s density; and, for a DF with a tail form, `tail_join`, the relative mismatch of the tail form against \(F\) at the table’s floor.

- *DF of a Method II model*: `top_form`, `slope_column` and `below_floor_join`, as for an untruncated DF, with the Method I model’s tier carried as the DF’s.

- *DF negative somewhere*: `top_form` and `slope_column`, both written as not a number, which places the DF in the tier refused.

- *Model, truncated by Method I* ([Section T:3.8](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation#tn-sec-model-checks)): `top_form` and `slope_column` of the truncated DF’s table, as for a DF; `edge_join`, the larger of the two relative mismatches at the edge of the truncated DF, the edge integral of \(\mathrm{d}F/\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K}\) against the difference table at the splice and the Taylor form against the edge integral at the switch; `df_clip`, the largest negative value of the truncated DF’s difference set to zero, relative to \(F(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t})\); and the three checks of the profile: `poisson_residual`, the largest relative residual of the potential and of the enclosed mass between rows against the integrals of the Poisson equation; `round_trip`, the largest relative difference between the density computed from the model’s DF and the profile’s density at half-decade radii and at every row toward the edge; `row_density`, a flag, zero where every bin of the potential and of the depth holds the rows that the row-count rule asks for, and infinite at any shortfall.

- *Model, untruncated*: `outer_join` and `eps`, the join of the outer rows and the offset of the potential, recorded as not judged because the model’s profile is the closed form on every row; and `poisson_residual`, `round_trip` and `row_density`, as for a truncated model, with the radii of trust.

- *Model of a Method II model*: `top_form`, as for a DF; `edge_join`, the relative mismatch of the edge law against the table’s bottom row; and `poisson_residual`, `round_trip` and `row_density`, as for a truncated model.

- *Velocity table of a sampler*: `row_error`, the table’s own error across rows, the larger of the error in the cumulative probability \(\mathcal{U}\) and the error relative to the scaled velocity \(x\); `polish_residual`, the largest absolute residual in \(\lambda_\mathcal{U}\) that the polish leaves at a node; the sampler carries the model’s tier.

- *Sampler of projected velocities*: `v_table`, the largest absolute difference between the interpolated velocity table’s cumulative probability and each check row’s own cumulative probability; `window`, the largest difference between the ends of the user-specified range read from the table and from each check row; `radius_quadrature`, the relative difference of the radial mass between the radial Gauss rule and a finer rule; `row_norm`, the largest departure of a row’s velocity distribution from unit norm; `annulus_cut`, the fraction of the annulus’s mass that lies beyond the table’s rows.

- *Line-of-sight table* ([Section T:6.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables#tn-sec-losvd-table)): `norm`, the worst relative difference of a row’s norm against the surface density; `second_moment`, the worst relative difference of a row’s second moment against the projected dispersion; `unjudged`, a flag, infinite where a row with positive surface density could not be judged; `t_converged`, a flag, infinite where a row’s rule along the line of sight ran out of doublings before the rule’s tests passed; `certificate`, the table’s last estimate of the table’s reading between rows, in units of the table’s tolerances, times the larger tolerance; `layer_floor`, the relative error at which the layers toward the \(L = 0\) point stop converging (zero where the layers converge).

- *Aperture distribution*: `norm`, the integral of the distribution by the distribution’s own weights less one; `second_moment`, the second moment divided by the distribution’s integral, against the aperture’s dispersion \(\sigma_\mathrm{los}^2\); the distribution carries the line-of-sight table’s tier.

- *Local velocity distribution*: `norm`, the integral of the distribution less one; `second_moment`, the second moment against \(\sigma_r^2 (3 - 2\beta)\); `halving`, the largest change of the distribution under the last doubling of the angle rule, relative to the distribution’s peak.

- *Draw*: `phase_space_bound`, every particle’s scaled velocity \(x \le 1\) and distance \(d \ge 0\) from the edge of the support; `velocity_construction`, every particle’s velocity within the support’s bound up to the rounding floor; both written as zero, because a draw in which any particle fails either check raises `AccuracyError`.

- *Superposition*: the members’ keys, each check the worst over the members, and the worst tier of the members as the tier it carries.

Each tier is read as in [Section T:0.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/principles#tn-sec-tiers).

## T:8.2 Tests against independent references

The exact forms are checked against references that owe nothing to the numerical pipeline. The symbolic derivatives of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) are compared with quadrature and differentiation in arbitrary precision at thirty digits; the derivatives of the anisotropy factor with the symbolic third derivative of its expression evaluated in arbitrary precision; the central series at the anchor with the symbolic derivatives of the closed-form density; and the closed-form DFs of the isotropic Hernquist and Plummer models with the table of the inversion; the closed form of the NFW profile at \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 1/2\) ([Section T:2.2.5](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df#tn-sec-nfw-half)) is checked where a Method II model uses that closed form, against the Method II model’s computed rows at the anchor. The two routes to every projected quantity ([Section T:6](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables#tn-sec-observables)) are held to \(10^{-6}\) against each other, and a run of the full pipeline is compared bit for bit with the stored products that it reproduces on the same backend; every file is read back and compared with what was written.

## T:8.3 The roundtrip test

The test of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Section 4, shown in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758), Fig. 8, starts from the untruncated isotropic NFW profile, computes the DF, integrates it to a density, and solves the Poisson equation with \(P(0) = 1\). Every curve is numerical, and the only analytical quantity is the target density.

- *PIANISTpy.* The standard untruncated isotropic product: the inverted DF, the velocity quadrature, and a numerical Poisson solve.

- *AGAMA.* All defaults: the multipole potential built from the density on its default grid with the radial extent detected automatically, the default isotropic quasi-spherical DF with the exact action finder, and the density from its moments routine.

- *galpy.* Its interpolated spherical potential on a grid denser and wider than its default, and its Eddington DF with every default. Its DF is zero beyond the default outer radius of that routine. galpy has no Poisson solver and therefore no density curve.

- *Fitting functions.* Passed through the same velocity quadrature and Poisson solve as the PIANISTpy DF.

The DF comparison of the figure’s upper panel is reproduced by the notebook that accompanies these notes; the density comparison of the lower panel is not.

## T:8.4 The accuracy tables run at every release

A fixed set of models, four tables of rows by columns over the exponents of the profile and the anisotropy models, is run unchanged at every release with both settings levels. The DF of each model is inverted, its density is computed back from it, and the roundtrip error is read on a dense grid of radii. Each cell records the maximum and the median over the stated range and the tier that the result itself reports, or the name of the refusal where the package refuses the model, or “excluded” where the model breaks the cusp bound; the grid states for every cell the outcome it expects, so that a release is compared with the last one cell by cell. A Type II model without a truncation has its DF only above \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\), and its cell gives the tier that the package reports over that support. The tables are published with the documentation; the measured values live there and in the notebooks, not in these notes.

# Release notes

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/release-notes

## Ver. 1.0.0

The initial public release of PIANISTpy, described in [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758).

### Known limitations

- Spherical, non-rotating systems with a double-power-law input density profile.

- One density profile per potential ([Upcoming features](https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/upcoming-features)).

- Gradients in the anisotropy parameters are available only for Method II models, whose input density profile
is the truncated density profile of another model. A Method I truncated model raises
`InputError`. Separately, for Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) Type II models, the
distribution function and every observable have no gradient in the anisotropy parameters
([End-to-end differentiability](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiability)).

- With `Settings(check_rows=True)`, the gradient of `losvd` and `aperture_losvd` recomputes each row of
the line-of-sight table that the gradient reads and requires the recomputed row to equal the stored row bit for
bit, and a JAX copy of the row’s computation to reproduce the row to \(10^{-12}\) of the row’s largest
value. On a GPU, whose order of summation does not promise the same bits, the comparison can fail a row and the
gradient raises `ResultError` instead of returning an inexact value ([Differentiable observables](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiable)). The
default, `check_rows=False`, recomputes and compares no row.

- The derivative of `losvd` and `aperture_losvd` through the line-of-sight table takes minutes to hours
([Differentiable observables](https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiable)).

Dependencies: the standard and the minimum versions are listed on [Install](https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/install).

# Accuracy by release

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/accuracy

The table below gives, for each release, the counts of the accuracy grid that the
[Accuracy tables](https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/accuracy) page describes. Each row gives the number of grid cells in each tier
(silent, recorded, warned, refused), the number of cells where the package raises an exception instead of
returning a result (the column “Refused with an error”), and the number of cells excluded because the model violates
the Cusp Slope–Central Anisotropy theorem ([An & Evans 2006b](https://doi.org/10.1086/501040)), which requires
the inner slope of the density profile, \(\gamma\), to be at least twice the central velocity anisotropy,
\(\beta_{\rm c}\) (i.e., \(\gamma \ge 2\beta_{\rm c}\)). Each row also links the full grid as CSV files, one for the default settings
and one for the quick settings, and the list of the grid’s models.

# Upcoming features

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/upcoming-features

The features listed below are planned or under development for releases after ver. 1.0.0.

- Generalization of the self-consistent models to systems of several components that share one truncated
potential, and to tracer populations in a fixed potential.

- The test problem of the isolated \(N\)-body runs of [Chiang+(2026d)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28758) as a
[GAMER](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/sty2586) test problem, with its analysis and plotting scripts.

- `losvd` and `aperture_losvd` on a `Model` that compute only the part of the line-of-sight table that the
requested radii or apertures need, instead of the whole table.

- Faster derivative evaluations of `losvd` and `aperture_losvd` through parallelization.

- A GPU-accelerated first build of the line-of-sight table.

- The likelihood on data sets of tens of thousands of projected radii or apertures, such as samples of individual
stars or integral-field spaxels.


---

# Contributing

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/contributing

Please use the [issue tracker](https://github.com/barrytchiang/PIANISTpy/issues) of the GitHub repository for
bug reports, questions and proposed changes. A bug report should include the version (`pianistpy.__version__`),
the inputs that reproduce the problem, and the full error message with the last log lines before the error. A
report of an accuracy warning also includes the result’s validation report.

## Before proposing a change

- Read the [style guide](https://github.com/barrytchiang/PIANISTpy/blob/main/STYLE_GUIDE.md). The style guide covers the names, the docstrings, the units, the
numerical rules and the checklist that every change is held to.

- Run the formatter, the linter and the type checker with `python -m ruff format pianistpy`,
`python -m ruff check pianistpy` and `python -m mypy`.

- Add a test for the change. A new function comes with a test of its result against an independent
reference: a closed form, a limit, or an identity that the result must satisfy.

## Rules for pull requests

- **Validate before filing.** A contributor should validate the changes with the test suite and the accuracy
checks, under both the default and the quick settings, and, for a change to a computation that runs on the GPU,
separately in the CPU-only mode and with the GPU enabled. The runtime options (verbosity, timing, number of
cores, compilation cache) must leave every result unchanged.

- **State every changed result.** If a code edit alters any result of the validation tests beyond rounding, the
pull request should state explicitly each result that changed and by how much.

- **LLM-assisted development.** Code written by or with the assistance of large language models is permitted. The
contributor must review every code change, every test added or changed, and the pull request description. A
pull request whose code, tests and description the contributor has not reviewed may be rejected.

# <no title>

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/_accuracy_files

The grid of ver. 1.0.0 is published as three files, each of which opens with a comment block that repeats the definitions below (`#` lines, which `pandas.read_csv(path, comment='#')` skips):

- [`grid_default.csv`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/_downloads/6f15053f3a7f4c7d100c986afa508c4e/grid_default.csv): the grid with the default settings level. One row is one model of the grid.

- [`grid_quick.csv`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/_downloads/2e7555df8c0babbc2a009c85f6173c54/grid_quick.csv): the same grid with the quick settings level, in the same columns.

- [`members.csv`](https://pianistpy.com/docs/_downloads/962e66e37a969157210bdebc01173211/members.csv): the list of the grid’s models with the place of each in the tables above and the outcome the grid expects of it. One row is one model.

The columns of the grid files, in their order:

`model`
the model’s key in the grid: its table (T1 the main grid, T2 anisotropy radius, T3 truncation energy, T4 limiting cases, the sections of the Accuracy tables page), its profile, its anisotropy model and its truncation

`settings level`
the settings level of the run: “default” or “quick” (the two tested levels of pianistpy.Settings)

`truncation method`
1 where the distribution function is inverted from the model’s own density (Method I, with or without a truncation); 2 where the model is a Method II model, the distribution function inverted from the truncated density of a Method I model

`anisotropy model`
the velocity anisotropy model: “iso” (isotropic), “constant” (constant anisotropy \(\beta_{\rm c}\)), “OM_I” and “OM_II” (Osipkov-Merritt of Type I and Type II), “COM_I” and “COM_II” (Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt of Type I and Type II)

`alpha`
the transition sharpness of the double power law

`beta`
the outer slope of the double power law

`gamma`
the inner slope of the double power law

`beta_c`
the central velocity anisotropy; 0 for the isotropic and the Osipkov-Merritt models

`r_a`
the anisotropy radius in scale radii; blank for the isotropic and the constant-anisotropy models

`k_t`
the truncation energy as a fraction of the central potential; blank for an untruncated model

`source model`
for a Method II model, the Method I model whose truncated density it is built on (its profile, anisotropy model and truncation energy); blank otherwise

`expected outcome`
what the grid expects of the model: “value” (a result is served), “value: not physical” (a result is served for a model that is not a physical equilibrium), “value: the Method I model’s DF within \(10^{-6}\), read by the package’s rule” (a Method II model whose distribution function equals its Method I model’s), or a refusal with the error the package raises (its kind, then the opening words of its message)

`physical`
whether the model is a physical equilibrium by the grid’s own criteria: True, False, or blank where the model is refused before the criteria apply; a result can be served for a model that is not physical

`outcome`
what the package did: “value” (the model was computed and the error of the density computed back from its distribution function measured); “refused: the package’s tier (checks)” (the model was computed and its validation report is in the tier refused, with the checks beyond \(10^{-2}\) listed); “refusal: <error>: <message>” (the package raised that error; no model exists)

`outcome as expected`
True where the outcome is the expected outcome, False where it is not (the Accuracy tables page marks such a cell)

`tier`
the tier of the model’s validation report: silent, every check at most \(10^{-6}\); recorded, at most \(10^{-4}\); warned, at most \(10^{-2}\); refused, beyond \(10^{-2}\); blank where the model is refused before a report exists

`tier of the distribution function`
the tier of the distribution function’s own report, read as the model’s tier (the model’s tier is at least this one, since a model’s report carries its distribution function’s checks)

`lowest energy of the support`
for a Type II model without a truncation, the energy \(P(R_{\rm a})\), as a fraction of the central potential, above which its distribution function is defined; the errors are read over that support only; blank otherwise

`median relative error, 1e-4 < R < 1e4`
the median over the radii \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{4}\) (\(R\) in scale radii) of the relative error of the density computed back from the distribution function against the model’s density; blank where no result exists

`maximum relative error, 1e-4 < R < 1e4`
the maximum of the same relative error over the radii \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{4}\)

`radius of the maximum, 1e-4 < R < 1e4`
the radius, in scale radii, at which the maximum over \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{4}\) is taken

`number of radii, 1e-4 < R < 1e4`
the number of radii over which the error is read in \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{4}\)

`radii with a non-finite error, 1e-4 < R < 1e4`
the number of those radii at which the computed density is not finite; 0 where every radius is finite

`median relative error, 1e-4 < R < 1e5`
the median over the radii \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{5}\) (\(R\) in scale radii) of the relative error of the density computed back from the distribution function against the model’s density; blank where no result exists

`maximum relative error, 1e-4 < R < 1e5`
the maximum of the same relative error over the radii \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{5}\)

`radius of the maximum, 1e-4 < R < 1e5`
the radius, in scale radii, at which the maximum over \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{5}\) is taken

`number of radii, 1e-4 < R < 1e5`
the number of radii over which the error is read in \(10^{-4} < R < 10^{5}\)

`radii with a non-finite error, 1e-4 < R < 1e5`
the number of those radii at which the computed density is not finite; 0 where every radius is finite

`median relative error, 1e-8 < R < 1e8`
the median over the radii \(10^{-8} < R < 10^{8}\) (\(R\) in scale radii) of the relative error of the density computed back from the distribution function against the model’s density; blank where no result exists

`maximum relative error, 1e-8 < R < 1e8`
the maximum of the same relative error over the radii \(10^{-8} < R < 10^{8}\)

`radius of the maximum, 1e-8 < R < 1e8`
the radius, in scale radii, at which the maximum over \(10^{-8} < R < 10^{8}\) is taken

`number of radii, 1e-8 < R < 1e8`
the number of radii over which the error is read in \(10^{-8} < R < 10^{8}\)

`radii with a non-finite error, 1e-8 < R < 1e8`
the number of those radii at which the computed density is not finite; 0 where every radius is finite

`refusal of the distribution function`
the package’s message where it refused to compute the model’s distribution function; blank where it did not

`refusal of the truncation`
the package’s message where it refused a truncation of the model: for a truncated model, its own truncation; for an untruncated model, the grid’s probe that asks the package to truncate it (a profile whose total mass diverges, outer slope at most 3, and a Type II model whose support ends at the anisotropy’s domain edge are refused by design); blank where nothing was refused

`refusal of the density check`
the package’s message where the density could not be computed back from the distribution function (a distribution function that is negative somewhere has no logarithm); blank otherwise

The columns of the model list, in their order:

`model`
the model’s key, as in the grid files

`table`
the table of the Accuracy tables page the model is in: 1 the main grid, 2 anisotropy radius, 3 truncation energy, 4 limiting cases (the page’s sections)

`row`
the key of the model’s row in that table, as the page labels it

`column`
the key of the model’s column in that table, as the page labels it

`alpha`
the transition sharpness of the double power law

`beta`
the outer slope of the double power law

`gamma`
the inner slope of the double power law

`anisotropy model`
the velocity anisotropy model, as in the grid files

`beta_c`
the central velocity anisotropy

`r_a`
the anisotropy radius in scale radii; blank where the model has none

`truncation method`
1 or 2, as in the grid files

`k_t`
the truncation energy as a fraction of the central potential; blank for an untruncated model

`source model`
for a Method II model, the Method I model it is built on; blank otherwise

`expected outcome`
what the grid expects of the model, as in the grid files
